questions.q: Software models need to represent the information that software transforms, the features users desire, the behavior of the system, and:
o: the test cases that will be run after delivery
the architecture and functions that enable the transformation to occur
the hardware on which the system will be deployed only
the budget and staffing plan for the project
questions.e: Software models represent the information the software transforms, the architecture and functions that enable the transformation, the features users desire, and the behavior of the system as the transformation takes place.

questions.q: Requirements models, also called analysis models, depict the software in which three domains?
o: The user domain, the business domain and the technical domain
The architectural domain, the interface domain and the component domain
The data domain, the hardware domain and the network domain
The information domain, the functional domain and the behavioral domain
questions.e: Requirements models represent customer requirements by depicting the software in the information, functional and behavioral domains. Design models instead represent the architecture, the user interface and component-level detail.

questions.q: Design models represent which characteristics of the software?
o: The project schedule, cost and risk
The architecture, the user interface and component-level detail
The information, functional and behavioral domains
The customer's viewpoint only
questions.e: Design models represent characteristics that help practitioners construct the software effectively: the architecture, the user interface and component-level detail.

questions.q: Which statement is a modelling principle?
o: Travel light - do not create more models than you need
Create as many models as possible to cover every viewpoint
Perfect the syntax of each model before considering its content
The primary goal of the software team is to create models
questions.e: The modelling principles include that the primary goal is to build software, not create models; travel light; strive for the simplest model; make models amenable to change; state an explicit purpose for each model; adapt models to the system at hand; build useful rather than perfect models; avoid dogmatism about syntax; trust your instincts; and get feedback as soon as you can.

questions.q: How many modelling principles are given in the standard list that begins 'the primary goal of the software team is to build software, not create models'?
o: Twelve
Eight
Ten
Five
questions.e: There are ten modelling principles, running from the primary goal of building software through to getting feedback as soon as you can.

questions.q: One modelling principle states that if a model communicates content successfully then:
o: representation is secondary, so one should not become dogmatic about the model's syntax
no further models are needed
the syntax must still be corrected before the model is used
the model should be rebuilt in a standard notation
questions.e: The principle is: do not become dogmatic about the syntax of the model; if it communicates content successfully, representation is secondary.

questions.q: The two levels of design are distinguished as:
o: preliminary design and final design
data design and process design
logical design and physical design
software architecture, the overall structure, and detailed design of individual components
questions.e: Software architecture is the overall structure of the software and the ways in which that structure provides conceptual integrity for a system. Detailed design describes the structure, properties and behaviour of individual components in enough detail for a developer to implement them easily.

questions.q: Within the software development life cycle, design is:
o: the first activity of the construction activity
the last activity within the modelling activity, setting the stage for construction
performed in parallel with requirements elicitation
performed after code generation and testing
questions.e: Design is the last software engineering action within the modelling activity and sets the stage for construction, that is code generation and testing. It translates the models created during requirements analysis into design models.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the three characteristics that guide the evaluation of a good design?
o: The design must be completed in a single iteration
The design must be expressed in a formal mathematical notation
The design must be a readable, understandable guide for those who generate code and for those who test and support the software
The design must specify the implementation language
questions.e: The three characteristics are: the design must implement all explicit requirements and accommodate all implicit requirements; it must be a readable, understandable guide for coders, testers and supporters; and it must provide a complete picture of the software, addressing the data, functional and behavioral domains from an implementation perspective.

questions.q: Besides implementing all explicit requirements in the analysis model, a design must also:
o: convert implicit requirements into explicit test cases
defer implicit requirements to the maintenance phase
exclude any requirement that was not written down
accommodate all of the implicit requirements desired by the customer
questions.e: The design must implement all of the explicit requirements contained in the analysis model and must accommodate all of the implicit requirements desired by the customer.

questions.q: According to the quality guidelines, a design should exhibit an architecture that has been created using recognizable architectural styles or patterns, is composed of components exhibiting good design characteristics, and:
o: avoids all component interaction
must be implemented strictly linearly
can be implemented in an evolutionary fashion
is fixed before requirements are analysed
questions.e: A design should exhibit such an architecture and be implementable in an evolutionary fashion, which facilitates implementation and testing. For smaller systems, design can sometimes be developed linearly.

questions.q: For which kind of system can design sometimes be developed linearly rather than in an evolutionary fashion?
o: Systems with many stakeholders
Distributed systems
Safety-critical systems
Smaller systems
questions.e: The evolutionary guideline carries the note that for smaller systems, design can sometimes be developed linearly.

questions.q: Which quality guideline concerns the partitioning of software?
o: A design should be modular, with the software logically partitioned into elements or subsystems
A design should be monolithic so that it can be grasped as a whole
A design should contain a single representation covering data and architecture together
A design should maximise the complexity of connections between components
questions.e: A design should be modular: the software should be logically partitioned into elements or subsystems. A separate guideline requires distinct representations of data, architecture, interfaces and components.

questions.q: According to the quality guidelines, interfaces in a design should:
o: be identical for all components
be derived after the components have been implemented
reduce the complexity of connections between components and with the external environment
expose the internal data structures of each component
questions.e: A design should lead to interfaces that reduce the complexity of connections between components and with the external environment.

questions.q: According to the quality guidelines, a design should be derived using:
o: a method chosen after the first code is written
whatever method the implementation language favours
a repeatable method driven by information obtained during software requirements analysis
the designer's intuition alone, since design is creative
questions.e: A design should be derived using a repeatable method that is driven by information obtained during software requirements analysis, and should be represented using a notation that effectively communicates its meaning.

questions.q: The quality attributes abbreviated FURPS stand for:
o: Functionality, uniformity, reliability, portability and scalability
Functionality, usability, reliability, performance and supportability
Flexibility, usability, reusability, performance and simplicity
Functionality, usefulness, robustness, portability and security
questions.e: The FURPS quality attributes, developed at Hewlett-Packard, are functionality, usability, reliability, performance and supportability; they represent a target for all software design.

questions.q: Within FURPS, which attribute combines extensibility, adaptability and serviceability?
o: Supportability
Reliability
Usability
Performance
questions.e: Supportability combines extensibility, adaptability and serviceability, which together represent the more common term maintainability; it also covers testability, compatibility, configurability, ease of installation and ease of problem localization.

questions.q: Within FURPS, usability is assessed by considering:
o: the frequency and severity of failure
processing speed, response time and throughput
the feature set and the security of the overall system
human factors, overall aesthetics, consistency and documentation
questions.e: Usability is assessed by considering human factors, overall aesthetics, consistency and documentation. Functionality covers the feature set, generality of functions and security; performance covers speed, response time, resource consumption, throughput and efficiency.

questions.q: Within FURPS, which measures include mean-time-to-failure and the ability to recover from failure?
o: Reliability
Supportability
Functionality
Performance
questions.e: Reliability is evaluated by measuring the frequency and severity of failure, the accuracy of output results, the mean-time-to-failure, the ability to recover from failure, and the predictability of the program.

questions.q: Quality attributes such as those in FURPS must be considered:
o: as design commences, not after the design is complete and construction has begun
only after construction has begun and performance can be measured
with equal weighting in every application
only for applications that stress security
questions.e: Not every quality attribute is weighted equally, but these attributes must be considered as design commences, not after the design is complete and construction has begun.

questions.q: During design, quality is assessed by conducting:
o: performance benchmarks on the design notation
a series of technical reviews, because there is no executable software to test
unit tests against the design document
customer acceptance testing of the design model
questions.e: The software cannot be tested during design because there is no executable software, so quality is assessed by conducting a series of technical reviews.

questions.q: In a technical review, which role is played by the person whose work product is being reviewed?
o: The moderator
The recorder
The producer
The review leader
questions.e: The review leader plans the meeting, sets an agenda and runs the meeting; the recorder takes notes; the producer is the person whose work product is being reviewed.

questions.q: How long does a technical review typically last, and how many people usually participate?
o: 15 to 30 minutes, with two participants
a full working day, with the whole team
60 to 90 minutes, with usually two, three or four participants
two to three hours, with at least six participants
questions.e: A technical review typically lasts between 60 and 90 minutes, and usually two, three or four people participate depending on the scope of the design information to be reviewed.

questions.q: Which principle warns that a designer should not be constrained by preconceptions, and instead should consider alternative approaches?
o: Design is not coding, coding is not design
The design should exhibit uniformity and integration
The design process should not suffer from 'tunnel vision'
The design should not reinvent the wheel
questions.e: The design principles attributed to Davis include that the design process should not suffer from tunnel vision, that the design should be traceable to the analysis model, that it should not reinvent the wheel, and that it should minimize the intellectual distance between the software and the real-world problem.

questions.q: Which design principle addresses behaviour when aberrant data, events or operating conditions are encountered?
o: The design should be traceable to the analysis model
The design should be structured to degrade gently
The design should exhibit uniformity and integration
The design should not reinvent the wheel
questions.e: A design should be structured to degrade gently, even when aberrant data, events or operating conditions are encountered; a separate principle requires it to be structured to accommodate change.

questions.q: Which design principle addresses the timing of quality assessment?
o: The design should be assessed by the customer rather than the team
The design should be assessed for quality as it is being created, not after the fact
The design should be assessed only once construction is complete
The design should be assessed only if defects are reported
questions.e: The design should be assessed for quality as it is being created, not after the fact, and it should be reviewed to minimize conceptual, that is semantic, errors.

questions.q: The principle to 'minimize the intellectual distance' concerns the distance between:
o: the analysis model and the test plan
the designer and the programmer
the architecture and the deployment environment
the software and the problem as it exists in the real world
questions.e: The design should minimize the intellectual distance between the software and the problem as it exists in the real world.

questions.q: Design reviews are conducted to minimize which kind of error in particular?
o: Compilation errors
Syntactic errors in the notation
Spelling errors in the documentation
Conceptual, that is semantic, errors
questions.e: The design should be reviewed to minimize conceptual, that is semantic, errors.

questions.q: The design error 'incorrectness' means that:
o: the design does not address quality requirements adequately
the design specification can be interpreted in more than one way
different design statements make conflicting assumptions
the design does not meet the users' requirements on functionality and features
questions.e: The four design errors are incorrectness (the design does not meet users' requirements on functionality and features), inconsistency (conflicting assumptions about functionality or data by different design decisions), ambiguity (different or ambiguous interpretations) and inferiority (quality requirements not adequately addressed).

questions.q: The design error 'inferiority' refers to a design that:
o: does not address quality requirements adequately, typically showing inefficiency and inflexibility
does not meet the users' functional requirements
can be interpreted in more than one way
contains conflicting assumptions about data
questions.e: Inferiority is where the design does not address quality requirements adequately; typical inferior quality problems include inefficiency and inflexibility.

questions.q: The design error 'ambiguity' causes problems because:
o: the design cannot be reviewed
the design cannot be traced to requirements
the design conflicts with the analysis model
inconsistent interpretations are made during implementation
questions.e: Ambiguity means different interpretations or an ambiguous design specification; it causes errors in the implementation of the design due to inconsistent interpretations made in the implementation process.

questions.q: Which conclusion about the nature of design is correct?
o: Design is a purely mechanical process with no creative element
Design is an iterative process and cannot be correct or complete on the first attempt
Design can be made correct and complete on the first attempt with sufficient rigour
Design always permits complete specification upfront
questions.e: Design is an iterative process that cannot be correct or complete at the first attempt; the designer must decide when to stop designing and move to implementation; design is a creative process; and completeness of design upfront might not be possible in certain situations.

questions.q: Producing a design is described as requiring the practice of diversification and then convergence. Diversification refers to:
o: the splitting of a design into independent subsystems
the production of several incompatible notations
the distribution of design work across several teams
the acquisition of a repertoire of alternatives - components, component solutions and knowledge
questions.e: Diversification is the acquisition of a repertoire of alternatives, the raw material of design: components, component solutions and knowledge contained in catalogs, textbooks and the mind. Convergence then picks elements from that repertoire to settle on one particular configuration of components.

questions.q: The Roman architecture critic Vitruvius held that well-designed buildings exhibit firmness, commodity and delight. Applied to software, 'commodity' means that:
o: a program should be inexpensive to produce
a program should have no bugs that inhibit its function
a program should be suitable for the purposes for which it was intended
the experience of using the program should be pleasurable
questions.e: Firmness means a program should have no bugs that inhibit its function; commodity means it should be suitable for its intended purposes; delight means the experience of using it should be pleasurable.

questions.q: Applied to software design, Vitruvius's criterion of 'firmness' means that:
o: a program should not have any bugs that inhibit its function
a program should be suitable for its intended purposes
the program should resist modification
using the program should be a pleasurable experience
questions.e: Firmness: a program should not have any bugs that inhibit its function. Commodity concerns suitability for purpose and delight concerns the pleasure of use.

questions.q: The importance of software design can be stated with a single word. Which?
o: Quality
Cost
Speed
Documentation
questions.e: Design is the place where quality is fostered in software engineering; it provides representations of software that can be assessed for quality, and is the only way to accurately translate stakeholders' requirements into a finished product.

questions.q: Which risk follows from building software without design?
o: An unstable system that fails when small changes are made and may be difficult to test
A system whose quality can be assessed too early
A system that is too rigid to fail but impossible to extend
A system that cannot be coded at all
questions.e: Without design you risk building an unstable system - one that will fail when small changes are made, one that may be difficult to test, and one whose quality cannot be assessed until late in the process when time is short and much money has been spent.

questions.q: Which characteristic is common to all software design methods?
o: A mechanism for translating the requirements model into a design representation
A fixed number of design iterations
A guarantee of an optimal design
A requirement that the design be expressed in UML
questions.e: All design methods share: a mechanism for translating the requirements model into a design representation; a notation for representing functional components and their interfaces; heuristics for refinement and partitioning; and guidelines for quality assessment.

questions.q: A procedural abstraction refers to:
o: a named collection of data that describes a data object
the overall structure of the software
a reorganization technique that simplifies the design
a sequence of instructions that have a specific and limited function, whose details are suppressed
questions.e: A procedural abstraction is a sequence of instructions with a specific and limited function; its name implies the function but the details are suppressed. The word 'open' for a door is the classic example.

questions.q: A data abstraction is:
o: a named collection of data that describes a data object
a crosscutting concern represented as a module
an interface that reduces connection complexity
a sequence of instructions with a specific and limited function
questions.e: A data abstraction is a named collection of data describing a data object. For the procedural abstraction 'open' one can define the data abstraction 'door', whose attributes might include door type, swing direction, opening mechanism, weight and dimensions.

questions.q: At the highest level of abstraction, a solution is stated:
o: in broad terms using the language of the problem environment
in a manner that can be directly implemented
using only implementation-oriented terminology
as a sequence of machine instructions
questions.e: At the highest level of abstraction a solution is stated in broad terms using the language of the problem environment; at lower levels more detail is given, and at the lowest level the solution is stated so it can be directly implemented.

questions.q: Software architecture is defined as the overall structure of the software and:
o: the sequence in which its modules are compiled
the notation used to document it
the ways in which that structure provides conceptual integrity for a system
the hardware on which it executes
questions.e: Architecture is the overall structure of the software and the ways in which that structure provides conceptual integrity for a system; in its simplest form it is the structure or organization of program components, the manner in which they interact, and the structure of the data they use.

questions.q: Which architectural property defines the components of a system and the manner in which those components are packaged and interact with one another?
o: Structural properties
Extra-functional properties
Framework models
Families of related systems
questions.e: Structural properties define the components of a system, such as modules, objects and filters, and how those components are packaged and interact. Extra-functional properties address how the architecture meets requirements for performance, capacity, reliability, security and adaptability. Families of related systems draw on repeatable patterns.

questions.q: Which architectural property addresses how the design achieves requirements for performance, capacity, reliability, security and adaptability?
o: Structural properties
Extra-functional properties
Dynamic models
Families of related systems
questions.e: Extra-functional properties address how the architectural design achieves requirements for performance, capacity, reliability, security, adaptability and other system characteristics.

questions.q: The architectural property 'families of related systems' means that the design should:
o: support only one system at a time
be derived from the implementation language
be identical for every system in a product line
draw upon repeatable patterns commonly encountered in similar systems, reusing architectural building blocks
questions.e: Families of related systems means the architectural design should draw upon repeatable patterns commonly encountered in the design of families of similar systems; in essence the design should have the ability to reuse architectural building blocks.

questions.q: Which kind of architectural model increases the level of design abstraction by identifying repeatable architectural design frameworks?
o: Structural models
Framework models
Process models
Dynamic models
questions.e: Structural models represent architecture as an organized collection of program components; framework models identify repeatable architectural design frameworks, that is patterns; dynamic models address behavioral aspects and how the configuration may change in response to external events; process models focus on the business or technical process; functional models represent the functional hierarchy.

questions.q: Which kind of architectural model addresses how the structure or system configuration may change as a function of external events?
o: Framework models
Structural models
Functional models
Dynamic models
questions.e: Dynamic models address the behavioral aspects of program architecture, indicating how the structure or system configuration may change as a function of external events.

questions.q: A pattern is described as an idea that:
o: applies to a single class or instance
must be reimplemented identically each time
has been useful in one practical context and will probably be useful in others
has been proven mathematically correct in all contexts
questions.e: A pattern is an idea that has been useful in one practical context and will probably be useful in others; a pattern addresses a recurring design problem that arises in specific design situations and presents a solution to it.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of patterns?
o: They guarantee optimal performance
They replace architectural documentation entirely
They remove the need for a design model
They provide a common vocabulary and understanding for design principles
questions.e: Patterns document existing, well-proven design experience; provide a common vocabulary and understanding for design principles; help document software architectures; support the construction of software with defined properties; help build complex and heterogeneous architectures; and help manage software complexity.

questions.q: Separation of concerns suggests that any complex problem:
o: must be solved as a whole to preserve consistency
should be delegated to a single expert
can be more easily handled if it is subdivided into pieces that can each be solved or optimized independently
requires a formal proof before decomposition
questions.e: Separation of concerns suggests that any complex problem can be more easily handled if subdivided into pieces that can each be solved or optimized independently. A concern is a feature or behavior specified as part of the requirements model.

questions.q: In the context of separation of concerns, a 'concern' is:
o: a feature or behavior specified as part of the requirements model for the software
a quality attribute defined after design
a risk identified during project planning
a defect reported by a stakeholder
questions.e: A concern is a feature or behavior that is specified as part of the requirements model for the software; separating concerns into smaller, more manageable pieces means a problem takes less effort and time to solve.

questions.q: Separation of concerns leads to a divide-and-conquer strategy because:
o: the perceived complexity of two combined problems is often greater than the sum of their separate complexities
complexity cannot be perceived at all
combining problems always reduces total complexity
complexity is strictly additive across problems
questions.e: The perceived complexity of two problems when combined is often greater than the sum of the perceived complexity when each is taken separately, which is why breaking a complex problem into manageable pieces makes it easier to solve.

questions.q: Modularity is described as the single attribute of software that:
o: allows a program to be intellectually manageable
makes a program portable across platforms
guarantees the absence of defects
determines the program's execution speed
questions.e: Modularity is the single attribute of software that allows a program to be intellectually manageable; monolithic software, a large program composed of a single module, cannot be easily grasped by a software engineer.

questions.q: Why can monolithic software not be easily grasped by a software engineer?
o: It has no interfaces to examine
It cannot be compiled by modern compilers
The number of control paths, span of reference, number of variables and overall complexity make understanding close to impossible
It executes too quickly to trace
questions.e: In monolithic software the number of control paths, span of reference, number of variables and overall complexity would make understanding close to impossible.

questions.q: Modularity is identified as the most common manifestation of which design concept?
o: Separation of concerns
Refactoring
Stepwise refinement
Information hiding
questions.e: Modularity is the most common manifestation of separation of concerns: software is divided into separately named and addressable components, sometimes called modules, that are integrated to satisfy problem requirements. Separation of concerns is also manifested in aspects, functional independence and refinement.

questions.q: Which is a listed advantage of modularity?
o: Higher integration cost
Increased number of control paths
Fault isolation
Greater span of reference
questions.e: The advantages of modularity include being easier to manage, easier to understand, reduced complexity, delegation or division of work, fault isolation, independent development, separation of concerns, and reuse.

questions.q: As the number of modules in a system increases, what happens to the two cost components?
o: The cost per module increases while the integration cost decreases
Both the cost per module and the integration cost decrease
Both the cost per module and the integration cost increase
The cost per module decreases while the cost to integrate the modules increases
questions.e: Given the same set of requirements, more modules means smaller individual size, so the effort to develop an individual module decreases; however, as the number of modules grows, the effort associated with integrating them also grows, producing a total cost curve with a minimum.

questions.q: The quantity M in the modularity cost analysis denotes:
o: the minimum number of modules required for modularity
the number of modules that results in minimum development cost, which cannot be predicted with assurance
the number of modules that can be integrated in one day
the maximum number of modules a system may have
questions.e: There is a number M of modules that would result in minimum development cost, but we do not have the necessary sophistication to predict M with assurance; the guidance is to stay in the vicinity of M, avoiding undermodularity and overmodularity.

questions.q: Information hiding suggests that modules be characterized by:
o: design decisions that each hides from all others
the global variables they declare
the number of lines of code they contain
the data structures they share with other modules
questions.e: The principle of information hiding suggests that modules be characterized by design decisions that each hides from all others; information such as algorithms and data contained within a module should be inaccessible to modules that have no need for it.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of information hiding?
o: When modifications are required, it reduces the chance of errors propagating to other modules
It removes the need for interfaces between modules
It increases the use of global data
It makes all module internals visible for easier debugging
questions.e: Information hiding reduces the likelihood of side effects, limits the global impact of local design decisions, emphasizes communication through controlled interfaces, discourages the use of global data, leads to encapsulation, and results in higher quality software. Its greatest benefits come when modifications are required during testing and later maintenance.

questions.q: Information hiding leads to which attribute of high quality design?
o: Inheritance
Polymorphism
Encapsulation
Global data sharing
questions.e: Information hiding leads to encapsulation, an attribute of high quality design, and discourages the use of global data.

questions.q: In object-oriented programming, information hiding is often achieved using:
o: global constants
access specifiers
inheritance hierarchies
interfaces only
questions.e: In object-oriented programming it can often be achieved with access specifiers: in a class whose name and city fields are public but whose age field is private, an external assignment to the age field is rejected.

questions.q: Functional independence is achieved by developing modules with:
o: many interrelated functions and rich interaction with other modules
no interfaces at all
single-minded function and an aversion to excessive interaction with other modules
all data declared globally for ease of access
questions.e: Functional independence is achieved by developing modules with single-minded function and an aversion to excessive interaction with other modules; each module addresses a specific sub-function of requirements and has a simple interface when viewed from other parts of the system.

questions.q: Functional independence is assessed using which two qualitative criteria?
o: Correctness and completeness
Modularity and hiding
Cohesion and coupling
Abstraction and refinement
questions.e: The two indicators of functional independence are cohesion, an indication of the relative functional strength of a module, and coupling, an indication of the relative interdependence among modules.

questions.q: Cohesion is an indication of:
o: the relative functional strength of a module
the depth of an abstraction hierarchy
the number of modules in a system
the relative interdependence among modules
questions.e: Cohesion is a qualitative indication of the degree to which a module focuses on just one thing: it indicates the relative functional strength of a module. Coupling indicates the relative interdependence among modules.

questions.q: A cohesive module ideally:
o: shares its internal data with all other modules
performs many unrelated functions so that it can be reused widely
has no interface to the rest of the program
does just one thing, requiring little interaction with other components
questions.e: A cohesive module performs a single task, requiring little interaction with other components in other parts of a program; stated simply, a cohesive module should ideally do just one thing. Modules that perform many unrelated functions are to be avoided.

questions.q: Which benefits follow from high cohesion?
o: The number of modules can be reduced to one
Modules can share more data with each other
Interfaces become more complex but faster
Changes are likely to be local to a module and the module is easier to understand in isolation
questions.e: High cohesion is good because changes are likely to be local to a module and because it is easier to understand a module in isolation; cohesion is a reflection of information hiding and functional independence.

questions.q: Coupling depends on which factors?
o: The interface complexity between modules, the point at which entry or reference is made, and what data pass across the interface
The programming language used
The total number of modules only
The number of lines of code in each module
questions.e: Coupling is an indication of interconnection among modules in a software structure. It depends on the interface complexity between modules, the point at which entry or reference is made to a module, and what data pass across the interface.

questions.q: High coupling causes which problems?
o: Reduced module size and faster compilation
Greater fault isolation
Simpler interfaces between modules
Change propagation, known as the ripple effect, difficulty in understanding, and difficult reuse
questions.e: High coupling causes change propagation - the ripple effect - difficulty in understanding, and difficult reuse. In software design one should strive for the lowest possible coupling.

questions.q: Stepwise refinement is a top-down design strategy in which:
o: the design is derived from the code
all modules are designed simultaneously at full detail
a macroscopic statement of function is decomposed stepwise until programming language statements are reached
programming language statements are generalised into abstractions
questions.e: Stepwise refinement, originally proposed by Niklaus Wirth, develops an application by successively refining levels of procedural detail: a hierarchy is developed by decomposing a macroscopic statement of function in a stepwise fashion until programming language statements are reached.

questions.q: Refinement is described as a process of:
o: translation, converting one notation into another
abbreviation, replacing detail with higher-level statements
verification, proving a design correct
elaboration, beginning with a high-level statement and providing more detail at each step
questions.e: Refinement is actually a process of elaboration: you begin with a statement of function defined at a high level of abstraction and then elaborate on it, providing more and more detail as each successive refinement occurs.

questions.q: How are abstraction and refinement complementary?
o: Both suppress low-level details at different times
Both reveal low-level details, but in different notations
Abstraction reveals low-level details while refinement suppresses them
Abstraction suppresses the need for outsiders to know low-level details, while refinement reveals those details as design progresses
questions.e: Abstraction enables you to specify procedure and data internally but suppress the need for outsiders to have knowledge of low-level details; refinement helps reveal low-level details as design progresses. Both allow a complete design model to be created as the design evolves.

questions.q: Requirement A is said to crosscut requirement B if:
o: A and B are implemented in the same module
A and B are specified by the same stakeholder
a software decomposition has been chosen in which B cannot be satisfied without taking A into account
B was written before A
questions.e: Requirement A crosscuts requirement B if a software decomposition, that is a refinement, has been chosen in which B cannot be satisfied without taking A into account.

questions.q: An aspect is defined as:
o: a representation of a single isolated requirement
a representation of a crosscutting concern
a design pattern applied to an interface
a module with no dependencies
questions.e: An aspect is a representation of a cross-cutting concern. In an ideal context an aspect is implemented as a separate module rather than as software fragments scattered or tangled throughout many components.

questions.q: In a web application where requirement A lets a registered user access camera video and requirement B requires that a registered user be validated before using the site, which relationship holds?
o: Both are aspects of each other symmetrically
The design representation of B crosscuts the design representation of A, so B is an aspect
Neither crosscuts the other, since they concern different modules
The design representation of A crosscuts that of B, so A is an aspect
questions.e: Requirement B is a generic security requirement applicable to all functions available to registered users, so the design representation of B cross-cuts the design representation of A, making B an aspect of the application.

questions.q: Fowler defines refactoring as the process of changing a software system so that it:
o: does not alter the external behavior of the code yet improves its internal structure
alters the external behavior while preserving the internal structure
adds new functionality without changing the design
is rewritten in a different programming language
questions.e: Fowler defines refactoring as the process of changing a software system in such a way that it does not alter the external behavior of the code or design, yet improves its internal structure.

questions.q: When software is refactored, the existing design is examined for:
o: compliance with the chosen programming language
redundancy, unused design elements, inefficient or unnecessary algorithms and poorly constructed data structures
missing requirements and incomplete test cases
opportunities to add new features
questions.e: When software is refactored the existing design is examined for redundancy, unused design elements, inefficient or unnecessary algorithms, poorly constructed or inappropriate data structures, and any other design failure that can be corrected to yield a better design.

questions.q: A first design iteration yields a component that performs three functions with only limited relationship to one another. This is a case of:
o: excessive abstraction, which adding detail would address
low cohesion, which refactoring into three separate highly cohesive components would address
high coupling, which merging the component with its callers would address
poor information hiding, which making the fields public would address
questions.e: Such a component exhibits low cohesion; refactoring it into three separate components, each exhibiting high cohesion, yields software that is easier to integrate, easier to test and easier to maintain.

questions.q: Although refactoring is intended not to alter external behavior, what precaution is needed?
o: The design must be frozen before refactoring begins
The entire system must be rewritten after each refactoring
No precaution is needed, since behavior is preserved by definition
Refactoring tools are used to analyze changes automatically and generate a test suite suitable for detecting behavioral changes
questions.e: Inadvertent side effects can and do occur, so refactoring tools are used to analyze changes automatically and to generate a test suite suitable for detecting behavioral changes.

questions.q: The dependency inversion principle states that high-level modules should not depend directly upon low-level modules; instead:
o: all modules should be merged to remove dependencies
low-level modules should depend directly on high-level modules
abstractions should depend on details, and details on abstractions
both should depend on abstractions, and abstractions should not depend on details
questions.e: The dependency inversion principle states that high-level modules should not depend directly upon low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions; abstractions should not depend on details; details should depend on abstractions.

questions.q: In a program where a control module coordinates a keystroke reader module and a printer writer module, how does dependency inversion reduce coupling?
o: The control module is merged with both worker modules
The worker modules are invoked through abstractions, implemented as abstract classes, which then point to the appropriate worker class
The worker modules call the control module directly
The control module is replaced by global variables
questions.e: Replacing direct dependence with abstractions, implemented in object-oriented software as abstract classes, means the control class invokes those abstractions, which point to the appropriate worker class. This approach reduces coupling and improves the testability of a design.

questions.q: In design for test, 'seams', sometimes called test hooks, are:
o: points at which the design is reviewed
the interfaces between a system and its users
locations in the detailed design where test code can probe state or isolate code under test from its production environment
the boundaries between the analysis model and the design model
questions.e: Seams are locations in the detailed design where you can insert test code that probes the state of your running software, or isolate code under test from its production environment so it can be exercised in a controlled context. They must be consciously designed at the component level.

questions.q: Advocates of test-driven development work in which cycle?
o: Design, implement, test, document
Write test code, fail the test, write enough code to pass, then pass the test
Write code, write tests, refactor, deploy
Write the whole design, then all tests, then all code
questions.e: Advocates of test-driven development write tests before implementing any other code, working in short, rapid-fire cycles of write test code, fail the test, write enough code to pass, then pass the test, following the credo 'test fast, fail fast, adjust fast'.

questions.q: Among the object-oriented design concepts, inheritance means that:
o: a class inherits only the attributes of its superclass, not its methods
responsibilities flow from subclasses to the superclass
a subclass may choose which responsibilities to inherit
all responsibilities of a superclass are immediately inherited by all subclasses
questions.e: In the object-oriented design concepts, inheritance means all responsibilities of a superclass are immediately inherited by all subclasses; messages stimulate some behavior to occur in the receiving object; and polymorphism greatly reduces the effort required to extend the design.

questions.q: Among the object-oriented design concepts, messages are described as constructs that:
o: define the attributes of the receiving object
stimulate some behavior to occur in the receiving object
hide the implementation of the sending object
create new subclasses at runtime
questions.e: Messages stimulate some behavior to occur in the receiving object; inheritance passes all superclass responsibilities to subclasses; polymorphism greatly reduces the effort required to extend the design.

questions.q: Which object-oriented design concept is described as greatly reducing the effort required to extend the design?
o: Messaging
Encapsulation
Polymorphism
Inheritance
questions.e: Polymorphism is characterised as greatly reducing the effort required to extend the design.

questions.q: Design classes are related to analysis classes in which way?
o: Design classes are refined during analysis to become analysis classes
Analysis classes are discarded once design classes are created
They are independent sets of classes with no relationship
Analysis classes are refined during design to become design classes, which add design detail helpful in class implementation
questions.e: Analysis classes are refined during design to become design classes; design classes provide design details helpful in class implementation, in the form of software infrastructure supporting the business solution. The level of abstraction of an analysis class is relatively high, while design classes present significantly more technical detail.

questions.q: How many different types of design classes can be developed, each representing a different layer of the design architecture?
o: Seven
Five
Three
Four
questions.e: Five different types of design classes can be developed: user interface classes, business domain classes, process classes, persistent classes and system classes.

questions.q: Which type of design class defines all abstractions necessary for human-computer interaction, often implementing it using metaphors?
o: Business domain classes
Process classes
User interface classes
System classes
questions.e: User interface classes define all abstractions necessary for human-computer interaction and often implement the HCI in the context of a metaphor.

questions.q: Which type of design class identifies the attributes and services required to implement some element of the business domain defined by one or more analysis classes?
o: Business domain classes
Process classes
Persistent classes
User interface classes
questions.e: Business domain classes identify the attributes and services, that is methods, required to implement some element of the business domain that was defined by one or more analysis classes.

questions.q: Which type of design class implements lower-level business abstractions required to fully manage the business domain classes?
o: User interface classes
Process classes
System classes
Persistent classes
questions.e: Process classes implement lower-level business abstractions required to fully manage the business domain classes.

questions.q: Which type of design class represents data stores that will persist beyond the execution of the software?
o: Process classes
System classes
Persistent classes
Business domain classes
questions.e: Persistent classes represent data stores, such as databases, that will persist beyond the execution of the software.

questions.q: Which type of design class implements software management and control functions that enable the system to operate and communicate within its computing environment and with the outside world?
o: Process classes
System classes
User interface classes
Persistent classes
questions.e: System classes implement software management and control functions that enable the system to operate and communicate within its computing environment and with the outside world.

questions.q: A well-formed design class has four characteristics. Which of the following is one of them?
o: High coupling
Monolithicity
Primitiveness
Redundancy
questions.e: The four characteristics of a well-formed design class are: complete and sufficient, primitiveness, high cohesion and low coupling.

questions.q: The characteristic 'complete and sufficient' for a design class means that:
o: the class contains every method any client might conceivably need
the class is complete only when it has at least five methods
the class contains no methods at all until clients request them
the class completely encapsulates all attributes and methods reasonably expected for it, and contains only methods sufficient to achieve its intent
questions.e: Completeness means a design class should be the complete encapsulation of all attributes and methods that can reasonably be expected to exist for the class based on its name; sufficiency ensures it contains only those methods sufficient to achieve the intent of the class, no more and no less.

questions.q: The characteristic 'primitiveness' for a design class means that:
o: the class should have no superclass
methods should focus on accomplishing one service, and once implemented the class should not provide another way to accomplish the same thing
the class should expose its attributes directly
the class should use only primitive data types
questions.e: Primitiveness means methods associated with a design class should be focused on accomplishing one service for the class; once the service has been implemented with a method, the class should not provide another way to accomplish the same thing.

questions.q: The Law of Demeter suggests that:
o: a method should only send messages to methods in neighbouring classes
each class should collaborate with every other class in the subsystem
a method should send messages to as many classes as possible to maximise reuse
classes should communicate only through global data
questions.e: The Law of Demeter, which addresses low coupling in a design class, suggests that a method should only send messages to methods in neighbouring classes; informally, each unit should only talk to its friends and should not talk to strangers.

questions.q: Why is a highly coupled design model, in which all design classes collaborate with all others, undesirable?
o: The system becomes impossible to compile
The system becomes difficult to implement, to test and to maintain over time
The classes lose their attributes
The design model cannot be drawn in UML
questions.e: If a design model is highly coupled, with all design classes collaborating with all other design classes, the system is difficult to implement, to test and to maintain over time; design classes within a subsystem should have only limited knowledge of other classes.

questions.q: Which five elements make up the design model?
o: Abstraction, modularity, hiding, cohesion and coupling elements
Data, architectural, interface, component-level and deployment-level design elements
Analysis, design, implementation, testing and deployment elements
Logical, process, physical, development and use-case elements
questions.e: The design model elements are data design elements, architectural design elements, interface elements, component-level design elements and deployment-level design elements.

questions.q: Data design, sometimes called data architecting, creates a model of data represented at:
o: the lowest possible level of abstraction, as physical storage layouts
the level of deployment hardware
the level of individual programming language statements
a high level of abstraction, the customer or user view of data, which is then refined into implementation-specific representations
questions.e: Data design creates a model of the data or information represented at a high level of abstraction - the customer or user view of data - which is then refined into more implementation-specific representations: a data model becomes a database architecture or data warehouse, and then data structures.

questions.q: Architectural design for software is likened to which part of building a house?
o: The choice of building site
The detailed wiring drawings for each room
The doors and windows
The floor plan
questions.e: Architectural design for software is the equivalent of the floor plan of a house: it gives an overall view of the software. Interface design is analogous to the detailed drawings for the doors, windows and external utilities, and component-level design to the detailed drawings for each room.

questions.q: From which three sources is the architectural model derived?
o: The customer, the developer and the tester
The data model, the interface model and the component model
The source code, the test plan and the deployment diagram
Information about the application domain, specific requirements model elements, and the availability of architectural patterns and styles
questions.e: The architectural model is derived from information about the application domain for the software to be built; specific requirements model elements such as data flow diagrams or analysis classes with their relationships and collaborations; and the availability of architectural patterns and styles.

questions.q: Which three types of interface are considered in interface design?
o: The hardware interface, the software interface and the network interface
The data interface, the control interface and the timing interface
The logical, process and physical interfaces
The user interface, external interfaces to other systems or devices, and internal interfaces between design components
questions.e: Interface design considers the user interface; external interfaces to other systems, devices, networks or other producers or consumers of information; and internal interfaces between various design components.

questions.q: Component-level design fully describes the internal detail of each software component by defining:
o: the business domain the component serves
data structures for all local data objects, algorithmic detail for all processing, and an interface allowing access to all component operations
the user interface metaphors used by the component
the hardware nodes on which the component will run
questions.e: To describe the internal detail of each component, component-level design defines data structures for all local data objects, algorithmic detail for all processing that occurs within a component, and an interface that allows access to all component operations.

questions.q: Deployment-level design elements indicate:
o: how components will communicate internally
how the user interface will be laid out
how software functionality and subsystems will be allocated within the physical computing environment
how data will be refined into data structures
questions.e: Deployment-level design elements indicate how software functionality and subsystems will be allocated within the physical computing environment that will support the software.

questions.q: A UML deployment diagram in 'descriptor form' means that it:
o: shows the deployment at a single instant in time
shows the computing environment but does not explicitly indicate configuration details
names each specific hardware configuration explicitly
shows only the software components, not the environment
questions.e: A deployment diagram in descriptor form shows the computing environment in general terms without explicitly indicating configuration details; instance form, used in later design stages or as construction begins, names each specific hardware configuration explicitly.

questions.q: The design model can be viewed in two dimensions. What does the process dimension indicate?
o: The level of detail of each element of the model
The number of design classes in each subsystem
The physical allocation of components to hardware
The evolution of the design model as design tasks are executed as part of the software process
questions.e: The process dimension indicates the evolution of the design model as design tasks are executed as part of the software process; the abstraction dimension represents the level of detail as each element of the analysis model is transformed into a design equivalent and refined iteratively.

questions.q: In the usual sequence of design model elements, which ordering holds?
o: Component-level design is completed first, then architecture is derived from it
Deployment design is completed before architectural design begins
Preliminary architectural design sets the stage, followed by interface design and component-level design, which often occur in parallel
All design model elements are developed in strict sequence with no overlap
questions.e: Model elements are not always developed sequentially: in most cases preliminary architectural design sets the stage and is followed by interface design and component-level design, which often occur in parallel. The deployment model is usually delayed until the design has been fully developed.

questions.q: In UML, an interface is defined as a specifier for:
o: the physical nodes on which a class is deployed
the inheritance relationships among classes
the internal data structures of a class
the externally visible operations of a class, component or other classifier, without specification of internal structure
questions.e: In UML an interface is a specifier for the externally visible, that is public, operations of a class, component or other classifier including subsystems, without specification of internal structure. More simply, it is a set of operations that describes some part of the behavior of a class and provides access to those operations.

questions.q: When part of a class's behavior is implemented by providing the operations declared in an interface, UML characterises this relationship as:
o: a generalization
a dependency
a realization
an aggregation
questions.e: A dashed line with an open triangle at its end indicates that the class provides the interface's operations as part of its behavior; in UML this is characterized as a realization.

questions.q: How is an interface shown in a UML class diagram?
o: As an <<interface>> stereotype, or as a small labelled circle connected to the class with a line
As a note attached with a dotted line
As a solid diamond on the association
As a dashed rectangle inside the class
questions.e: The interface is shown as an <<interface>> stereotype or as a small, labelled circle connected to the class with a line, and is defined with no attributes and the set of operations necessary to achieve the behavior concerned.

questions.q: Which representation can be used for the detailed procedural flow of a component?
o: An entity-relationship diagram only
A use-case diagram only
Pseudocode, a flowchart or a box diagram
A deployment diagram only
questions.e: A UML activity diagram can represent processing logic, and detailed procedural flow for a component can be represented using either pseudocode or another diagrammatic form such as a flowchart or box diagram. Data structures are usually modeled using pseudocode or the implementation language.

questions.q: The data/class design transforms class models into:
o: use cases and activity diagrams
deployment diagrams and hardware nodes
architectural styles and patterns
design class realizations and the requisite data structures required to implement the software
questions.e: The data/class design transforms class models into design class realizations and the requisite data structures required to implement the software; the objects and relationships defined in the CRC diagram and the data content in class attributes provide the basis for data design.

questions.q: The architectural design defines the relationship between major structural elements, the styles and patterns that can be used, and:
o: the user interface metaphors
the constraints that affect the way in which the architecture can be implemented
the physical hardware on which components execute
the algorithms used inside each component
questions.e: The architectural design defines the relationship between major structural elements of the software, the architectural styles and patterns that can be used to achieve the requirements, and the constraints that affect the way in which the architecture can be implemented.

questions.q: Object-oriented design describes the software solution in terms of:
o: data structures followed by the functions that act on them
a single monolithic control flow
hardware nodes and their connections
collaborating objects with responsibilities
questions.e: Object-oriented design describes the software solution in terms of collaborating objects with responsibilities, drawing on concepts such as objects, classes, encapsulation, states, inheritance, composition and polymorphism.

questions.q: Which statement captures the structural difference between the structured and object-oriented paradigms?
o: In structured design data and functions are placed together, whereas object-oriented design separates them
Neither paradigm distinguishes data from functions
In structured design data and functions are kept separately, whereas in object-oriented design the related data and functions of an object are placed together within one unit
Both paradigms place data and functions together, but use different notations
questions.e: In structured design, data and functions are kept separately, usually with all data placed before any functions are written, so it is sometimes not intuitively known which data works with which function. In object-oriented design the related data and functions of an object are placed together within one unit.

questions.q: The benefit of object orientation described as 'naturalness' means that:
o: the object-oriented paradigm models the real world better because everything in the real world is an object
objects are created automatically by the compiler
object-oriented code requires no training to read
object-oriented designs need no documentation
questions.e: Naturalness means the object-oriented paradigm models the real world better because everything in the real world is an object. Reusability means using existing classes or components in future designs without much effort, and object orientation also enjoys all the benefits of the modular approach.

questions.q: In object orientation, dependencies can be handled by finding commonalities through:
o: global variables and shared files
procedure calls and parameter lists
inheritance and polymorphism
data flow diagrams
questions.e: Object orientation enjoys all the benefits of the modular approach, and dependencies can be handled by finding the commonalities through inheritance and polymorphism; built-in libraries are a further benefit.

questions.q: An object is defined as:
o: an entity that has a state and a defined set of operations which operate on that state
a template that declares attributes and services
a notation for representing a software design
a message sent between two classes
questions.e: An object is an entity that has a state and a defined set of operations which operate on that state. Objects are created according to some object class definition, which serves as a template including declarations of all the attributes and services associated with objects of that class.

questions.q: An object class definition serves as:
o: a message passed between objects
an instance of an object with a particular state
a physical node in a deployment diagram
a template for objects, including declarations of all the attributes and services associated with objects of that class
questions.e: An object class definition serves as a template for objects; it includes declarations of all the attributes and services which should be associated with an object of that class.

questions.q: In object-oriented design, objects are described as independent entities that:
o: expose their state so that other objects can manage them
contain only functions, with data held externally
share a single global state
encapsulate state and representation information and manage themselves
questions.e: Objects are abstractions of real-world or system entities that manage themselves; they are independent and encapsulate state and representation information. System functionality is expressed in terms of object services, and objects communicate by message passing.

questions.q: Conceptually, objects communicate by message passing. A message consists of:
o: the name of the service requested, copies of the information required to execute it, and the name of a holder for the result
the sender's identity and the receiver's physical address
the class definition of the receiving object
the complete state of the sending object
questions.e: A message carries the name of the service requested by the calling object, copies of the information required to execute the service, and the name of a holder for the result of the service.

questions.q: In practice, messages between objects are often implemented by:
o: shared global variables read by both objects
files written by the sender and read by the receiver
procedure calls, where the name is the procedure name and the information is the parameter list
network packets in all cases
questions.e: In practice, messages are often implemented by procedure calls: the name becomes the procedure name and the information becomes the parameter list.

questions.q: UML is best described as:
o: a software process model for iterative development
a standard notation to represent software design, based on object-oriented approaches, with syntax rules
a programming language for implementing object-oriented designs
a database modelling language
questions.e: UML, the Unified Modelling Language, is a standard notation to represent software design. It is based on object-oriented approaches, has syntax rules, and can be extended using stereotypes.

questions.q: UML can be extended using which mechanism?
o: Preprocessor directives
Stereotypes
Inheritance of diagrams
Macros
questions.e: UML has syntax rules and can be extended using stereotypes.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of UML?
o: It eliminates the need for requirements analysis
It generates executable code automatically
It applies only to new systems, not existing ones
It provides unambiguous and consistent notation and is a de facto standard
questions.e: UML lets you specify, visualize and document models of software systems - current and new systems, structure and design, behavior and interaction - and it is a de facto standard with unambiguous and consistent notation, and serves as documentation.

questions.q: In the typical sequence of UML usage, which diagram is used for business modelling?
o: The class diagram
The activity diagram
The use case diagram
The deployment diagram
questions.e: Business modelling uses an activity diagram; requirements capture uses a use case diagram; requirements analysis uses use case details and a class diagram; initial design uses sequence diagrams and a second version of the class diagram; system architecture uses a deployment diagram.

questions.q: Which UML diagram is used for system architecture in the typical sequence of UML usage?
o: The deployment diagram
The state diagram
The use case diagram
The activity diagram
questions.e: System architecture uses the deployment diagram, while architecture design uses packages and subsystems and detailed design uses collaboration and component diagrams.

questions.q: UML modelling is commonly organised around which set of views?
o: The five-layer model
The 4+1 view model
The three-tier model
The seven-view model
questions.e: UML modelling is organised around the 4+1 view model, whose views are the use-case view, logical view, dynamic or process view, implementation view and deployment view.

questions.q: Which concern belongs to the use-case view?
o: Gathering and documenting functional requirements, and identifying actors and their association to use cases
Dividing logical entities into actual software components
Identifying entities, attributes, operations and multiplicity
Showing the hardware topology on which the system executes
questions.e: The use-case view covers gathering requirements, both functional and non-functional; documenting functional requirements with use case diagrams and use case description documents; identifying actors and their association to use cases; and creating different levels of use cases to encourage reuse.

questions.q: Which concern belongs to the logical view?
o: Mapping components onto hardware nodes
Capturing the internal organization of components in a configuration management tool
Identifying entities used in the use cases together with their attributes, operations, relations and multiplicity
Describing the concurrency and communication mechanisms
questions.e: The logical view identifies the entities or things used in the use cases, together with their attributes, operations, entity relations and multiplicity; the aim is to create a class diagram.

questions.q: Which concern belongs to the dynamic view?
o: Allocating subsystems to hardware nodes
Capturing the package and class hierarchy as held in a development environment
Identifying attributes and multiplicity of entities
Identifying the objects involved and the interactions, that is messages, between them using public operations
questions.e: The dynamic view identifies the objects involved, identifies interactions - messages - using public operations, and describes how things work. UML dynamic views express and model the behaviour of a system over time, through state machine, interaction and activity diagrams.

questions.q: The implementation view concentrates on:
o: gathering functional and non-functional requirements
describing the concurrency of the architecture
taking the logical view and dividing the logical entities into actual software components
showing the hardware topology on which the system executes
questions.e: The implementation view takes the logical view and divides the logical entities into actual software components, using components, component diagrams, and a hierarchy of classes and packages.

questions.q: In the deployment view, hardware elements are called:
o: components
nodes
packages
actors
questions.e: The deployment view shows the hardware topology, such as computers and devices, on which the physical system executes; hardware elements are called nodes, and the view is composed of deployment diagrams.

questions.q: After the UML models have been created, the important next steps are to:
o: discard the models once code has been written
convert all models into a single class diagram
refine all models through iterations, implement the models by translating into code, and deploy the software within its operational environment
freeze the models and forbid further change
questions.e: The three points emphasised are: refine all models through iterations; implement the models by translating them into code; and deploy the software within its operational environment.

questions.q: Which of the following is an object-oriented concept named among the fundamentals of object-oriented design?
o: Composition
Pipelining
Marshalling
Normalization
questions.e: The object-oriented concepts named are objects, classes, encapsulation, states, inheritance, composition and polymorphism.

questions.q: Use cases serve which purposes?
o: Describing functional system specifications, providing a starting point for system design, providing a basis for verification tests and giving the customer a quick checkout
Specifying the hardware topology and deployment nodes
Documenting the internal algorithms of each component
Measuring the performance of the finished system
questions.e: Use cases describe functional system specifications, provide a starting point for system design including the GUI, provide a basis for system verification tests, and provide a quick checkout for the customer.

questions.q: Use cases are documented in which two forms?
o: A domain model and a deployment diagram
A use case diagram and a detailed use case document
A class diagram and a sequence diagram
An activity diagram and a state diagram
questions.e: Use cases are captured as a use case diagram and a detailed use case document.

questions.q: A use case diagram shows:
o: the hardware on which the system is deployed
the system boundary, the main functionalities, and the external entities that can interact with the system
the order in which messages are exchanged over time
the internal class structure of the system
questions.e: A use case diagram is a UML artifact representing the overall system specifications: a way to conceive and illustrate the use cases, showing the system boundary, main functionalities and the external entities that can interact with the system.

questions.q: Which notations are used in a use case diagram?
o: States, transitions, guards and actions
System boundary, actors, use cases and flow of information or stimulus
Classes, attributes, operations and multiplicity
Nodes, components, artifacts and connectors
questions.e: The notations used are the system boundary, actors, use cases, and the flow of information or stimulus.

questions.q: An actor is defined as:
o: an internal class that controls the system's behaviour
a sequence of actions that yields an observable result
a document describing system events and responses
an external agent that interacts with the system, stimulating it with input events or receiving something from it
questions.e: An actor is an external agent that interacts with the system; it stimulates the system with input events, or receives something from it. More generally, an actor is something with behaviour such as a person, computer system or organization, for example a cashier.

questions.q: A use case describes a process:
o: from the user's point of view, expressed in the user's language
from the tester's point of view, expressed as assertions
from the developer's point of view, expressed in implementation terms
from the database's point of view, expressed as transactions
questions.e: A use case describes a process from the user's point of view expressed in the user's language; it is a collection of interactions between the system and actors, and an end-to-end process description that includes many steps or transactions.

questions.q: A use case document is best described as:
o: a narrative document describing the sequence of system events and the system responses originating from the initiating actors
a list of hardware nodes and their configurations
a table of attributes and their data types
a diagram showing the system boundary and actors
questions.e: A use case document is a narrative document that describes the sequence of system events and the system responses originating from the initiating actors of the system; a use case tells a story of actors using a system, and is a sequence of actions a system performs that yields an observable result of value to a particular actor.

questions.q: A scenario is defined as:
o: an external agent with behaviour
a specific sequence of actions and interactions between actors and the system under discussion
a collection of related success and failure scenarios
a diagram of system boundaries
questions.e: A scenario is a specific sequence of actions and interactions between actors and the system under discussion, such as successfully purchasing items with cash. A use case is a collection of related success and failure scenarios that describe actors using a system to support a goal.

questions.q: A use case is formally defined as:
o: a single successful sequence of interactions with the system
a collection of related success and failure scenarios that describe actors using a system to support a goal
a specific sequence of actions between one actor and one class
the normal flow of processing only
questions.e: A use case is a collection of related success and failure scenarios that describe actors using a system to support a goal; an individual scenario is one specific sequence of actions and interactions.

questions.q: The main success scenario of a use case represents:
o: the system's response to invalid input only
the normal flow of processing
every possible deviation from normal processing
the steps taken when an error occurs
questions.e: The main success scenario is the normal flow of processing. Alternate scenarios describe the alternate course of action if the normal flow deviates, such as informing the customer and asking for another payment method if credit authorization is rejected.

questions.q: In defining use cases, which step comes first?
o: Define use cases that satisfy user goals
Choose the system boundary
Identify each actor's user goals
Tabulate findings in the Vision artifact
questions.e: The sequence is: choose the system boundary; identify primary actors; for each actor identify their user goals; tabulate findings in the Vision artifact; and define use cases that satisfy user goals, naming them according to their goal.

questions.q: Primary actors are those that:
o: appear only in alternate scenarios
are internal to the system boundary
supply data to the system without any goals of their own
have user goals fulfilled through using services of the system
questions.e: Primary actors are those that have user goals fulfilled through using services of the system; for each actor one then identifies their user goals.

questions.q: Use cases should be named according to:
o: the user goal they satisfy
the actor who initiates them
the order in which they were discovered
the class that implements them
questions.e: Use cases that satisfy user goals are defined and named according to their goal.

questions.q: In a fully dressed use case, preconditions state:
o: the technologies by which data may be entered
what must be true before the use case begins, such as the cashier being identified and authenticated
the alternative flows that may be taken
what will be true after the use case completes successfully
questions.e: A fully dressed use case lists the primary actor, stakeholders and interests, preconditions - for example that the cashier is identified and authenticated - a success guarantee or postconditions, the main success scenario, extensions, special requirements, a technology and data variations list, and open issues.

questions.q: In a fully dressed use case, which section records items such as 'sale is saved' and 'tax correctly calculated'?
o: The special requirements
The preconditions
The success guarantee, that is the postconditions
The technology and data variations list
questions.e: The success guarantee, or postconditions, records what will be true once the use case succeeds, such as the sale being saved and the tax correctly calculated.
