questions.q: In a fully dressed use case, an entry such as 'identifier entered by bar code scanner' belongs in which section?
o: The special requirements
The technology and data variations list
The preconditions
The stakeholders and interests
questions.e: The technology and data variations list records items such as an identifier being entered by bar code scanner; special requirements records items such as a touch screen user interface.

questions.q: In a point-of-sale Process Sale use case, after the cashier indicates that item entry is complete, the next step is that:
o: the system determines the item price
the system calculates and presents the sale total
the cashier records the identifier for each item
the customer gives a cash payment
questions.e: The main success scenario runs: the customer arrives with items; the cashier records each item identifier and quantity; the system determines the price and adds the item to the running transaction, presenting description and price; on completion of item entry the cashier indicates completion; the system calculates and presents the sale total; the cashier tells the customer the total; the customer gives a cash payment.

questions.q: In a point-of-sale sale use case, an extension stating that the sales transaction is modified by removing items and the total recalculated covers which situation?
o: The cashier was not authenticated
The credit authorization was rejected
The customer did not have enough cash
An invalid item identifier was entered
questions.e: The extensions include: if an invalid identifier is entered, indicate an error; if the customer did not have enough cash, modify the sales transaction by removing items and recalculate the total; and cancel the sales transaction on the customer's request if they did not have enough cash.

questions.q: After defining the use cases, the next step in the logical view is to:
o: write the detailed algorithms for each operation
cross the system boundary and open the system black box, thinking of the whole system in terms of entities, concepts or objects
allocate subsystems to hardware nodes
design the graphical user interface layouts
questions.e: After defining the use cases, the next step is to cross the system boundary: open the system black box and think of the whole system in terms of entities, concepts or objects.

questions.q: A domain model is best described as:
o: a representation of the software components that implement the system
a representation of real-world things, not software components, illustrating meaningful concepts in a problem domain
a model of the hardware on which the system runs
a model of the sequence of messages over time
questions.e: A domain model represents entities and illustrates meaningful concepts in a problem domain; it is a representation of real-world things, not software components. It is a set of static structure diagrams in which no operations are defined, and it may show concepts, associations between concepts, and attributes of concepts.

questions.q: Which statement about a domain model is correct?
o: It is derived from the deployment diagram
It defines both attributes and operations for every concept
It is a set of static structure diagrams in which no operations are defined
It shows the dynamic flow of messages between objects
questions.e: A domain model is a set of static structure diagrams; no operations are defined in it. It may show concepts, associations between concepts and attributes of concepts.

questions.q: An attribute is defined as:
o: an operation that an object can perform
a logical data value of an object
a multiplicity constraint on an association
a relationship between two concepts
questions.e: An attribute is a logical data value of an object; for example, because a sales receipt normally includes a date and time, the Sale concept would need date and time attributes.

questions.q: In a domain model, attributes should preferably be:
o: complex domain concepts such as Sale or Airport
collections of other attributes
references to other objects in all cases
pure data values such as Boolean, Date, Number and String, and simple attributes such as colour or zip code
questions.e: Attributes should be kept simple: the type of an attribute should not normally be a complex domain concept such as Sale or Airport. Attributes in a domain model should preferably be pure data values - Boolean, Date, Number, String - and simple attributes such as colour, phone number, zip code or universal product code.

questions.q: How are the operations, that is method names, for each class identified?
o: By analysing the interaction diagrams
By reading the domain model attributes
By listing all actors in the use case diagram
By examining the deployment diagram
questions.e: Operation or method names are added by analysing the interaction diagrams; the methods for each class can be identified by analysing those diagrams.

questions.q: An association is defined as:
o: a relationship between concepts that indicates some meaningful and interesting connection
the number of instances of one type related to another
a logical data value held by an object
a message sent from one object to another
questions.e: The relationships between the entities identified earlier are known as associations: an association is a relationship between concepts that indicates some meaningful and interesting connection. Associations can be named and can be identified using a common association list.

questions.q: Multiplicity defines:
o: the total number of instances of a type that can ever exist
the number of operations a class may declare
how many instances of a type A can be associated with one instance of a type B, at a particular moment in time
the number of attributes a concept may have
questions.e: Multiplicity defines how many instances of a type A can be associated with one instance of a type B at a particular moment in time; for example, a single instance of a Store can be associated with many - zero or more - Item instances.

questions.q: In a store-and-items example, 'many (zero or more)' as a multiplicity means that:
o: a single Item instance may belong to many stores
the number of items is fixed when the store is created
a single Store instance may be associated with no items at all, or with any number of them
a single Store instance must be associated with at least one item
questions.e: Multiplicity of 'many', described as zero or more, means a single instance of a Store can be associated with no items or with any number of Item instances at a particular moment in time.

questions.q: UML dynamic views are used to express and model the behaviour of a system over time through which three kinds of diagram?
o: State machine, interaction and activity diagrams
Use case, component and deployment diagrams
Class, object and package diagrams
Domain, data flow and entity-relationship diagrams
questions.e: UML dynamic views express and model the behaviour of a system over time, presented through state machine, interaction and activity diagrams.

questions.q: State machine diagrams can be used to model the behaviour of:
o: a class, a subsystem or an entire application
only the hardware on which the system runs
only an entire application
only a single class
questions.e: State machine diagrams capture the behaviour of a software system and can be used to model the behaviour of a class, subsystem or entire application; they also provide an excellent way to model communications with external entities via a protocol or event-based system.

questions.q: State machines provide an excellent way to model communications with external entities via:
o: a protocol or event-based system
a file transfer mechanism
a direct procedure call
a shared database
questions.e: State machines provide an excellent way to model communications with external entities via a protocol or event-based system.

questions.q: In a state machine, a door that may be open or closed changes state:
o: at fixed time intervals
upon the triggering of an event
only when the system restarts
whenever any attribute changes
questions.e: A door can have either an open or a closed state during its life-cycle, and it changes state upon the triggering of an event.

questions.q: A transition in a state machine may carry:
o: a guard condition for triggering an event, as well as an action fired by the transition
only an action, never a guard condition
neither a guard condition nor an action
only a guard condition, never an action
questions.e: A transition can have a guard condition for triggering an event as well as an action fired by the transition.

questions.q: What is the relationship between a substate and its enclosing superstate?
o: Substates and superstates have entirely independent transitions
A substate inherits the transitions of its superstate
A superstate inherits the transitions of its substates
A substate may not have any transitions of its own
questions.e: A state allows nesting to contain substates, and a substate inherits the transitions of its superstate, the enclosing state. So within an Active state, whatever substate the object is in, an 'on hook' event causes a transition to the idle state.

questions.q: Interaction diagrams illustrate:
o: the flow of objects and synchronization in parallel processing
how states change in response to events
the hardware topology of the system
how objects interact via messages
questions.e: Interaction diagrams illustrate how objects interact via messages; they can be collaboration or communication diagrams, or sequence diagrams.

questions.q: Communication diagrams illustrate object interactions in which format?
o: A graph or network format
A kind of fence format
A hierarchical tree format
A tabular format
questions.e: Communication diagrams illustrate object interactions in a graph or network format, whereas sequence diagrams illustrate interactions in a kind of fence format.

questions.q: Sequence diagrams illustrate interactions in which format?
o: A Petri net format
A swimlane format
A kind of fence format
A graph or network format
questions.e: Sequence diagrams illustrate interactions in a kind of fence format, providing a sequential map of message passing between objects over time.

questions.q: Communication diagrams were previously known as:
o: activity diagrams
state charts
collaboration diagrams
sequence diagrams
questions.e: Communication diagrams were previously known as collaboration diagrams. They provide a bird's eye-view of a collection of collaborating objects and show the message flow between objects in an object-oriented application, also implying the basic associations between classes.

questions.q: Besides showing message flow, communication diagrams also imply:
o: the sequence of use case extensions
the state transitions of each object
the basic associations, that is relationships, between classes
the physical deployment of objects onto nodes
questions.e: Communication diagrams show the message flow between objects in an object-oriented application and also imply the basic associations, that is relationships, between classes.

questions.q: Sequence diagrams are used to display the interaction among:
o: packages, components and subsystems
states, events and guards
nodes, devices and networks
users, screens, objects and entities within the system
questions.e: Sequence diagrams display the interaction among users, screens, objects and entities within the system, providing a sequential map of message passing between objects over time.

questions.q: In an interaction diagram, how is a conditional message shown?
o: By following a sequence number with a conditional clause in square brackets
By drawing the message as a dashed line
By following a sequence number with a star
By placing the message inside a diamond
questions.e: A message can be conditional, shown by following a sequence number with a conditional clause in square brackets; iteration is indicated by following the sequence number with a star. A message can also be sent from an object to itself.

questions.q: In an interaction diagram, how is iteration indicated?
o: By repeating the message arrow twice
By drawing a loop around the message
By following the sequence number with a star
By following the sequence number with a plus sign
questions.e: Iteration is indicated by following the sequence number with a star.

questions.q: Can a message in an interaction diagram be sent from an object to itself?
o: Yes, a message can be sent from an object to itself
Only if the object is a controller class
No, messages must always have distinct sender and receiver
Only in sequence diagrams, never in communication diagrams
questions.e: A message can be sent from an object to itself.

questions.q: An activity diagram is described as an extension of which older notation, combined with Petri nets?
o: The entity-relationship diagram
The data flow diagram
The flow chart diagram
The state transition table
questions.e: An activity diagram is an extension of the old flow chart diagram combined with Petri nets.

questions.q: Activity diagrams emphasize:
o: the static structure of classes and their relationships
the states an individual object passes through
the allocation of software to hardware
the flow of objects and synchronization of the flow in support of parallel processing
questions.e: Activity diagrams are important for modeling system functions and emphasize the flow of objects and the synchronization of that flow in support of parallel processing.

questions.q: The aim of the logical view, when identifying entities, attributes, operations, relations and multiplicity, is to produce:
o: a sequence diagram
a state machine diagram
a class diagram
a deployment diagram
questions.e: In the logical view one identifies entities and things used in the use cases together with attributes, operations, entity relations and multiplicity; the aim is to create a class diagram.

questions.q: In the dynamic view, which kind of operations are used when identifying interactions between objects?
o: Static operations only
Private operations
Protected operations
Public operations
questions.e: The dynamic view identifies the objects involved and identifies interactions, that is messages, using public operations, in order to describe how things work.

questions.q: Each pattern is described as a three-part rule expressing a relation between:
o: a certain context, a problem and a solution
a class, an object and a message
an intent, a participant and a consequence
a style, a pattern and an idiom
questions.e: Each pattern is a three-part rule which expresses a relation between a certain context, a problem and a solution. The context is the design situation giving rise to a design problem, the problem is the set of forces repeatedly arising in that context, and the solution is a configuration to balance those forces.

questions.q: In the three-part structure of a pattern, the 'problem' is:
o: the set of forces repeatedly arising in the context
the configuration that balances the forces
the structure with components and relationships
the design situation giving rise to a design problem
questions.e: The context is the design situation giving rise to a design problem; the problem is the set of forces repeatedly arising in the context; the solution is a configuration to balance the forces, comprising a structure with components and relationships plus run-time behaviour.

questions.q: In the three-part structure of a pattern, the solution comprises:
o: the forces arising in the context
a structure with components and relationships, plus run-time behaviour
the design situation that gives rise to the problem
the intent and the participants only
questions.e: The solution is a configuration to balance the forces: a structure with components and relationships, together with run-time behaviour.

questions.q: Patterns identify and specify abstractions that are:
o: specific to one programming language
identical to the level of single classes
above the level of single classes and instances, or of components
below the level of single statements
questions.e: Patterns document existing, well-proven design experience and identify and specify abstractions that are above the level of single classes and instances, or of components.

questions.q: Patterns are grouped into which three categories?
o: Creational, structural and behavioral patterns
Interactive, distributed and adaptable patterns
Structural, dynamic and functional patterns
Architectural patterns, design patterns and idioms
questions.e: The categories of patterns are architectural patterns, design patterns and idioms.

questions.q: An architectural pattern expresses a fundamental structural organization schema for software systems by:
o: defining a vocabulary of design elements and configuration rules only
refining the relationships between the components of a subsystem
describing how to implement particular aspects of components using the features of a given language
providing a set of predefined subsystems, specifying their responsibilities, and including rules and guidelines for organizing the relationships between them
questions.e: An architectural pattern expresses a fundamental structural organization schema for software systems: it provides a set of predefined subsystems, specifies their responsibilities, and includes rules and guidelines for organizing the relationships between them.

questions.q: Architectural patterns are characterised in which way?
o: They act as templates for a complete software architecture and represent a fundamental design decision
They are low-level patterns specific to a programming language
They apply only to the user interface layer
They are medium-scale patterns independent of programming language
questions.e: Architectural patterns act as templates for a complete software architecture, are a fundamental design decision, and also affect the architecture of the subsystems.

questions.q: A design pattern provides a scheme for:
o: refining the subsystems or components of a software system, or the relationships between them
implementing a particular aspect using the features of one language
organizing a complete software architecture into predefined subsystems
defining the hardware topology of a system
questions.e: A design pattern provides a scheme for refining the subsystems or components of a software system, or the relationships between them; it describes a commonly recurring structure of communicating components that solves a general design problem within a particular context.

questions.q: Design patterns are characterised as:
o: large-scale patterns that determine the whole architecture
patterns that apply only to distributed systems
medium-scale patterns that are independent of a particular programming language or paradigm
low-level patterns tied to the features of a specific language
questions.e: Design patterns are medium-scale patterns, independent of a particular programming language or programming paradigm; many provide structures for decomposing more complex services or components, such as Observer or Publisher-Subscriber.

questions.q: An idiom is defined as:
o: a template for a complete software architecture
a medium-scale pattern independent of any language
a low-level pattern specific to a programming language, describing how to implement particular aspects using that language's features
a named collection of architectural design decisions
questions.e: An idiom is a low-level pattern specific to a programming language; it describes how to implement particular aspects of components or the relationships between them using the features of the given language. Idioms deal with the implementation of particular design issues.

questions.q: Swapping two variable values with 'temp = a; a = b; b = temp;' in most languages, versus '($a, $b) = ($b, $a);' in Perl, illustrates which category of pattern?
o: An architectural pattern
An idiom
A style
A design pattern
questions.e: Swapping variable values is a classic idiom: a low-level pattern whose expression depends on the features of the particular programming language.

questions.q: According to the Gang of Four, the intent of the Adapter pattern is to:
o: convert the interface of a class into another interface that the clients expect, letting classes work together despite incompatible interfaces
provide a unified interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem
define a one-to-many dependency between objects
encapsulate what varies in a class of its own
questions.e: The Adapter pattern's intent is to convert the interface of a class into another interface that the clients expect; Adapter lets classes work together that could not otherwise because of incompatible interfaces. Its one-line summary is: create a new interface.

questions.q: The 'Gang of Four' refers to the four authors of which 1994 book?
o: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software
Software Architecture in Practice
Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code
Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture
questions.e: The Gang of Four are Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides, authors of Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software, Addison-Wesley, 1994.

questions.q: In the Adapter pattern's key features, the problem is characterised as:
o: a subsystem that is too complex for its clients to use
a system that has the wrong data but the right interface
a list of objects that must be notified of a state change
a system that has the right data and behavior but the wrong interface
questions.e: The Adapter addresses a system that has the right data and behavior but the wrong interface; it is typically used when you have to make something a derivative of an abstract class. The solution is a wrapper with the desired interface.

questions.q: In the Adapter pattern, the solution is described as:
o: a central object that notifies dependants
an abstract class encapsulating what varies
a new simplified interface onto a subsystem
a wrapper with the desired interface
questions.e: The Adapter provides a wrapper with the desired interface.

questions.q: In the Adapter pattern's participants and collaborators, which description is correct?
o: The Adapter adapts the interface of an Adaptee to match that of the Adapter's Target, so the Client can use the Adaptee as if it were a type of Target
The Target adapts the Adapter to match the Client's interface
The Adaptee adapts the interface of the Target to match that of the Client
The Client adapts its own interface to match the Adaptee
questions.e: The Adapter adapts the interface of an Adaptee to match that of the Adapter's Target, which is the class it derives from; this allows the Client to use the Adaptee as if it were a type of Target.

questions.q: The consequence of applying the Adapter pattern is that:
o: subjects may notify observers about events they do not need
preexisting objects can fit into new class structures without being limited by their interfaces
the design gains cohesion but loses flexibility
the subsystem becomes simpler but some functionality may be unavailable
questions.e: The Adapter pattern allows for preexisting objects to fit into new class structures without being limited by their interfaces.

questions.q: How is the Adapter pattern implemented?
o: Contain the existing class in another class, have the containing class match the required interface, and call the methods of the contained class
Derive the existing class directly from the required interface
Define a new interface and have the client implement it
Modify the existing class's method names to match the interface
questions.e: The implementation is: contain the existing class in another class; have the containing class match the required interface and call the methods of the contained class.

questions.q: A class easyCircles provides displayIt(), fillIt() and undisplayIt(), but a Shape hierarchy requires display(), fill() and undisplay(). The class cannot be derived from. What is the recommended approach?
o: Require clients to call easyCircles directly
Derive a new Circle class from Shape that contains an easyCircles object and passes requests through to it
Rename the methods of easyCircles to match the Shape interface
Make easyCircles the superclass of Shape
questions.e: The approach is to derive a new class Circle from Shape, have Circle contain an easyCircles object, and have Circle pass requests made to it on through to the contained easyCircles object - the Adapter pattern.

questions.q: In the shapes example, why do client objects benefit from dealing only with 'shapes'?
o: It lets clients deal with all these objects in the same way and lets new kinds of shapes be added later without changing the clients
It makes the client code run faster
It allows clients to access shape internals directly
It removes the need for a display method
questions.e: Treating all objects as shapes allows client objects to deal with all of them in the same way and enables different kinds of shapes to be added in the future without having to change the clients; the client is freed from knowing details.

questions.q: Which behaviours are specified for the Shapes hierarchy in the adapter example?
o: Create, read, update and delete a shape
Encrypt, decrypt, sign and verify
Set and get a shape's location, display, fill, set the colour, and undisplay a shape
Attach, detach, notify and update
questions.e: The behaviours specified are: set a shape's location, get a shape's location, display a shape, fill a shape, set the colour of a shape, and undisplay a shape. These are declared in the interface and implemented in derived classes, used polymorphically.

questions.q: According to the Gang of Four, the intent of the Facade pattern is to:
o: provide a unified interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem, defining a higher-level interface that makes the subsystem easier to use
encapsulate the concept that varies in its own class
convert the interface of a class into another interface that clients expect
define a one-to-many dependency so dependants are notified automatically
questions.e: The Facade pattern's intent is to provide a unified interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem; Facade defines a higher-level interface that makes the subsystem easier to use.

questions.q: The Facade pattern applies when you:
o: have a single class whose interface does not match what clients expect
need to notify a varying list of objects that an event has occurred
have a set of related classes and want to shield the rest of the system from their details
need to swap an algorithm at runtime
questions.e: Facade applies when you have a set of related classes and want to shield the rest of the system from these details; Facade provides a simplified interface and encapsulates a subsystem.

questions.q: In the Facade pattern's key features, the problem is characterised as:
o: having a system with the right data and behavior but the wrong interface
needing to use only a subset of a complex system, or needing to interact with the system in a particular way
needing to notify a varying list of objects of an event
having several classes that do the same thing with different method names
questions.e: The Facade addresses needing to use only a subset of a complex system, or needing to interact with the system in a particular way. Its intent is to simplify how an existing system is used by defining your own interface.

questions.q: What is the stated consequence, including the drawback, of applying the Facade pattern?
o: The Facade exposes all subsystem functionality, at the cost of complexity
The Facade removes the subsystem entirely
The Facade guarantees improved performance but reduces readability
The Facade simplifies the use of the required subsystem, but because it is not complete, certain functionality may be unavailable to the client
questions.e: The Facade simplifies the use of the required subsystem; however, because the Facade is not complete, certain functionality may be unavailable to the client.

questions.q: How is the Facade pattern implemented?
o: Add a notify method to the existing subsystem
Define a new class, or classes, that has the required interface and have this new class use the existing system
Contain the existing class in a wrapper that matches the client's interface
Replace the existing system with a simpler one
questions.e: The implementation is to define a new class, or classes, that has the required interface, and have this new class use the existing system.

questions.q: The caveat that the Facade approach 'works with subsets' means that:
o: it works only when the client is a subset of the subsystem
it works only when using a subset of the system's capabilities, or interacting with it in a particular way
it works only for subsystems with fewer than ten classes
it works only when the system is a subset of another system
questions.e: This approach works only when using a subset of the system's capabilities or when interacting with it in a particular way; the Facade provides a collection of easier-to-understand methods.

questions.q: Which is a listed variation on the Facade pattern?
o: Converting incompatible interfaces so classes can work together
Supplementing existing functions with new routines, and acting as an encapsulating layer
Defining a one-to-many dependency between a subject and its observers
Deferring the binding of a method call until runtime
questions.e: The variations include reducing the number of objects a client must work with, having one Facade work for many objects, supplementing existing functions with new routines, and acting as an encapsulating layer. Used as an encapsulating layer, the Facade can also hide the system, allowing system usage to be tracked and systems to be swapped out.

questions.q: Using a Facade as an encapsulating layer makes which two things possible?
o: Converting interfaces and deriving new classes
Registering and deregistering observers
Tracking system usage and swapping out systems
Encrypting and signing messages
questions.e: The Facade can also be used to hide, or encapsulate, the system, which allows system usage to be tracked and systems to be swapped out.

questions.q: What problem is common to both the Adapter and Facade patterns?
o: A subsystem must be distributed across several machines
An algorithm must be selected at runtime
A client object needs to be notified when a subject changes state
A client object needs to use another, preexisting object with the wrong interface
questions.e: Both address a client object using another, preexisting object with the wrong interface; the Adapter matches an existing object to a particular required interface, while the Facade defines a new, simplified interface onto a subsystem.

questions.q: According to the Gang of Four, the intent of the Observer pattern is to:
o: provide a unified interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem
define a many-to-one dependency so that many objects update a single dependant
define a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all its dependants are notified and updated automatically
convert the interface of a class into another interface clients expect
questions.e: The Observer pattern's intent is to define a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all its dependants are notified and updated automatically. Simply stated, it handles notification automatically.

questions.q: The Observer pattern also goes by which other names?
o: Adapter and Wrapper
Dependants and Publish-Subscribe
Facade and Encapsulator
Strategy and Policy
questions.e: The Observer pattern also goes by the names Dependants and Publish-Subscribe.

questions.q: In Java, the Observer pattern is implemented with which language constructs?
o: The Publisher and Subscriber abstract classes
The Observer interface and the Observable class
The Subject interface and the Dependant class
The Notifier class and the Listener interface
questions.e: The pattern can be found in the notify process in COM; it is implemented in Java with the Observer interface and the Observable class; and in rule-based expert systems it is often implemented with daemon rules.

questions.q: In rule-based expert systems, the Observer pattern is often implemented with:
o: inference chains
daemon rules
decision tables
forward chaining only
questions.e: In rule-based, expert systems, observers are often implemented with daemon rules.

questions.q: In applying the Observer pattern, which two things are varying?
o: The programming language and the platform
The data format and the network protocol
The different kinds of objects needing notification, and their different interfaces
The number of subjects and the frequency of events
questions.e: Two things are varying: different kinds of objects, since there is a list of objects that need to be notified of a change in state and they tend to belong to different classes; and different interfaces, since belonging to different classes they tend to have different interfaces.

questions.q: The first step in applying the Observer pattern is to make the observers behave in the same way. In C# and Java this is done by:
o: making all observers subclasses of the subject
implementing a common interface
declaring all observers as abstract classes
using multiple inheritance
questions.e: All observers must have the same interface. In C# and Java this is implemented with an interface; in C++, inheritance is used.

questions.q: In the Observer pattern, which two methods must the Subject define so that observers can register themselves?
o: notify() and update()
subscribe() and publish()
register() and getState()
attach(Observer) and detach(Observer)
questions.e: The Subject defines attach(Observer), which adds the given observer to its list of observers, and detach(Observer), which removes the given observer from that list.

questions.q: In the Observer pattern, which method does each Observer implement, and which does the Subject implement to notify them?
o: Each Observer implements getState(); the Subject implements setState()
Each Observer implements update(); the Subject implements notify(), which iterates its list of Observers and calls update() on each
Each Observer implements notify(); the Subject implements update()
Each Observer implements attach(); the Subject implements detach()
questions.e: Each Observer implements a method called update(), which should contain the code to handle the event. The Subject implements a notify() method that goes through its list of Observers and calls update() for each of them.

questions.q: Besides notification, what else must the Subject provide so that Observers can act?
o: A method that removes the Subject from the system
A method that lets Observers modify the Subject's state directly
Methods that allow the Observers to get whatever information they need from the Subject
A method that creates new Observers on demand
questions.e: You must also add method or methods to the Subject that allow the Observers to get whatever information they need; each Observer typically calls getState, and there would usually be several methods to obtain the needed information.

questions.q: In an e-commerce application where a welcome e-mail must be sent and the customer's address verified when a new customer is added, what is the problem with hard-coding these calls into the Customer class?
o: The Customer class cannot contain method calls
Requirements always change, so each new action to be taken for a new customer would require changing Customer
Hard-coded calls execute too slowly
The actions cannot be implemented in the same language
questions.e: If the required actions were known in advance, the behaviour could be hard-coded into the Customer class, which would call the other objects to have the corresponding actions take place. But requirements always change, which is the challenge the Observer pattern answers.

questions.q: In that e-commerce example, what is the responsibility of the AddrVerification class?
o: It creates welcome letters for newly added customers
It notifies all observers when a customer is added
It stores the list of observers for the Customer class
It verifies the address of any customer that asks it to
questions.e: AddrVerification verifies the address of any customer that asks it to; WelcomeLetter creates welcome letters for customers letting them know they were added to the system.

questions.q: In the e-commerce Observer implementation, when do the Observers attach themselves to the Customer class?
o: When the Customer's notify method is first called
When they are instantiated
When the application shuts down
When a new Customer is added
questions.e: The Observers attach themselves to the Customer class when they are instantiated; when a new Customer is added, the notify method calls these Observers, and each Observer then calls getState for the information it needs.

questions.q: In the Observer pattern's key features, the problem is characterised as:
o: needing to notify a varying list of objects that an event has occurred
needing to select among several algorithms at runtime
having a system with the right data but the wrong interface
needing to use a subset of a complex system
questions.e: The Observer addresses needing to notify a varying list of objects that an event has occurred. The solution is that observers delegate the responsibility for monitoring for an event to a central object, the Subject.

questions.q: In the Observer pattern's solution, what do the Observers delegate, and to whom?
o: They delegate their registration to the Adapter
They delegate their state to the other Observers
They delegate the responsibility for monitoring for an event to a central object, the Subject
They delegate the handling of the event to the Subject
questions.e: Observers delegate the responsibility for monitoring for an event to a central object: the Subject.

questions.q: Which statement about participants and collaborators in the Observer pattern is correct?
o: The Subject discovers its Observers by scanning the system at startup
The Observers know the Subject but the Subject never knows the Observers
The Subject knows its Observers because the Observers register with it
A central registry, not the Subject, holds the Observers
questions.e: The Subject knows its Observers because the Observers register with it; the Subject must notify the Observers when the event occurs; and the Observers are responsible both for registering with the Subject and for getting the information from the Subject when notified.

questions.q: In the Observer pattern, for what are the Observers responsible?
o: Detecting the event themselves without the Subject
Maintaining the Subject's list of observers
Notifying the Subject when the event occurs
Registering with the Subject and getting the information from the Subject when notified
questions.e: The Observers are responsible both for registering with the Subject and for getting the information from the Subject when notified.

questions.q: Which is a stated consequence of the Observer pattern?
o: Subjects may tell Observers about events they do not need to know, if some Observers are interested in only a subset of events
The number of Observers must be fixed at compile time
Observers may be notified before the event has actually occurred
The Subject must know the concrete class of every Observer
questions.e: The consequences are that Subjects may tell Observers about events they do not need to know if some Observers are interested in only a subset of events, and that extra communication may be required if Subjects notify Observers which then go back and request additional information.

questions.q: Why may extra communication be required when using the Observer pattern?
o: Because registration must be repeated for each event
Because Subjects notify Observers, which then go back and request additional information
Because every Observer must notify every other Observer
Because the Subject must poll each Observer for its state
questions.e: Extra communication may be required if Subjects notify Observers which then go back and request additional information from the Subject.

questions.q: Which pattern is sometimes needed alongside Observer, in order to implement the Observer interface for all of the observer-type objects?
o: The Facade pattern
The Adapter pattern
The Strategy pattern
The Layers pattern
questions.e: In the Observer pattern's implementation notes, the Adapter pattern is sometimes needed to be able to implement the Observer interface for all of the Observer-type objects.

questions.q: In the Observer implementation, what is the correct sequence once the event occurs?
o: The Subject attaches itself to each Observer, then each Observer polls the Subject
Objects that want to know attach themselves to the Subject beforehand, and when the event occurs the Subject tells the Observers it has occurred
A central registry detects the event and bypasses the Subject
The Observers detect the event directly and inform the Subject
questions.e: The implementation is: have objects - Observers - that want to know when an event happens attach themselves to another object - the Subject - that is watching for the event or that triggers it; when the event occurs, the Subject tells the Observers that it has occurred.

questions.q: In a Java Observer implementation, 'interface MyObserver { void update(Customer myCust); }' serves which purpose?
o: It stores the list of registered observers
It provides the customer state to the observers
It defines the Subject's attach and detach operations
It gives every observer the same interface so the Subject can call update on each without knowing its concrete class
questions.e: Making the observers behave in the same way means giving them all the same interface; in Java this is done with an interface such as MyObserver declaring update, which concrete observers like AddrVerification and WelcomeLetter then implement.

questions.q: The guideline 'program to an interface, not an implementation' is:
o: A constraint of the layered style
A rule for naming design classes
A principle of designing for change
A consequence of the Adapter pattern
questions.e: The design-for-change guidelines are: program to an interface, not an implementation; favor object aggregation over class inheritance; and consider what should be variable in your design.

questions.q: Which guideline for design for change concerns the choice between aggregation and inheritance?
o: Favor class inheritance over object aggregation
Avoid both aggregation and inheritance
Use inheritance only for interfaces
Favor object aggregation over class inheritance
questions.e: The guideline is to favor object aggregation over class inheritance, alongside programming to an interface rather than an implementation.

questions.q: The guideline 'consider what should be variable in your design' is described as the opposite of:
o: focusing on the cost of redesign
focusing on the implementation details
focusing on the interface of a class
focusing on the cause of redesign
questions.e: Rather than considering what might force a change to a design - focusing on the cause of redesign - you consider what you want to be able to change without redesign. The focus is on encapsulating the concept that varies, a theme of many design patterns.

questions.q: The theme shared by many design patterns, highlighted in the design-for-change guidelines, is:
o: maximising the depth of the inheritance hierarchy
minimising the number of classes
encapsulating the concept that varies
eliminating all interfaces
questions.e: The focus is on encapsulating the concept that varies, a theme of many design patterns.

questions.q: Which long-term issues do several software projects tend to ignore, motivating the Strategy pattern?
o: Documentation and training
Security and privacy
Speed of execution and memory use
Ease of maintenance and ability to change
questions.e: Several software projects tend to ignore long-term issues such as ease of maintenance or ability to change, which is the motivation for designing for change and applying the Strategy pattern.

questions.q: In the order-processing case study, what are the functions of the SalesOrder class?
o: Authenticating users, authorizing access, and auditing actions
Allowing the order to be filled out with a GUI, handling tax calculations, and processing the order and printing a sales receipt
Managing the database connection, caching results, and balancing load
Verifying addresses, sending welcome letters, and logging transactions
questions.e: The functions of SalesOrder are: allow for filling out the order with a GUI; handle tax calculations; and process the order and print a sales receipt. The system must process sales orders in many different countries.

questions.q: Which three naive approaches to new taxation rules does the Strategy pattern replace?
o: Aggregation, delegation and polymorphism
Copy and paste, switches or ifs on a variable specifying the case, and inheritance
Logging, monitoring and alerting
Refactoring, unit testing and code review
questions.e: The naive responses to new requirements for taxation rules are copy and paste; switches or ifs on a variable specifying the case; and inheritance, that is making a derived class that does it the new way.

questions.q: Based on the guiding principles, what should be done with the part of the design that varies?
o: Find what varies and move it into a switch statement in the client
Find what varies, encapsulate it in a class of its own, and contain that class in another class, favoring aggregation
Find what varies and replicate it in each subclass
Find what varies and hard-code each case as a separate program
questions.e: Based on the guiding principles: find what varies and encapsulate it in a class of its own, then contain this class in another class, favoring aggregation.

questions.q: In the Strategy implementation of the tax example, what does the TaskController class do?
o: It prints the sales receipt for each order
It works out which country applies, obtains the appropriate tax rules object, and passes it to the SalesOrder's process method
It calculates the tax amount itself for each country
It stores the tax rules in a database table
questions.e: The TaskController's process method emulates a processing task controller: it figures out which country you are in, obtains a CalcTax object via getTaxRulesForCountry, creates a SalesOrder and calls mySO.process(myTax). In real life the tax rules would be obtained based on the country, with the logic either in the controller or in a configuration file.

questions.q: In the Strategy implementation of the tax example, how does SalesOrder compute the tax?
o: It switches on a country code and computes the tax inline
It receives a CalcTax object as a parameter to process and calls taxToUse.taxAmount(itemNumber, price)
It inherits the tax calculation from a country-specific superclass
It instantiates the correct CalcTax subclass itself based on the country
questions.e: SalesOrder's process method takes a CalcTax parameter and, given the tax object to use, calculates the tax by calling taxToUse.taxAmount(itemNumber, price). The varying behaviour is thus supplied from outside rather than decided inside SalesOrder.

questions.q: In the tax example, how is the varying tax behaviour declared, and how is a country-specific rule supplied?
o: CalcTax is a concrete class whose taxAmount method switches on the country
CalcTax declares an abstract taxAmount method, and concrete classes such as CanTax and USTax extend CalcTax to implement it
Each country's rule is a static method on SalesOrder
CalcTax is an enumeration of country codes
questions.e: CalcTax is declared with an abstract method 'abstract public double taxAmount(long itemSold, double price)', and concrete implementations such as CanTax extend CalcTax and implement taxAmount with the rules for that country. Note that although one slide title calls CalcTax an interface, the code declares it as an abstract class.

questions.q: What advantages are claimed for applying the Strategy pattern to the tax example?
o: It improves cohesion, aids flexibility, and makes it easier to shift responsibilities
It guarantees faster tax computation
It removes the need for a task controller
It reduces the number of classes and the total lines of code
questions.e: The advantages given are that it improves cohesion and aids flexibility, and that it makes it easier to shift responsibilities.

questions.q: Why does encapsulating the tax rules in their own class hierarchy improve cohesion?
o: It removes the need for the SalesOrder class
It places all tax rules together with the order-filling GUI code
Each class then has a single responsibility: SalesOrder processes orders while each CalcTax subclass handles one country's rules
It reduces the number of methods per class to one
questions.e: Finding what varies and encapsulating it in a class of its own leaves SalesOrder responsible only for processing the order while each concrete tax class is responsible for one country's rules, which improves cohesion and makes responsibilities easier to shift.

questions.q: As the size and complexity of software systems increases, which design issue becomes more significant than the choice of algorithms and data structures?
o: The design and specification of overall system structure
The size of the development team
The selection of a programming language
The choice of compiler optimisation settings
questions.e: As size and complexity increase, the design and specification of overall system structure become a more significant issue than the choice of algorithms and data structures; this is the software architecture level of design.

questions.q: Which of the following are structural issues at the architecture level?
o: System organization as a composition of components, protocols for communication, and interaction through interfaces
Variable naming, indentation and commenting
Test case selection and coverage measurement
Loop unrolling, inlining and register allocation
questions.e: Structural issues include system organization as a composition of components, protocols for communication, and interaction through interfaces; this is the software architecture level of design.

questions.q: Software architecture involves the description of the elements from which the system is built, the interactions among those elements, the patterns that guide their composition, and:
o: the test cases for each element
the hardware budget
the algorithms inside each element
the constraints on the patterns
questions.e: Software architecture is a natural evolution of design abstractions; it involves the description of elements from which the system is built, interactions among those elements, patterns that guide their composition, and constraints on the patterns. It considers the system as a collection of components and their interactions.

questions.q: Which of the following are examples of architectural components?
o: Classes, attributes and methods only
Loops, conditionals and assignments
Clients, servers, databases and layers
Nodes, devices and cables
questions.e: Components are such things as clients and servers, databases and layers. Interactions among components can be procedure calls, shared variable access, and so on.

questions.q: Which of the following are examples of interactions among architectural components?
o: Procedure calls and shared variable access
Compilation and linking
Encryption and hashing
Inheritance and polymorphism
questions.e: Interactions among components can be procedure calls, shared variable access, and similar mechanisms. At the architectural level one also considers system-level issues such as capacity, consistency and performance.

questions.q: IEEE standard 1471-2000 defines architecture as the fundamental organization of a system embodied in its components, their relationships to each other and to the environment, and:
o: the languages in which it is written
the principles guiding its design and evolution
the processes by which it is tested
the hardware on which it is deployed
questions.e: IEEE standard 1471-2000 defines architecture as the fundamental organization of a system embodied in its components, their relationships to each other and to the environment, and the principles guiding its design and evolution.

questions.q: Len Bass defines software architecture as the structure or structures of the system comprising software elements, the externally visible properties of those elements, and:
o: the stakeholders who requested them
the algorithms they implement
the constraints on their deployment
the relationships among them
questions.e: Bass's definition is that the software architecture of a program or computing system is the structure or structures of the system, which comprise software elements, the externally visible properties of those elements, and the relationships among them.

questions.q: Software architecture is said to define which properties of a software system?
o: The syntactic properties of the source code
The internal algorithmic properties
The lexical properties of its identifiers
The observable properties
questions.e: Software architecture defines the observable properties of a software system; software architecting means the process of creating software architectures.

questions.q: Which statement captures the relationship between architecture and design?
o: All design is architecture, but not all architecture is design
All architecture is design, but not all design is architecture
Architecture and design are entirely distinct activities
Architecture replaces design in modern practice
questions.e: All architecture is design, not all design is architecture. Architectural design is outward looking, focusing on stakeholders rather than technology, and architecture does not describe the complete characteristics of components, whereas design does.

questions.q: Architectural design is described as 'outward looking' because it focuses on:
o: components, not systems
technology, not stakeholders
code, not models
stakeholders, not technology
questions.e: Architectural design is outward looking: the focus is on stakeholders, not technology.

questions.q: Which distinguishes architecture from the classical design phase in terms of component description?
o: Both describe components completely but at different times
Neither describes component characteristics
Architecture describes the complete characteristics of components, whereas design does not
Architecture does not describe the complete characteristics of components, whereas design does
questions.e: Architecture doesn't describe the complete characteristics of components - design does.

questions.q: How has the software architecting process changed the position of design in the life cycle?
o: It has moved design to after implementation
It has replaced the traditional design phase entirely
It has expanded the traditional design phase to include a phase immediately preceding traditional high-level design, which may at times overlap it
It has merged design with requirements elicitation
questions.e: The software architecting process has expanded the traditional design phase to include a phase that immediately precedes the traditional high-level design phase and will at times overlap this phase, depending on the architectural view.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the influences on an architecture in the architectural business cycle?
o: The office layout of the development team
The architects' background and experience
The choice of version control system
The size of the source code repository
questions.e: The influences are system stakeholders, the developing organization, the architects' background and experience, and the technical environment. The ramifications of these influences are to know your constraints and to engage stakeholders early.

questions.q: What are the two stated ramifications of architectural influences?
o: Fix the architecture before requirements, and avoid change
Know your constraints, and engage stakeholders early
Hire experienced architects, and outsource implementation
Choose the newest technology, and minimise documentation
questions.e: The ramifications of influences on architecture are to know your constraints and to ensure the early engagement of stakeholders.

questions.q: An architectural pattern is described as a description of element and relation types together with:
o: a complete implementation in a chosen language
a list of the stakeholders who requested them
the hardware on which they must run
a set of constraints on how they may be used
questions.e: An architectural pattern is a description of element and relation types together with a set of constraints on how they may be used; these constraints define a set or family of architectures that satisfy them, and such patterns exhibit known quality attributes.

questions.q: In the client-server architectural pattern, how is coordination described?
o: By the protocol the server uses
By direct inheritance between client and server
By the order of compilation
By a shared global data structure
questions.e: In client-server, the client and server are the two elements, coordination is described by the protocol the server uses, and multiple clients can exist.

questions.q: Which four questions are asked when reading a software architecture?
o: The nature of the elements, their responsibilities, the significance of the connections, and the significance of the layout
The author, the date, the version and the reviewer
The number of elements, their size, their cost and their schedule
The language, the compiler, the platform and the database
questions.e: The four questions are: what is the nature of the elements; what are the responsibilities of the elements; what is the significance of the connections; and what is the significance of the layout.

questions.q: Software architecture is described as the crucial bridge between:
o: coding and deployment
requirements and design
design and testing
stakeholders and shareholders
questions.e: Among the reasons for software architecture are communication among stakeholders, early design decisions, and a transferable abstraction of a system; architecture is the crucial bridge between requirements and design.

questions.q: Software architecture is said to involve understanding domains, problems and solutions, making design decisions and trade-offs, and:
o: selecting the development tools
managing the project budget
delivering working systems
writing the detailed algorithms
questions.e: Software architecture involves understanding domains, problems and solutions; making design decisions and trade-offs; and delivering working systems.

questions.q: Software architecture is concerned with which three things?
o: Processes, threads and locks
Stakeholders, system-level structures and system qualities
Requirements, code and tests
Classes, objects and messages
questions.e: Software architecture is concerned with stakeholders, system-level structures and system qualities.

questions.q: Stakeholders are defined as those who:
o: operate the system after deployment only
pay for the system's development only
write the system's code
care if the system gets built, whether with a positive or a negative interest
questions.e: Stakeholders are those who care if the system gets built; the interest can be positive or negative, and stakeholders include people, groups and entities. Systems are built for stakeholders, so design decisions must reflect their needs.

questions.q: System-level structures are described as the traditional deliverable of the software architect, and are represented as:
o: a set of test cases
a set of views, which separate concerns, communicate effectively and organize deliverables and activities
a single comprehensive diagram
a list of components and their line counts
questions.e: System-level structures are the traditional deliverable of the software architect; there are many structures - functional, deployment, information and others - and they are represented as a set of views, which separate concerns, communicate effectively and organize deliverables and activities.

questions.q: System qualities, the non-functional characteristics sometimes called the '-illities', are often crucial to stakeholders because:
o: slow functions don't get used and unavailable systems stop the business
they are the easiest properties to measure
they determine the implementation language
they are specified before functional requirements
questions.e: System qualities are non-functional characteristics such as performance, security and availability. They are often crucial to stakeholders because slow functions don't get used and unavailable systems stop the business.

questions.q: Which of the following is included among the concerns that quality involves?
o: Compilation speed
Aesthetic concerns
Version numbering
Source code line count
questions.e: Quality involves functionality, usability, resilience, performance, reuse, comprehensibility, economic and technology constraints and trade-offs, and aesthetic concerns.

questions.q: Software architecture views are analogous to:
o: the different programming languages used in a project
the different test levels in a test plan
the different types of blueprints made in building architecture
the different releases of a product
questions.e: Software architecture is commonly organized in views, which are analogous to the different types of blueprints made in building architecture.

questions.q: What is the relationship between a view and a viewpoint?
o: Views are instances of viewpoints, where a viewpoint exists to describe the architecture from the perspective of a given set of stakeholders and their concerns
A viewpoint is a view rendered in UML
Views and viewpoints are synonyms
Viewpoints are instances of views, each describing one diagram
questions.e: Views are instances of viewpoints, where a viewpoint exists to describe the architecture from the perspective of a given set of stakeholders and their concerns.

questions.q: Which view captures the structure of the application using class diagrams or equivalents?
o: The physical view
The logical view
The development view
The process view
questions.e: The logical view describes the architecturally significant elements of the architecture and the relationships between them; it essentially captures the structure of the application using class diagrams or equivalents.

questions.q: Which view focuses on describing the concurrency and communications elements of an architecture?
o: The process view
The physical view
The logical view
The development view
questions.e: The process view focuses on describing the concurrency and communications elements of an architecture; in IT applications the main concerns are multi-threaded or replicated components and the synchronous or asynchronous communication mechanisms used.

questions.q: Which view depicts how the major processes and components are mapped on to the application's hardware?
o: The logical view
The physical view
The process view
The development view
questions.e: The physical view depicts how the major processes and components are mapped on to the application's hardware; it might show how the database and web servers are distributed across a number of server machines.

questions.q: Which view captures the internal organization of the software components as they are held in a development environment or configuration management tool?
o: The physical view
The process view
The logical view
The development view
questions.e: The development view captures the internal organization of the software components, typically as held in a development environment or configuration management tool; for example a nested package and class hierarchy for a Java application.

questions.q: Which ways of representing software architecture are identified?
o: Spreadsheets, databases and reports
Source code, object code and executables
Class diagrams, sequence diagrams and use case diagrams only
Textual representation, graphical representation and architecture description languages
questions.e: Software architecture can be represented through textual representation, graphical representation and architecture description languages, with the question raised of whether UML serves as an ADL.

questions.q: An architecture description language is defined as:
o: a set of notations, languages, standards and conventions for an architectural model, with a formal syntax and an assigned semantic interpretation
a configuration file format for deployment
a graphical notation with no formal syntax
a general-purpose programming language used to implement an architecture
questions.e: An ADL is a set of notations, languages, standards and conventions for an architectural model; it is designed specifically for the representation and analysis of software architectures, defines a formal syntax for expressing architectures, and assigns a semantic interpretation.

questions.q: Which ADL is a Society of Automotive Engineers standard?
o: Wright
Acme
Darwin
AADL
questions.e: AADL is a Society of Automotive Engineers standard; Wright and Acme were developed at Carnegie Mellon, xADL at UCI, and Darwin at Imperial College London.

questions.q: Which two ADLs were developed at Carnegie Mellon?
o: Wright and Acme
Darwin and Wright
Acme and Darwin
AADL and xADL
questions.e: Wright and Acme were both developed by Carnegie Mellon; xADL was developed by UCI and Darwin by Imperial College London.

questions.q: Which ADL was developed at Imperial College London?
o: xADL
AADL
Darwin
Acme
questions.e: Darwin was developed by Imperial College London; xADL was developed by UCI.

questions.q: An architectural style is defined as a named collection of architectural design decisions that are applicable in a given development context, constrain architectural design decisions specific to a particular system within that context, and:
o: fix the implementation language for each resulting system
elicit beneficial qualities in each resulting system
guarantee the absence of defects in each resulting system
determine the project schedule for each resulting system
questions.e: An architectural style is a named collection of architectural design decisions that are applicable in a given development context, constrain architectural design decisions specific to a particular system within that context, and elicit beneficial qualities in each resulting system.

questions.q: Shaw and Garlan describe architectural styles as recurring organizational patterns and idioms whose established, shared understanding of common design forms is:
o: a sign of stagnation in a discipline
a constraint only on legacy systems
the mark of a mature engineering field
unique to software engineering
questions.e: Styles are recurring organizational patterns and idioms; the established, shared understanding of common design forms is the mark of a mature engineering field. Medvidovic and Taylor describe a style as an abstraction of recurring composition and interaction characteristics in a set of architectures.

questions.q: Which is one of the basic properties of an architectural style?
o: A vocabulary of design elements, such as component and connector types and data elements
A guarantee of linear scalability
A single permitted programming language
A fixed number of components in every system
questions.e: The basic properties of styles are: a vocabulary of design elements, such as component and connector types and data elements, for example pipes, filters, objects and servers; a set of configuration rules; a semantic interpretation; and possible analyses of systems built in the style.

questions.q: In the basic properties of a style, configuration rules are:
o: topological constraints that determine allowed compositions of elements
the names given to component and connector types
the analyses enabled by the constrained design space
the semantic meanings assigned to compositions
questions.e: A set of configuration rules consists of topological constraints that determine allowed compositions of elements, for example that a component may be connected to at most two other components.

questions.q: In the basic properties of a style, a semantic interpretation means that:
o: compositions of design elements have well-defined meanings
the style can be expressed in a formal grammar
the style can be analysed for performance
each element has a unique name
questions.e: A semantic interpretation means compositions of design elements have well-defined meanings; a further property is the possible analyses of systems built in a style.

questions.q: Which benefit of using styles is illustrated by the observation that a phrase such as 'client-server' conveys a lot of information?
o: Code reuse
Interoperability
Design reuse
Understandability of system organization
questions.e: The benefits of using styles are design reuse, code reuse, understandability of system organization - where a phrase such as client-server conveys a lot of information - interoperability supported by style standardization, style-specific analyses enabled by the constrained design space, and visualizations matching engineers' mental models.

questions.q: Which benefit of styles is supported by style standardization?
o: Visualizations
Interoperability
Style-specific analyses
Design reuse
questions.e: Interoperability is supported by style standardization, while style-specific analyses are enabled by the constrained design space.

questions.q: Which benefit of styles arises specifically from shared implementations of the invariant aspects of a style?
o: Interoperability
Design reuse
Code reuse
Understandability
questions.e: Code reuse comes from shared implementations of invariant aspects of a style, whereas design reuse comes from well-understood solutions applied to new problems.

questions.q: Main program and subroutines, object-oriented organization, and hierarchical layers are all examples of which family of styles?
o: Data-centered systems
Data-flow systems
Independent components
Call and return systems
questions.e: Call and return systems include main program and subroutines, object-oriented, and hierarchical layers. Data-flow systems include batch sequential and pipe and filter; data-centered systems or repositories include databases and blackboard; virtual machines include interpreters and rule-based systems; independent components include communicating processes, event-based systems and publish-subscribe.

questions.q: Interpreters and rule-based systems are examples of which family of styles?
o: Peer-to-peer
Data-flow systems
Virtual machines
Call and return systems
questions.e: Virtual machines as a style family includes interpreters and rule-based systems.

questions.q: Databases and blackboard are examples of which family of styles?
o: Data-flow systems
Independent components
Virtual machines
Data-centered systems, also called repositories
questions.e: Data-centered systems, also called repositories, include databases and blackboard.

questions.q: Communicating processes, event-based systems and publish-subscribe are examples of which family of styles?
o: Data-centered systems
Derived styles
Call and return systems
Independent components
questions.e: Independent components include communicating processes, event-based systems and publish-subscribe. CORBA is an example of a 'derived' style.

questions.q: In the object-oriented style, what are the components and connectors?
o: Components are layers; connectors are protocols of layer interaction
Components are filters; connectors are pipes
Components are clients and servers; connectors are RPC protocols
Components are objects with data and associated operations; connectors are messages and method invocations
questions.e: In the object-oriented style the components are objects - data and associated operations - and the connectors are messages and method invocations.

questions.q: What are the style invariants of the object-oriented style?
o: Servers do not know the number or identities of clients
Announcers are unaware of their events' effects
Objects are responsible for their internal representation integrity, and the internal representation is hidden from other objects
Filters are independent and have no knowledge of up- or down-stream filters
questions.e: The object-oriented style invariants are that objects are responsible for their internal representation integrity and that the internal representation is hidden from other objects.

questions.q: Which are the stated disadvantages of the object-oriented style?
o: Batch organization of processing and a lowest common denominator on data transmission
Components relinquish computation control to the system
Objects must know the identities of servers, and side effects can arise in object method invocations if an object's identity changes
Layers may have to be skipped and performance suffers
questions.e: The object-oriented style's advantages are the infinite malleability of object internals and system decomposition into sets of interacting agents; its disadvantages are that objects must know the identities of servers, and side effects in object method invocations if an object's identity changes.

questions.q: In the client-server style, which statement about knowledge of identity is correct?
o: Both clients and servers know each other's identities
Neither clients nor servers know any identities
Servers do not know the number or identities of clients, while clients know the server's identity
Clients do not know the server's identity, while servers know all client identities
questions.e: In the client-server style the components are clients and servers; servers do not know the number or identities of clients, clients know the server's identity, and the connectors are RPC-based network interaction protocols.

questions.q: In the client-server style, the connectors are:
o: the human hand carrying tapes
pipes carrying data streams
messages and method invocations
RPC-based network interaction protocols
questions.e: The connectors in the client-server style are RPC-based network interaction protocols.

questions.q: In the batch sequential style, separate programs are executed in order and data is passed:
o: incrementally as each record is produced
as an aggregate from one program to the next, upon completion of the producing program's execution
by remote procedure call
through shared memory accessed concurrently
questions.e: In batch sequential, separate programs are executed in order and data is passed as an aggregate from one program to the next. The data elements are explicit aggregate elements passed on completion of the producing program's execution.

questions.q: In the batch sequential style, the connectors were historically described as:
o: network protocols with content-based routing
pipes conveying data streams
a central blackboard data structure
the human hand carrying tapes between the programs, also known as sneaker-net
questions.e: The connectors in batch sequential are 'the human hand' carrying tapes between the programs, also known as sneaker-net. Its typical use is transaction processing in financial systems, and it is called the granddaddy of styles.

questions.q: Batch sequential is typically used for:
o: interactive graphical applications
transaction processing in financial systems
artificial intelligence reasoning
real-time control systems
questions.e: The typical use of batch sequential is transaction processing in financial systems; it is described as the granddaddy of styles.

questions.q: In the pipe and filter style, what are the components and connectors?
o: Components are peers; connectors are network messages
Components are objects; connectors are messages
Components are filters that transform input data streams into output data streams; connectors are pipes, which are conduits for data streams
Components are pipes; connectors are filters
questions.e: In pipe and filter, the components are filters that transform input data streams into output data streams, possibly producing output incrementally, and the connectors are pipes, conduits for data streams.

questions.q: What are the style invariants of the pipe and filter style?
o: Filters are independent with no shared state, and a filter has no knowledge of up- or down-stream filters
Filters must know the identity of the next filter in the chain
Filters share a central data structure that drives control
Filters must be executed in a fixed order determined at compile time
questions.e: The pipe and filter style invariants are that filters are independent, with no shared state, and that a filter has no knowledge of up- or down-stream filters.

questions.q: Which is an example of the pipe and filter style?
o: The UNIX shell command 'ls invoices | grep -e August | sort'
A database with multiple concurrent clients
A set of peers exchanging network messages
An operating system organised into privilege rings
questions.e: Examples of pipe and filter include the UNIX shell, signal processing, distributed systems and parallel programming; the shell pipeline 'ls invoices | grep -e August | sort' is one concrete instance.

questions.q: Which variations of the pipe and filter style are identified?
o: Layers, which expose an API to the layer above
Blackboards, which share a central data structure
Pipelines, which are linear sequences of filters, with bounded pipes limiting data and typed pipes strongly typing data
Peers, which act as both client and server
questions.e: The variations are pipelines - linear sequences of filters - with bounded pipes limiting the amount of data on a pipe and typed pipes making the data strongly typed.

questions.q: Which advantages are claimed for the pipe and filter style?
o: System behavior is a succession of component behaviors, allowing filter addition, replacement and reuse, and certain analyses such as throughput, latency and deadlock
Highly efficient one-way dissemination of information
Low coupling achieved by having announcers unaware of event effects
Increasing abstraction levels and evolvability across layers
questions.e: Pipe and filter advantages are that system behavior is a succession of component behaviors - allowing filter addition, replacement and reuse, since any two filters can be hooked together - and that certain analyses are possible, such as throughput, latency and deadlock.

questions.q: Which are the stated disadvantages of the pipe and filter style?
o: Components relinquish computation control to the system
Layers may have to be skipped
Objects must know the identities of servers
Batch organization of processing, which hampers interactive applications, and a lowest common denominator on data transmission
questions.e: The disadvantages of pipe and filter are the batch organization of processing - a problem for interactive applications - and the lowest common denominator on data transmission.

questions.q: Compilers are traditionally viewed as pipeline systems consisting of which stages?
o: Preprocessing, compilation, assembly and linking
Lexical analysis, parsing, semantic analysis and code generation
Tokenising, indexing, searching and ranking
Reading, validating, transforming and writing
questions.e: Compilers are traditionally viewed as pipeline systems: lexical analysis, parsing, semantic analysis and code generation.
