questions.q: In the blackboard style, which two kinds of component exist, and what drives system control?
o: A central data structure called the blackboard and components operating on it, with control entirely driven by the blackboard state
Publishers and subscribers, with control driven by subscriptions
Filters and pipes, with control driven by the arrival of data
Clients and servers, with control driven by the server's protocol
questions.e: In the blackboard style there are two kinds of components - the central data structure called the blackboard and components operating on the blackboard - and system control is entirely driven by the blackboard state.

questions.q: Which systems typically use the blackboard style?
o: Integrated development environments responding to breakpoints
Financial transaction processing systems
Artificial intelligence systems, integrated software environments and compiler architecture
Operating systems and virtual machines
questions.e: Blackboard is typically used for AI systems, integrated software environments such as Interlisp, and compiler architecture.

questions.q: In the implicit invocation or event-based style, how is behaviour triggered?
o: By a central blackboard whose state drives all control
By passing aggregate data from one program to the next
By event announcement instead of method invocation, with listeners registering interest and the system invoking all registered methods implicitly
By explicit remote procedure calls from clients to servers
questions.e: In the implicit invocation or event-based style, event announcement replaces method invocation: listeners register interest in and associate methods with events, and the system invokes all registered methods implicitly. Component interfaces are methods and events, and invocation is either explicit or implicit in response to events.

questions.q: What are the style invariants of the implicit invocation or event-based style?
o: Servers do not know the identities of clients
Filters have no knowledge of up- or down-stream filters
Announcers are unaware of their events' effects, and no assumption is made about processing in response to events
Announcers must know which listeners will respond and in what order
questions.e: The style invariants are that announcers are unaware of their events' effects, and that no assumption is made about processing in response to events.

questions.q: Which are the stated disadvantages of the implicit invocation style?
o: Layers may have to be skipped, reducing performance
Objects must know the identities of servers
Batch organization of processing hampers interactivity
Components relinquish computation control to the system, with no knowledge of which components will respond or the order of responses
questions.e: The disadvantages are that components relinquish computation control to the system, with no knowledge of what components will respond to an event and no knowledge of the order of responses. The advantages are component reuse and system evolution, both at construction time and at run time.

questions.q: Which advantages are claimed for the implicit invocation or event-based style?
o: Increasing abstraction levels across layers
Highly efficient one-way information dissemination
Throughput, latency and deadlock analyses
Component reuse and system evolution, both at system construction-time and at run-time
questions.e: The advantages of implicit invocation are component reuse and system evolution, both at system construction-time and at run-time.

questions.q: An integrated development environment in which an editor and a variable monitor each respond when a breakpoint is hit illustrates which style?
o: The implicit invocation or event-based style
The batch sequential style
The pipe and filter style
The blackboard style
questions.e: The debugging process in an IDE illustrates the implicit invocation style: the editor and the variables monitor behave appropriately on a breakpoint because they have registered interest in that event, rather than being called explicitly.

questions.q: In the publish-subscribe style, what do subscribers and publishers each do?
o: Subscribers and publishers exchange roles on each message
Subscribers register and deregister to receive specific messages or content, and publishers broadcast messages to subscribers either synchronously or asynchronously
Subscribers poll publishers at a fixed interval
Subscribers broadcast requests and publishers answer them synchronously
questions.e: In publish-subscribe, subscribers register or deregister to receive specific messages or specific content, and publishers broadcast messages to subscribers either synchronously or asynchronously.

questions.q: In the publish-subscribe style, what are the components and the data elements?
o: Components are publishers, subscribers and proxies for managing distribution; data elements are subscriptions, notifications and published information
Components are peers; data elements are network messages
Components are layers; data elements are service requests
Components are filters and pipes; data elements are data streams
questions.e: In publish-subscribe the components are publishers, subscribers and proxies for managing distribution, and the data elements are subscriptions, notifications and published information. Connectors are typically a network protocol, and content-based subscription requires sophisticated connectors.

questions.q: Which qualities does the publish-subscribe style yield?
o: Strong synchronous consistency between publishers and subscribers
Minimal network usage through polling
Guaranteed ordering of all notifications
Highly efficient one-way dissemination of information with very low coupling of components
questions.e: Publish-subscribe yields highly efficient one-way dissemination of information with very low coupling of components. Subscribers connect to publishers either directly or receive notifications via a network protocol from intermediaries.

questions.q: In the peer-to-peer style, peers are described as:
o: filters with no shared state
components that are strictly either clients or servers but never both
independent components having their own state and control thread, which can act as either clients or servers
layers exposing APIs to the layer above
questions.e: In peer-to-peer, state and behavior are distributed among peers which can act as either clients or servers; peers are independent components having their own state and control thread. Connectors are network protocols, often custom, and the data elements are network messages.

questions.q: In the peer-to-peer style, the connectors are:
o: shared variables in a blackboard
method invocations between objects
pipes carrying data streams
network protocols, often custom
questions.e: The connectors in peer-to-peer are network protocols, often custom, and the data elements are network messages.

questions.q: In the layered style, how does each layer act?
o: As a filter transforming a data stream
As a server providing services to layers above and as a client consuming services of the layers below
As a peer to every other layer
As a client to the layers above and a server to the layers below
questions.e: In the layered style - a hierarchical system organization described as multi-level client-server - each layer exposes an interface or API to be used by the layers above, and each layer acts as a server to layers above and a client of the layers below. The connectors are protocols of layer interaction.

questions.q: Which style results from fully opaque layers?
o: The peer-to-peer style
The blackboard style
The virtual machine style
The pipe and filter style
questions.e: The virtual machine style results from fully opaque layers; operating systems are the example given for the layered style.

questions.q: Which advantage of the layered style concerns the scope of change?
o: Changes in a layer require the whole system to be rebuilt
Changes in a layer affect all layers above it
Changes in a layer affect at most the adjacent two layers
Changes in a layer affect no other layer at all
questions.e: Among the advantages of the layered style are increasing abstraction levels, evolvability, the fact that changes in a layer affect at most the adjacent two layers, reuse, permitted alternative implementations of a layer as long as the interface is preserved, and standardized layer interfaces for libraries and frameworks.

questions.q: Which is a stated disadvantage of the layered style?
o: Servers must know the identities of clients
Announcers are unaware of their events' effects
Layers may have to be skipped, and determining the correct abstraction level is difficult
Filters cannot be hooked together arbitrarily
questions.e: The disadvantages of the layered style are that it is not universally applicable, performance, that layers may have to be skipped, and the difficulty of determining the correct abstraction level.

questions.q: Different implementations of a layer are permitted in the layered style as long as:
o: the layer below is also reimplemented
the interface is preserved
the number of layers stays the same
the implementation language is unchanged
questions.e: Different implementations of a layer are allowed as long as the interface is preserved; this, together with standardized layer interfaces for libraries and frameworks, supports reuse.

questions.q: Architectural patterns are grouped into which four categories?
o: Logical, process, physical and development
Creational, structural, behavioral and concurrency
Call and return, data-flow, data-centered and virtual machines
From mud to structure, distributed systems, interactive systems and adaptable systems
questions.e: The architectural pattern categories are from mud to structure, distributed systems, interactive systems and adaptable systems.

questions.q: Patterns in the 'from mud to structure' category support:
o: the extension of applications and adaptability to evolving technology
a controlled decomposition of an overall system task into cooperating sub-tasks
infrastructure for distributed applications
the structuring of systems featuring human-computer interaction
questions.e: Patterns in the from mud to structure category support a controlled decomposition of an overall system task into cooperating sub-tasks. One often has a large set of requirements with competing interests and overlapping aspects - a 'ball of mud' - and although the system can be decomposed by functionality, quality attributes must still be met.

questions.q: The 'ball of mud' problem that 'from mud to structure' patterns address arises because:
o: the system has too few requirements to structure
a large set of requirements brings competing interests, overlapping aspects and problems that are difficult to work with
the hardware platform is undecided
the implementation language lacks modularity constructs
questions.e: Often there is a large set of requirements and it is difficult to work with competing interests, overlapping aspects and problems - a ball of mud. Although the system can be decomposed based on functionalities, one has to ensure quality attributes are met.

questions.q: Which pattern belongs to the distributed systems category, and which two are referred to from other categories?
o: Blackboard belongs to it, and it refers to Broker and Layers
Pipes and Filters belongs to it, and it refers to MVC and Reflection
Microkernel belongs to it, and it refers to Broker and Layers
Broker belongs to it, and it refers to Microkernel and Pipes and Filters
questions.e: The distributed systems category provides infrastructure for distributed applications; it includes one pattern, Broker, and refers to two patterns in other categories: Microkernel and Pipes and Filters.

questions.q: Which patterns belong to the interactive systems category?
o: Model-View-Controller and Presentation-Abstraction-Control
Broker and Microkernel
Layers, Pipes and Filters and Blackboard
Reflection and Microkernel
questions.e: The interactive systems category supports the structuring of software systems that feature human-computer interaction; its patterns include MVC and Presentation Abstraction Controller.

questions.q: Which patterns belong to the adaptable systems category?
o: Reflection and Microkernel
Broker and Pipes and Filters
MVC and Presentation-Abstraction-Control
Layers and Blackboard
questions.e: The adaptable systems category contains patterns that support extension of applications and adaptability to evolving technology and changing functional requirements; its patterns include Reflection and Microkernel.

questions.q: Within the 'from mud to structure' category, which pattern is useful for problems for which no deterministic solution strategies are known?
o: Pipes and Filters
Layers
Blackboard
Broker
questions.e: The Blackboard pattern is useful for problems for which no deterministic solution strategies are known; in Blackboard, several specialised subsystems assemble their knowledge to build a possibly partial or approximate solution.

questions.q: In the Blackboard pattern, what do the specialised subsystems do?
o: They assemble their knowledge to build a possibly partial or approximate solution
They each transform a data stream and pass it to the next
They broadcast notifications to registered subscribers
They each expose an API to the subsystem above
questions.e: In Blackboard, several specialised subsystems assemble their knowledge to build a possibly partial or approximate solution.

questions.q: Within the 'from mud to structure' category, the Pipes and Filters pattern provides a structure for systems that:
o: can be decomposed into groups of sub-tasks at particular levels of abstraction
have no known deterministic solution strategy
require infrastructure for distribution
process a stream of data, with each processing step encapsulated in a filter component and data passed through pipes between adjacent filters
questions.e: The Pipes and Filters pattern provides a structure for systems that process a stream of data; each processing step is encapsulated in a filter component and data is passed through pipes between adjacent filters. Recombining filters allows families of related systems to be built.

questions.q: Recombining filters in the Pipes and Filters pattern allows you to:
o: convert the system into a layered architecture
eliminate the need for pipes
guarantee real-time response
build families of related systems
questions.e: Recombining filters allows you to build families of related systems.

questions.q: The Layers architectural pattern helps to structure applications that:
o: require human-computer interaction
process a stream of data through successive transformations
have no deterministic solution strategy
can be decomposed into groups of subtasks in which each group is at a particular level of abstraction
questions.e: The Layers architectural pattern helps to structure applications that can be decomposed into groups of subtasks in which each group of subtasks is at a particular level of abstraction.

questions.q: What is the context for applying the Layers pattern?
o: A large system that requires decomposition
A system whose requirements are fully stable
A small system with a single responsibility
A system with no quality attribute requirements
questions.e: The context for the Layers pattern is a large system that requires decomposition. Networking protocols are the best known examples of layered architecture.

questions.q: Which are cited as the best known examples of layered architecture?
o: Compilers
Networking protocols
Expert systems
Relational databases
questions.e: Networking protocols are the best known examples of layered architecture.

questions.q: Which characteristics describe the problem the Layers pattern addresses?
o: A system whose dominant characteristic is a mix of low- and high-level issues, where high-level operations rely on lower-level ones
A system with no portability requirements
A system in which all operations are at the same level of abstraction
A system that must process an unbounded stream of data
questions.e: The problem is a system whose dominant characteristic is a mix of low- and high-level issues, where high-level operations rely on the lower-level ones. Such systems often also require horizontal structuring orthogonal to their vertical subdivision, and portability to other platforms is also desired.

questions.q: Which force must be balanced when applying the Layers pattern?
o: Responsibilities should be distributed randomly to avoid clustering
Late source code changes should not ripple through the system, so changes should be confined to one component without affecting others
All components should be able to access all others directly
The number of layers should be maximised
questions.e: The forces to balance are: late source code changes should not ripple through the system, confining changes to one component without affecting others; parts of the system should be exchangeable; and similar responsibilities should be grouped to help understandability and maintainability.

questions.q: Which force in the Layers pattern concerns grouping of responsibilities?
o: Responsibilities should be spread evenly across all layers
Dissimilar responsibilities should be grouped to maximise reuse
Similar responsibilities should be grouped to help understandability and maintainability
Each responsibility should be in its own layer
questions.e: Similar responsibilities should be grouped to help understandability and maintainability.

questions.q: In the Layers pattern's solution, how are the services at a given layer composed?
o: Services at Layer J are composed of services from the layer above
Services at Layer J are composed of services from every lower layer directly
Most of the services at Layer J are composed of the services provided by the next lower layer, Layer J-1
Services at each layer are independent of all other layers
questions.e: The solution is to divide the system into an appropriate number of layers and put them on top of each other; most of the services at a particular layer, Layer J, are composed of the services provided by the next lower layer, Layer J-1.

questions.q: In the Layers pattern's solution, what is required of the components within an individual layer?
o: They shall be implemented in the same programming language
They shall each work at a different level of abstraction
They shall all work at the same level of abstraction
They shall communicate only with components in other layers
questions.e: All constituent components within an individual layer shall work at the same level of abstraction.

questions.q: In the Layers pattern's first dynamic scenario, what happens when Layer N cannot carry out a client request on its own?
o: It calls the next lower layer, Layer N-1, for supporting subtasks, and replies are passed back to the next higher layer
It bypasses the intermediate layers and calls Layer 1 directly
It forwards the request to the layer above
It rejects the request and returns an error to the client
questions.e: In Scenario I, a client issues a request to Layer N; Layer N cannot carry out the request on its own so it calls the next Layer N-1 for supporting subtasks; Layer N-1 performs these tasks and may send a request to the next lower layer; replies are passed back to the next higher layer.

questions.q: In the Layers pattern's second dynamic scenario, bottom-up communication starts when, for example, a device driver detects input. What are such bottom-up transmissions called?
o: Notifications, in contrast to requests which travel the other way
Requests, in contrast to notifications which travel the other way
Callbacks, in contrast to events
Interrupts, in contrast to signals
questions.e: Scenario II illustrates bottom-up communication: the chain of actions starts at Layer 1, for example when a device driver detects input; Layer 1 translates the input to an internal format and transmits it to the next higher layer. Bottom-up transmission is termed 'notifications'; the other direction is 'requests'.

questions.q: In the Layers pattern's step-wise implementation, which step comes first?
o: Name the layers and assign tasks to each of them
Design an error-handling strategy
Specify an interface for each layer
Define the abstraction criterion and determine the number of abstraction levels
questions.e: The step-wise refinement approach, in which not all steps are mandatory, runs: define the abstraction criterion and determine the number of abstraction levels; name the layers and assign tasks; specify the services; specify an interface for each layer; refine and structure individual layers; specify the communication between adjacent layers; decouple adjacent layers; design an error-handling strategy.

questions.q: In the Layers pattern's step-wise implementation, which step comes last?
o: Refine and structure individual layers
Design an error-handling strategy
Decouple adjacent layers
Specify the communication between adjacent layers
questions.e: The last of the eight implementation steps is to design an error-handling strategy; it is preceded by decoupling adjacent layers.

questions.q: Which is a known use of the Layers pattern?
o: Compilers and lexical analysers
Financial transaction batch processing
Virtual machines, APIs and information systems
Artificial intelligence reasoning systems
questions.e: The known uses given are virtual machines, APIs, information systems, and Windows enterprise operating systems such as NT, 2000, XP and Server, which are noted as being structured as the Microkernel pattern.

questions.q: Which are the stated benefits of the Layers pattern?
o: Automatic error handling and fault tolerance
Reuse of layers, support for standardization, dependencies kept local, and exchangeability
Guaranteed efficiency and minimal work
Unlimited abstraction depth with no cost
questions.e: The benefits of the Layers pattern are reuse of layers, support for standardization, dependencies being kept local, and exchangeability.

questions.q: Which are the stated liabilities of the Layers pattern?
o: Loss of modularity and loss of abstraction
Cascades of changing behaviour, lower efficiency, unnecessary work, and difficulty of establishing the correct granularity of layers
Complete dependence on a single vendor's platform
Inability to reuse any layer
questions.e: The liabilities are cascades of changing behaviour, lower efficiency, unnecessary work, and the difficulty of establishing the correct granularity of layers.

questions.q: The liability 'cascades of changing behaviour' in the Layers pattern refers to the risk that:
o: layers cannot be reused across systems
the number of layers grows without limit
a change in one layer propagates through others, undermining the benefit of local dependencies
layers must be skipped for performance reasons
questions.e: Although dependencies are kept local, one liability of the Layers pattern is cascades of changing behaviour, alongside lower efficiency, unnecessary work, and difficulty establishing the correct granularity of layers.

questions.q: Functionality and quality attributes are described as:
o: mutually exclusive, so a system can have one or the other
equivalent, so improving functionality necessarily improves quality
orthogonal, so the architect's choices determine the desired level of quality for a particular function
dependent, so quality is fixed once functionality is fixed
questions.e: Functionality is the basic statement of the system's capability, services and behaviour; various quality attributes need to be accommodated in the architecture. Functionality and quality attributes are orthogonal, and the architect's choices determine the desired level of quality for a particular function.

questions.q: Which statement about achieving quality at the architectural level is correct?
o: Architecture alone fully determines the quality of the delivered system
Quality is independent of both architecture and implementation
Quality can only be evaluated after implementation is complete
Qualities can be designed in and evaluated at architectural level, but architecture on its own cannot achieve quality, so attention must be paid to detail
questions.e: Achieving quality has to be considered throughout design, implementation and deployment: qualities can be designed in and evaluated at architectural level, but architecture on its own cannot achieve quality, so attention has to be paid to detail.

questions.q: Which usability decision is architectural rather than non-architectural?
o: The screen layout
The ability to cancel an operation, undo operations, or re-use data previously entered
Whether to provide a radio button or a check box
The choice of typeface
questions.e: Non-architectural usability decisions concern making the user interface clear and easy to use - radio button or check box, screen layout, typeface. Architectural decisions may include the ability to cancel an operation, undo operations, or re-use data previously entered.

questions.q: Modifiability can be determined by:
o: the frequency of inter-component communication
the number of event sources and arrival patterns
the ability to mask or repair faults
how functionality is divided and by coding techniques within a module
questions.e: Modifiability can be determined by how functionality is divided and by coding techniques within a module. Performance, by contrast, depends on the frequency of inter-component communication, what functionality is allocated to each component, the allocation of shared resources, the choice of algorithms and how those algorithms are coded.

questions.q: Which factor does performance depend on?
o: The frequency of inter-component communication
The probability of detecting an attack
The clarity of the user interface layout
The coding techniques used inside a single module only
questions.e: Performance depends on the frequency of inter-component communication, including what functionality has been allocated to each component, the allocation of shared resources, the choice of algorithms and how those algorithms are coded.

questions.q: Why are portability and performance considered conflicting quality attributes?
o: Portable systems cannot use shared resources at all
Portability requires that all algorithms be rewritten
Performance requires platform-specific code that cannot be isolated
Isolating system dependencies and introducing wrappers or converters adds data transformations and message passing, which lowers performance
questions.e: The conflict arises because achieving portability means isolating system dependencies and introducing wrappers or converters, which brings more data transformations and message passing, and hence lower performance.

questions.q: Quality attributes are divided into which three classes?
o: Functional, non-functional and technical qualities
Internal, external and interface qualities
Qualities of the system, business qualities and architectural qualities
Runtime, design-time and deployment-time qualities
questions.e: The classes are qualities of the system - availability, modifiability, performance, security, testability and usability; business qualities such as time to market, which are affected by the architecture; and architectural qualities such as conceptual integrity, which are about the architecture itself.

questions.q: Which of the following is a quality of the system rather than a business or architectural quality?
o: Testability
Conceptual integrity
Buildability
Time to market
questions.e: The qualities of the system are availability, modifiability, performance, security, testability and usability. Time to market is a business quality, and conceptual integrity and buildability are architectural qualities.

questions.q: Which three problems does an architect face with quality attributes?
o: The definitions provided for an attribute are not operational, attribute concerns overlap, and each quality attribute has a separate vocabulary
Attributes cannot be measured, cannot be designed and cannot be tested
Attributes are too numerous, too vague and too technical
Attributes conflict, cost money and take time
questions.e: The three main problems from an architect's view are that the definitions provided for an attribute are not operational, that attribute concerns overlap, and that there is a separate vocabulary for each quality attribute.

questions.q: Which of the architect's three quality-attribute problems are solved by using quality attribute scenarios?
o: None of them; scenarios address a different issue
The third only: separate vocabulary for each attribute
All three problems
The first two: non-operational definitions and overlapping attribute concerns
questions.e: The first two problems - non-operational definitions and overlapping attribute concerns - can be solved by using quality attribute scenarios. The solution to the third problem, separate vocabulary for each quality attribute, is a brief description of each attribute in terms of its underlying concerns.

questions.q: A quality attribute scenario is defined as:
o: a general description of an attribute in plain language
a test case for a non-functional requirement
a tactic that influences a quality attribute response
a quality-attribute-specific requirement consisting of six parts
questions.e: A quality attribute scenario is a quality-attribute-specific requirement consisting of six parts: stimulus, source of stimulus, environment, artifact, response and response measure.

questions.q: In a quality attribute scenario, the 'stimulus' is:
o: the entity that generated the condition
the conditions under which the condition occurs
the activity undertaken after the condition arrives
a condition that needs to be considered when it arrives at a system
questions.e: The stimulus is a condition that needs to be considered when it arrives at a system; the source of stimulus is the entity - a human, a computer system or any other actuator - that generated the stimulus.

questions.q: In a quality attribute scenario, the 'artifact' is:
o: the activity undertaken after the stimulus arrives
the thing that is stimulated, which may be the whole system or some pieces of it
the measurable outcome of the response
the entity that generated the stimulus
questions.e: Some artifact is stimulated; this may be the whole system or some pieces of it.

questions.q: Why must the response in a quality attribute scenario have a response measure?
o: So that the environment can be classified
So that the artifact can be located
So that the requirement can be tested, since the response should be measurable in some fashion
So that the stimulus can be identified
questions.e: The response is the activity undertaken after the arrival of the stimulus; when the response occurs it should be measurable in some fashion so that the requirement can be tested.

questions.q: Quality attribute scenarios come in which two forms?
o: Internal scenarios and external scenarios
General scenarios and concrete scenarios
Positive scenarios and negative scenarios
Static scenarios and dynamic scenarios
questions.e: Quality attribute scenarios are expressed as general scenarios and as concrete scenarios.

questions.q: Availability is concerned with:
o: system failure and its associated consequences
the ease with which a user can accomplish a task
the cost of making changes to a system
the system's resistance to unauthorized use
questions.e: Availability is concerned with system failure and its associated consequences; a system failure occurs when the system no longer delivers a service consistent with its specification.

questions.q: A system failure occurs when:
o: any internal fault is present in the system
an unauthorized user attempts access
the system no longer delivers a service consistent with its specification
the system's performance degrades below its average
questions.e: A system failure occurs when the system no longer delivers a service consistent with its specification.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a fault from a failure?
o: Neither faults nor failures are observable by the user
A fault is observable by the user and a failure is not
A failure is observable by the system's user and a fault is not; a fault may become a failure if not corrected or masked
Faults and failures are both observable by the user
questions.e: A fault may become a failure if not corrected or masked. A failure is observable by the system's user and a fault is not; when a fault does become observable, it becomes a failure.

questions.q: The availability of a system is typically defined as:
o: the number of failures divided by the operating time
mean time to repair divided by mean time to failure
one minus the mean time to failure
mean time to failure divided by the sum of mean time to failure and mean time to repair
questions.e: The availability of a system is the probability that it will be operational when it is needed, typically defined as the mean time to failure divided by the sum of the mean time to failure and the mean time to repair.

questions.q: Which of these are concerns about failure that availability addresses?
o: How many statements are covered by tests
How many users the system can support concurrently
How failure is detected, how frequently it may occur, and how long a system is allowed to be out of operation
How quickly changes can be deployed
questions.e: The concerns about failure are how system failure is detected, how frequently it may occur, what happens when a failure occurs, how long a system is allowed to be out of operation, and how failures can be prevented.

questions.q: In an availability scenario, what distinction does the source of stimulus make?
o: Between internal and external indications of faults or failure
Between authorized and unauthorized users
Between periodic and stochastic arrival patterns
Between design time and runtime
questions.e: For availability, the source of stimulus differentiates between internal and external indications of faults or failure.

questions.q: In an availability scenario, a fault in which a component fails to respond to an input is classed as:
o: timing
crash
response
omission
questions.e: The availability stimulus types are omission, where a component fails to respond to an input; crash, where the component repeatedly suffers omission faults; timing, where a component responds but the response is early or late; and response, where a component responds with an incorrect value.

questions.q: In an availability scenario, a fault in which a component repeatedly suffers omission faults is classed as:
o: crash
timing
response
omission
questions.e: A crash fault is one in which the component repeatedly suffers omission faults.

questions.q: In an availability scenario, a fault in which a component responds but the response is early or late is classed as:
o: omission
response
timing
crash
questions.e: A timing fault is one in which a component responds but the response is early or late; a response fault is one in which a component responds with an incorrect value.

questions.q: In an availability scenario, what does the artifact specify?
o: The possible reactions to the failure
The source of the fault indication
The resource required to be highly available, such as a processor, communication channel, process or storage
The state of the system when the fault occurs
questions.e: For availability, the artifact specifies the resource that is required to be highly available, such as a processor, communication channel, process or storage. The environment is the state of the system when the fault or failure occurs.

questions.q: Which of these is a possible availability response?
o: Measuring the percentage of executable statements executed
Recomputing the response with a different algorithm for speed
Switching to a degraded mode with either less capacity or less function
Authenticating the user who caused the fault
questions.e: Possible reactions to a system failure include logging the failure, notifying selected users or other systems, and switching to a degraded mode with either less capacity or less function.

questions.q: An availability response measure can specify:
o: the probability of identifying an attacker
an availability percentage, a time to repair, or the times during which the system must be available
the number of errors a user makes
the percentage of executable statements executed
questions.e: An availability response measure can specify an availability percentage, or a time to repair, or the times during which the system must be available.

questions.q: In the availability scenario overview, 'normal operation' and 'degraded mode' are values of which scenario portion?
o: Artifact
Stimulus
Environment
Response
questions.e: For availability, the environment takes values such as normal operation and degraded mode, meaning fewer features or a fall-back solution. The artifact takes values such as the system's processors, communication channels, persistent storage and processes.

questions.q: Which of these is a possible availability response in the scenario overview?
o: Grant or withdraw permission to access data
Aggregate data and commands for efficient use
Disable sources of events that cause fault or failure according to defined rules
Provide access to state values for a test harness
questions.e: For availability the system should detect the event and do one or more of: record it; notify appropriate parties including the user and other systems; disable sources of events that cause fault or failure according to defined rules; be unavailable for a pre-specified interval depending on the criticality of the system; or continue to operate in normal or degraded mode.

questions.q: 'An unanticipated external message is received by a process during normal operation. The process informs the operator of the receipt of the message and continues to operate with no downtime.' This is a concrete scenario for which quality attribute?
o: Availability
Modifiability
Security
Performance
questions.e: This is the concrete availability scenario derived from the general availability scenario: an unanticipated external message received during normal operation, with the process informing the operator and continuing to operate with no downtime.

questions.q: Which availability response measures are identified in the scenario overview?
o: The time interval when the system must be available, availability time, the time interval in which the system can be in degraded mode, and repair time
Latency, deadline, throughput, jitter and miss rate
Task time, number of errors and user satisfaction
Percent executable statements executed and time to perform tests
questions.e: For availability the response measures are the time interval when the system must be available, availability time, the time interval in which the system can be in degraded mode, and repair time.

questions.q: Modifiability is fundamentally about:
o: resistance to unauthorized usage
the timing of responses
the cost of change
the ease of demonstrating faults
questions.e: Modifiability is about the cost of change. The artifact question asks what can change: a change can occur to any aspect of a system.

questions.q: Which of these can change, as the artifact of a modifiability scenario?
o: Only the user interface of the system
The functions the system computes, the platform it exists on, and the environment within which it operates
Only the source code of the system
Only the hardware on which the system runs
questions.e: A change can occur to any aspect of a system: the functions the system computes; the platform it exists on, meaning hardware, operating system and middleware; and the environment within which it operates, meaning the systems it must interoperate with and the protocols it uses.

questions.q: Which question must the architect answer about the likelihood of change?
o: Which changes are likely, which of these are to be supported and which are not
Which developer will make each change
How much each change will cost in money alone
How many lines of code each change will touch
questions.e: The architect needs to identify which changes are likely, which of these are to be supported, and which are not.

questions.q: Traditionally a change is made to source code by a developer. At what other times can changes be made?
o: Only at design time
Only during compile and build
During compile, during build, during configuration setup and during execution
Only during configuration setup
questions.e: Changes can be made during compile, using compile-time switches; during build, by choice of libraries; during configuration setup, by techniques including parameter setting; and during execution, by parameter setting. A change can also be made by an end user or a system administrator.

questions.q: In a modifiability scenario, who are the possible sources of stimulus?
o: One of a number of independent sources
End user, developer and system administrator
Internal to the system and external to the system
Unit developer, increment integrator and system verifier
questions.e: For modifiability the sources are end user, developer and system administrator. 'Internal or external to the system' is the availability source, and 'unit developer, increment integrator, system verifier' is the testability source.

questions.q: In a modifiability scenario, the stimulus is characterised as a wish to:
o: display, change or delete information or reduce availability of services
add, delete or modify, or to vary functionality, a quality attribute or capacity
learn system features or use the system efficiently
complete a phase of system development
questions.e: For modifiability the stimulus is that someone wishes to add, delete or modify, or to vary functionality, a quality attribute or capacity.

questions.q: In a modifiability scenario, the environment takes which values?
o: At runtime, compile time, build time and design time
Online or offline, connected or disconnected, firewalled or open
At runtime or configure time
Normal mode and overload mode
questions.e: For modifiability the environment is at runtime, compile time, build time or design time. 'Normal mode and overload mode' belongs to performance, and 'online or offline, connected or disconnected, firewalled or open' belongs to security.

questions.q: In a modifiability scenario, the four-part response begins with which step?
o: Deploying the modification
Locating the places in the architecture to be modified
Testing the modification
Making the modification without affecting other functionality
questions.e: The modifiability response is: locate places in the architecture to be modified; make the modification without affecting other functionality; test the modification; deploy the modification.

questions.q: In a modifiability scenario, the response measures are:
o: task time, number of errors and user satisfaction
cost in terms of the number of elements affected, effort and money, and the extent to which the change affects other functions or quality attributes
latency, deadline, throughput, jitter and miss rate
availability percentage and repair time
questions.e: The modifiability response measures are cost - in terms of the number of elements affected, effort and money - and the extent to which this affects other functions or quality attributes.

questions.q: 'A developer wishes to change the user interface to make a screen's background colour blue. The change will be made to the code at implementation time, will take less than three hours to make and test, and no side effect changes will occur in the behavior.' Which quality attribute does this scenario address?
o: Usability
Modifiability
Testability
Performance
questions.e: This is the sample modifiability scenario: it names the source (a developer), the artifact (the user interface), the environment (implementation time) and the response measure (less than three hours, with no side effects).

questions.q: Performance is fundamentally about:
o: resistance to attack
timing
cost of change
ease of testing
questions.e: Performance is about timing: an event - interrupts, messages, requests from users or the passage of time - occurs and the system must respond to it.

questions.q: Which are identified as complications in performance?
o: The number of event sources and the event arrival pattern
The number of developers and the build frequency
The number of attack vectors and the attacker's resources
The number of user errors and the task time
questions.e: Events such as interrupts, messages, requests from users or the passage of time occur and the system must respond to them; the complications in performance are the number of event sources and the event arrival pattern.

questions.q: In a performance scenario, the stimulus is characterised as:
o: a wish to add, delete, modify or vary functionality
an attempt to display, change or delete data
omission, crash, timing or response faults
periodic events arrive, sporadic events arrive, or stochastic events arrive
questions.e: For performance the stimulus is that periodic, sporadic or stochastic events arrive; the source is one of a number of independent sources, possibly from within the system.

questions.q: In a performance scenario, the environment takes which values?
o: Normal mode and overload mode
Runtime, compile time, build time and design time
Normal operation and degraded mode
At runtime or configure time
questions.e: For performance the environment is normal mode or overload mode; the artifact is the system and the response is that the system processes the stimuli or changes level of service.

questions.q: In a performance scenario, the response measures are:
o: task time, number of errors and user satisfaction
availability percentage and repair time
cost, effort and money
latency, deadline, throughput, jitter, miss rate and data loss
questions.e: The performance response measures are latency, deadline, throughput, jitter, miss rate and data loss.

questions.q: 'Users initiate 1,000 transactions per minute stochastically under normal operations, and these transactions are processed with an average latency of two seconds.' Which attribute does this scenario address?
o: Availability
Performance
Usability
Modifiability
questions.e: This is the sample performance scenario: 1,000 transactions per minute arriving stochastically under normal operations, processed with an average latency of two seconds.

questions.q: Security is defined as a measure of the system's ability to:
o: accommodate changes at the lowest possible cost
demonstrate its faults through testing
detect and repair faults without downtime
resist unauthorized usage while still providing its services to legitimate users
questions.e: Security is a measure of the system's ability to resist unauthorized usage while still providing its services to legitimate users.

questions.q: Which forms can an attack take?
o: Only denial of service to legitimate users
An unauthorized attempt to access data or service, modifying data, or denying service to legitimate users
Only modification of system source code
Only unauthorized access to data
questions.e: An attack can be an unauthorized attempt to access data or service, to modify data, or to deny service to legitimate users.

questions.q: In a security scenario, the artifact is:
o: system services and data within the system
the whole system only
the system's processors and communication channels
a piece of design, a piece of code or a complete application
questions.e: For security the artifact is system services and data within the system.

questions.q: In a security scenario, how is the source characterised?
o: An individual or system that is correctly identified, identified incorrectly or of unknown identity, who is internal or external, authorized or not, with access to limited or vast resources
One of a number of independent sources, possibly from within the system
Internal or external indications of faults
End user, developer or system administrator
questions.e: For security the source is an individual or system that is correctly identified, identified incorrectly or of unknown identity; who is internal or external, authorized or not authorized; and with access to limited resources or vast resources.

questions.q: In a security scenario, the stimulus is characterised as an attempt to:
o: add, delete, modify or vary functionality
learn system features or use the system efficiently
complete a phase of system development
display data, change or delete data, access system services, or reduce availability to system services
questions.e: For security the stimulus is that the source tries to display data, change or delete data, access system services, or reduce availability to system services.

questions.q: In a security scenario, the environment takes which values?
o: Online or offline, connected or disconnected, firewalled or open
Normal operation or degraded mode
Normal mode or overload mode
Runtime, compile time, build time or design time
questions.e: For security the environment is either online or offline, connected or disconnected, firewalled or open.

questions.q: Which of the following is a security response?
o: Switching to a degraded mode with less capacity
Recognizing an unexplainable high demand for services, informing a user or another system, and restricting availability of services
Locating the places in the architecture to be modified
Providing access to state values for a test harness
questions.e: Security responses include authenticating the user; hiding the user's identity; blocking or allowing access to data or services; granting or withdrawing permission; recording accesses, modifications or attempts by identity; storing data in an unreadable format; and recognizing an unexplainable high demand for services, informing a user or another system, and restricting availability of services.

questions.q: Which of the following is a security response measure?
o: The percent of executable statements executed
The latency and throughput of transactions
The number of elements affected by a change
The time, effort or resources required to circumvent security measures, with the probability of success
questions.e: Security response measures include the time, effort or resources required to circumvent security measures with the probability of success; the probability of detecting an attack; the probability of identifying the individual responsible; the percentage of services still available under a denial-of-service attack; restoring data or services; and the extent to which data or services were damaged or legitimate access denied.

questions.q: 'A correctly identified individual tries to modify system data from an external site; the system maintains an audit trail and the correct data is restored within one day.' Which attribute does this scenario address?
o: Testability
Security
Modifiability
Availability
questions.e: This is the sample security scenario: a correctly identified individual attempting modification from an external site, with an audit trail maintained and correct data restored within one day.

questions.q: In the summary of quality attribute stimuli, which stimulus corresponds to availability?
o: Periodic, stochastic or sporadic events
An unexpected event, or the nonoccurrence of an expected event
A request to add, delete, change or vary functionality
Completion of a phase of system development
questions.e: In the summary of stimuli, performance is stimulated by periodic, stochastic or sporadic events; availability by an unexpected event or the nonoccurrence of an expected event; modifiability by a request to add, delete, change or vary functionality, platform, quality attribute or capacity; security by attempts to display, modify, change or delete information, access services, or reduce availability; and testability by completion of a phase of system development.

questions.q: In the summary of quality attribute stimuli, which stimulus corresponds to testability?
o: Completion of a phase of system development
A wish to learn system features
Periodic, stochastic or sporadic events
An unexpected event or nonoccurrence of an expected event
questions.e: Testability is stimulated by the completion of a phase of system development.

questions.q: Testability refers to:
o: the proportion of code covered by automated tests
the probability that software contains no faults at all
the cost of running a complete test suite
the ease with which software can be made to demonstrate its faults through testing
questions.e: Testability refers to the ease with which software can be made to demonstrate its faults through testing; more precisely, assuming the software has at least one fault, it refers to the probability that it will fail on its next test execution.

questions.q: Testability is defined more precisely as the probability that, assuming the software has at least one fault:
o: it will pass its next test execution
the fault will be repaired without side effects
the fault will be located within one hour
it will fail on its next test execution
questions.e: Testability refers to the probability, assuming the software has at least one fault, that it will fail on its next test execution.

questions.q: What proportion of cost is said to relate to testing?
o: 40 percent
10 percent
20 percent
60 percent
questions.e: 40 percent of cost relates to testing, which is part of why anything the architect can do to reduce it yields significant benefit.

questions.q: A test harness is defined as:
o: a document listing the test cases to be executed
specialized software designed to exercise the software under test
a hardware rig used to simulate system load
a measure of the probability of failure
questions.e: A test harness is specialized software designed to exercise the software under test.

questions.q: In a testability scenario, the artifact takes which values?
o: The system's processors, communication channels and storage
A piece of design, a piece of code, or a complete application
The system user interface, platform and environment
System services and data within the system
questions.e: For testability the artifact is a piece of design, a piece of code, or a complete application.

questions.q: In a testability scenario, the source takes which values?
o: End user, developer and system administrator
Unit developer, increment integrator, system verifier, client acceptance tester and system user
Internal to the system and external to the system
One of a number of independent sources
questions.e: For testability the sources are the unit developer, increment integrator, system verifier, client acceptance tester and system user.

questions.q: In a testability scenario, the stimulus takes which values?
o: A wish to add, delete, modify or vary functionality
Analysis, architecture, design, class or subsystem integration completed, or system delivered
An attempt to display, change or delete data
Periodic, sporadic or stochastic events arriving
questions.e: For testability the stimulus is that analysis, architecture, design, class or subsystem integration is completed, or the system is delivered.

questions.q: In a testability scenario, the environment takes which values?
o: Normal mode or overload mode
At runtime or configure time
Online or offline, connected or disconnected
At design time, at development time, at compile time, or at deployment time
questions.e: For testability the environment is at design time, at development time, at compile time, or at deployment time.

questions.q: In a testability scenario, the response is that the system:
o: records the event and notifies appropriate parties
locates and makes the modification, then tests and deploys it
provides access to state values, provides computed values, and prepares the test environment
authenticates the user and blocks access to data
questions.e: For testability the response is that the system provides access to state values, provides computed values and prepares the test environment.

questions.q: Which of the following is a testability response measure?
o: The ratio of successful operations to total operations
The number of elements affected by a change
The latency and jitter of transactions
The length of the longest dependency chain in a test
questions.e: Testability response measures include the percent of executable statements executed, the probability of failure if a fault exists, the time to perform tests, the length of the longest dependency chain in a test, and the length of time to prepare the test environment.

questions.q: 'A unit tester performs a unit test on a completed system component that provides an interface for controlling its behaviour and observing its output; 85% path coverage is achieved within three hours.' Which attribute does this scenario address?
o: Performance
Modifiability
Testability
Usability
questions.e: This is the testability scenario: a unit tester, a completed component with an interface for controlling behaviour and observing output, and a response measure of 85% path coverage within three hours.

questions.q: Usability is concerned with how easy it is for the user to accomplish a desired task and:
o: the probability that a fault will be demonstrated
the kind of user support the system provides
the cost of changing the user interface
the system's resistance to unauthorized use
questions.e: Usability is concerned with how easy it is for the user to accomplish a desired task and the kind of user support the system provides.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the concerns of usability?
o: Minimizing the time to repair a fault
Minimizing the probability of a successful attack
Minimizing the number of elements affected by a change
Minimizing the impact of errors
questions.e: The usability concerns are learning system features, using a system efficiently, minimizing the impact of errors, adapting the system to user needs, and increasing confidence and satisfaction.

questions.q: In a usability scenario, the source of stimulus is:
o: the system administrator
the developer
the system verifier
the end user
questions.e: For usability the artifact is the system, the source is the end user, and the environment is at runtime or configure time.

questions.q: In a usability scenario, the environment takes which values?
o: At design time or compile time
Normal mode or overload mode
At runtime or configure time
Online or offline
questions.e: For usability the environment is at runtime or configure time.

questions.q: In a usability scenario, the stimulus is characterised as the user wanting to:
o: add, delete, modify or vary functionality
display, change or delete data
learn system features, use the system efficiently, minimize the impact of errors, adapt the system, or feel comfortable
complete a phase of system development
questions.e: For usability the stimulus is that the user wants to learn system features, use the system efficiently, minimize the impact of errors, adapt the system, or feel comfortable.

questions.q: Which usability responses support the goal 'minimize impact of errors'?
o: Display system state and work at the user's pace
Aggregation of data and commands, and re-use of already entered data
Customizability and internationalization
Undo, cancel, recover from system failure, recognize and correct user error, retrieve a forgotten password, and verify system resources
questions.e: To minimize impact of errors the system offers undo, cancel, recover from system failure, recognize and correct user error, retrieve forgotten password and verify system resources. Customizability and internationalization support 'adapt system'; display system state and working at the user's pace support 'feel comfortable'.

questions.q: Which usability responses support the goal 'adapt system'?
o: Comprehensive searching and distinct views
Display system state and work at the user's pace
Customizability and internationalization
Undo, cancel and recovery from system failure
questions.e: Customizability and internationalization are the responses listed for 'adapt system'.

questions.q: Which usability responses support the goal 'feel comfortable'?
o: Display system state and work at the user's pace
Customizability and internationalization
Undo, cancel and error correction
Aggregation of data and commands
questions.e: Displaying system state and working at the user's pace are the responses listed for 'feel comfortable'.

questions.q: Which usability responses support the goal 'use system efficiently'?
o: Undo, cancel and recovery from system failure

Aggregation of data or commands, re-use of already entered data, efficient navigation within a screen, distinct views with consistent operations, comprehensive searching and multiple simultaneous activities
Display of system state and pacing to the user
Customizability and internationalization
questions.e: To support 'use system efficiently' the system offers aggregation of data and/or commands, re-use of already entered data and/or commands, support for efficient navigation within a screen, distinct views with consistent operations, comprehensive searching and multiple simultaneous activities.

questions.q: Which of the following is a usability response measure?
o: The probability of detecting an attack
The length of the longest dependency chain in a test
The ratio of successful operations to total operations
The time interval during which the system must be available
questions.e: Usability response measures are task time, number of errors, number of problems solved, user satisfaction, gain of user knowledge, ratio of successful operations to total operations, and amount of time or data lost.

questions.q: 'A user, wanting to minimize the impact of an error, wishes to cancel a system operation at runtime; cancellation takes place in less than one second.' Which attribute does this scenario address?
o: Performance
Modifiability
Usability
Availability
questions.e: This is the sample usability scenario: a user wanting to minimize the impact of an error cancels a system operation at runtime, with cancellation taking place in less than one second.

questions.q: Which of the following is a business quality?
o: Conceptual integrity
Testability
Buildability
Projected lifetime of the system
questions.e: The business qualities are time to market, cost and benefit, projected lifetime of the system, targeted market, rollout schedule, and integration with legacy systems.

questions.q: Which of the following is a business quality rather than a system or architectural quality?
o: Usability
Availability
Integration with legacy systems
Correctness and completeness
questions.e: Integration with legacy systems is a business quality, alongside time to market, cost and benefit, projected lifetime of the system, targeted market and rollout schedule.

questions.q: Conceptual integrity, as an architectural quality, is defined as:
o: the property that the system can be completed by the available team in a timely manner
the probability that the system is operational when needed
the underlying theme or vision that unifies the design of the system at all levels
the property that all requirements and resource constraints can be met
questions.e: Conceptual integrity is the underlying theme or vision that unifies the design of the system at all levels. The other architectural qualities are correctness and completeness, and buildability.

questions.q: The architectural quality 'correctness and completeness' means that the architecture:
o: allows the system to be completed by the available team in a timely manner
allows for all of the system's requirements and runtime resource constraints to be met
contains no design errors of any kind
unifies the design of the system at all levels
questions.e: Correctness and completeness allows for all of the system's requirements and runtime resource constraints to be met.

questions.q: The architectural quality 'buildability' means that the architecture:
o: makes the system easy for end users to learn
guarantees that all requirements can be met
allows the system to be completed by the available team in a timely manner and remains open to certain changes as development progresses
unifies the design at all levels under a single vision
questions.e: Buildability allows the system to be completed by the available team in a timely manner; it also enables the system to be open to certain changes as development progresses.

questions.q: A tactic is defined as:
o: a notation for documenting an architecture
a measurable requirement for a quality attribute
a design decision that influences the control of a quality attribute response
a complete architectural pattern
questions.e: A tactic is a design decision that influences the control of a quality attribute response; a collection of tactics is called an architectural strategy.

questions.q: A collection of tactics is called:
o: an architectural strategy
a quality attribute scenario
an architectural style
an architectural pattern
questions.e: A collection of tactics is called an architectural strategy. Each tactic is a design option for the architect.

questions.q: How can tactics influence one another, and how do they relate to patterns?
o: Tactics can refine other tactics, and patterns package tactics
Tactics are independent of each other and of patterns
Tactics can replace other tactics, and tactics package patterns
Patterns refine tactics, and tactics package styles
questions.e: The influences of tactics can be that tactics refine other tactics and that patterns package tactics; tactics are organised for each quality attribute as a hierarchy.

questions.q: Availability, defined as an aspect of dependability, refers to the ability of a system to:
o: detect every fault within a fixed time
operate without any faults ever occurring
recover instantly from any failure
mask or repair faults such that the cumulative service outage period does not exceed a required value over a specified time interval
questions.e: Availability refers to the ability of a system to mask or repair faults such that the cumulative service outage period does not exceed a required value over a specified time interval. This makes the concept of failure subject to the judgment of an external agent, possibly a human.

questions.q: Dependability is defined as the ability to:
o: measure the frequency of failures accurately
avoid failures that are more frequent and more severe than is acceptable
repair every fault before it becomes a failure
avoid all failures entirely
questions.e: Dependability is the ability to avoid failures that are more frequent and more severe than is acceptable. Availability builds upon the concept of reliability by adding the notion of recovery - when the system breaks, it repairs itself by various means.

questions.q: Availability is said to build upon the concept of reliability by adding:
o: the notion of integrity
the notion of recovery
the notion of performance
the notion of confidentiality
questions.e: Availability builds upon the concept of reliability by adding the notion of recovery: when the system breaks, it repairs itself by various means. The broad perspective of availability is often called reliability, although it may encompass additional considerations such as downtime due to periodic maintenance.

questions.q: A Service Level Agreement specifies:
o: the functional requirements the system must satisfy
the quality attribute scenarios to be tested
the tactics the architect must apply
the availability level that is guaranteed and usually the penalties if the agreement is violated
questions.e: The Service Level Agreement specifies the availability level that is guaranteed and, usually, the penalties that the computer system or hosting service will suffer if the SLA is violated.

questions.q: In the quoted cloud-service agreement, what annual uptime percentage is committed, and what is the remedy if it is not met?
o: At least 99.999 percent, with a full refund
At least 99.95 percent during the service year, with eligibility for a service credit
At least 99 percent, with contract termination
At least 99.5 percent, with free support
questions.e: The quoted agreement commits commercially reasonable efforts to make the service available with an annual uptime percentage of at least 99.95 percent during the service year; if that commitment is not met, the customer is eligible to receive a service credit.

questions.q: Availability tactics are said to involve which three things?
o: Redundancy, health monitoring to detect a failure, and recovery when a failure is detected
Record, playback and stubbing
Caching, concurrency and scheduling
Authentication, authorization and auditing
questions.e: Availability involves redundancy, health monitoring to detect a failure, and recovery when a failure is detected. Many of the tactics are available in standard execution environments such as operating systems, application servers, middleware packages, development platforms and database management systems.

questions.q: Availability tactics fall into which three major categories?
o: Fault isolation, fault masking and fault logging
Detection, correction and reporting
Monitoring, alerting and repairing
Fault detection, fault recovery and fault prevention
questions.e: The major categories are fault detection, fault recovery - which divides into preparation and repair, and reintroduction - and fault prevention.

questions.q: The ping/echo tactic refers to:
o: an asynchronous request/response message pair exchanged between nodes to determine reachability and round-trip delay
assigning the state of a local clock to an event immediately after it occurs
checking the validity or reasonableness of a component's outputs
a periodic one-way message emitted by one component and listened for by another
questions.e: Ping/echo refers to an asynchronous request/response message pair exchanged between nodes, used to determine reachability and the round-trip delay through the associated network path; one component issues a ping and expects to receive back an echo within a predefined time. Pings are often sent by a system monitor, and standard implementations exist for nodes interconnected via IP.

questions.q: The monitor tactic refers to a component that:
o: raises an exception when a timing constraint is missed
monitors the state of health of various other parts of the system, such as processors, processes, input/output and memory
runs a previously failed component alongside working ones
emits a periodic message that another component listens for
questions.e: A monitor is a component used to monitor the state of health of various other parts of the system: processors, processes, input/output, memory and so on. A system monitor can detect failure or congestion in the network or other shared resources, for example from a denial-of-service attack, and it orchestrates software using other detection tactics; it can initiate self-tests or detect faulty time stamps and missed heartbeats.

questions.q: The heartbeat tactic, also called a dead man timer, works by:
o: assigning a local clock value to each event as it occurs
two components exchanging a request/response pair to measure round-trip delay
placing a known data pattern after an object's variable-length parameters
one component emitting a message periodically while another component listens for it
questions.e: In the heartbeat tactic one component emits a heartbeat message periodically and another component listens for it; the heartbeat can also carry data.

questions.q: The time stamp tactic is used primarily to detect:
o: incorrect sequences of events in distributed message-passing systems
overwriting of memory allocated to an object's parameters
inconsistency among redundant components' outputs
unreachable nodes on a network
questions.e: The time stamp tactic is used to detect incorrect sequences of events, primarily in distributed message-passing systems; a time stamp can be established by assigning the state of a local clock to the event immediately after the event occurs. Simple sequence numbers can also be used if time information is not important.

questions.q: What may be used in place of time stamps when time information is not important?
o: Simple sequence numbers
Parameter fences
Checksums
Heartbeats
questions.e: Simple sequence numbers can also be used for detecting incorrect sequences of events, if time information is not important.

questions.q: The sanity checking tactic checks:
o: whether a component has exceeded its timing constraints
whether redundant components agree on their outputs
the validity or reasonableness of specific operations or outputs of a component, most often at interfaces
whether a node is reachable over the network
questions.e: Sanity checking checks the validity or reasonableness of specific operations or outputs of a component; it is typically based on knowledge of the internal design, the state of the system or the nature of the information under scrutiny, and is most often employed at interfaces to examine a specific information flow.

questions.q: Exception detection refers to the detection of a system condition that:
o: reduces the number of available components
changes the system's configuration
increases the system's resource consumption
alters the normal flow of execution
questions.e: Exception detection refers to the detection of a system condition that alters the normal flow of execution; the exception handler typically executes in the same process that introduced the exception.

questions.q: The parameter fence tactic works by:
o: computing a checksum over the component's state
using a base class that defines functions for type-length-value formatted parameters
placing an a priori data pattern immediately after any variable-length parameters of an object, allowing runtime detection of overwriting
raising an exception when a component misses its timing constraints
questions.e: The parameter fence tactic incorporates an a priori data pattern placed immediately after any variable-length parameters of an object; this allows runtime detection of overwriting the memory allocated for the object's variable-length parameters.

questions.q: The parameter typing tactic employs a base class that defines functions to add, find and iterate over parameters in which format?
o: Key-value pair formatted parameters
Comma-separated value formatted parameters
Type-length-value, or TLV, formatted message parameters
Fixed-width binary parameters
questions.e: Parameter typing employs a base class defining functions that add, find and iterate over type-length-value, or TLV, formatted message parameters; derived classes use those base class functions to provide parameter typing according to each parameter's structure. Strong typing to build and parse messages gives higher availability than treating messages as byte buckets.

questions.q: The timeout tactic raises an exception when:
o: a component's output fails a reasonableness check
a component detects that it or another component has failed to meet its timing constraints
a heartbeat message is not received
redundant components disagree on their outputs
questions.e: Timeout is a tactic that raises an exception when a component detects that it or another component has failed to meet its timing constraints; for example, a component awaiting a response from another can raise an exception if the wait time exceeds a certain value.

questions.q: The condition monitoring tactic involves checking conditions in a process or device, or validating assumptions made during the design. What constraint applies to the monitor itself?
o: The monitor must itself be simple, and ideally provable, to ensure it does not introduce new software errors
The monitor must run on separate hardware in all cases
The monitor must be as complex as the system it monitors
The monitor must be written in a different language
questions.e: Condition monitoring prevents a system from producing faulty behavior by monitoring conditions; the computation of checksums is a common example. However, the monitor must itself be simple, and ideally provable, to ensure that it does not introduce new software errors.

questions.q: The computation of checksums is a common example of which fault detection tactic?
o: Voting
Parameter typing
Sanity checking
Condition monitoring
questions.e: The computation of checksums is a common example of the condition monitoring tactic.

questions.q: The most common realization of the voting tactic is triple modular redundancy, in which:
o: three components do the same thing on identical inputs and forward their outputs to voting logic that detects inconsistency
three components each perform a different task and their results are combined
a primary component informs two standbys of state updates
three copies of the data are kept in different repositories
questions.e: Triple modular redundancy employs three components that do the same thing, each receiving identical inputs, forwarding their output to voting logic used to detect any inconsistency among the three output states. Faced with an inconsistency the voter reports a fault and must also decide what output to use: it can let the majority rule or choose some computed average of the disparate outputs.

questions.q: When the voter in a triple modular redundancy scheme detects an inconsistency, how may it decide what output to use?
o: It must always discard all three outputs
It must always recompute the result itself
It must always select the first output received
It can let the majority rule, or choose some computed average of the disparate outputs
questions.e: Faced with an inconsistency the voter reports a fault; it must also decide what output to use, and it can let the majority rule or choose some computed average of the disparate outputs.

questions.q: Why is replication, the simplest form of voting, limited in what it can protect against?
o: Because the voter cannot compare identical outputs
Because the components must run on the same processor
Because only two components are used, a tie cannot be broken
Because the components are exact clones, there is no diversity, so it cannot protect against design or implementation errors
questions.e: Replication is the simplest form of voting; the components are exact clones of each other. Multiple identical copies can be effective against random hardware failures, but cannot protect against design or implementation errors in hardware or software, because there is no form of diversity embedded in the tactic.

questions.q: Functional redundancy is a form of voting intended to address which issue?
o: Specification errors in the requirements
Common-mode failures, that is design or implementation faults, in hardware or software components
Network congestion between nodes
Random hardware failures only
questions.e: Functional redundancy addresses common-mode failures - design or implementation faults - in hardware or software components: the components must always give the same output given the same input, but they are diversely designed and diversely implemented.

questions.q: Analytic redundancy differs from functional redundancy in that it:
o: applies only to hardware components
requires all components to share a single requirement specification
permits diversity among the components' inputs and outputs as well as their private sides, tolerating specification errors by using separate requirement specifications
requires components to be exact clones of one another
