questions.e: Analytic redundancy permits not only diversity among components' private sides but also diversity among the components' inputs and outputs; this tactic is intended to tolerate specification errors by using separate requirement specifications.

questions.q: In active redundancy, also called hot spare:
o: a standby platform is configured to replace many different failed components
one primary component responds and informs standbys of state updates
all redundant components respond to events in parallel and are therefore all in the same state, with the response from only one component used
a previously failed component runs in shadow mode before returning to service
questions.e: In active redundancy, or hot spare, all redundant components respond to events in parallel, so they are all in the same state; the response from only one component is used, usually the first to respond, and the rest are discarded. It is often used in client/server configurations such as database management systems where quick responses are necessary even when a fault occurs.

questions.q: In passive redundancy, also called warm spare, who is responsible for synchronization?
o: The system monitor
The voting logic
The primary component
Each standby component individually
questions.e: In passive redundancy, also called warm restart, dual redundancy or triple redundancy, one component - the primary - responds to events and informs the standbys of state updates they must make. When a fault occurs the system must first ensure the backup state is sufficiently fresh before resuming services. Synchronization is the responsibility of the primary component.

questions.q: In passive redundancy, how does forcing switchovers periodically, for example once a day or once a week, affect the system?
o: It decreases the availability of the system
It increases the availability of the system
It has no effect on availability
It eliminates the need for synchronization
questions.e: Forcing switchovers periodically - for example once a day or once a week - increases the availability of the system.

questions.q: The spare, or cold spare, tactic consists of:
o: all redundant components responding in parallel to every event
a primary component informing standbys of state updates
a component run in shadow mode before restoration
a standby spare computing platform configured to replace many different failed components
questions.e: In the spare, or cold spare, tactic a standby spare computing platform is configured to replace many different failed components.

questions.q: Why is simply crashing a poor way to handle a detected exception?
o: It requires additional hardware
It takes longer than any alternative
It prevents the exception from being logged
It is terrible from the point of view of availability, usability, testability and plain good sense
questions.e: Once an exception has been detected the system must handle it in some fashion; the easiest thing it can do is simply to crash, but that is a terrible idea from the point of availability, usability, testability and plain good sense. There are much more productive possibilities.

questions.q: Exception handling mechanisms range from simple function return codes to exception classes containing information such as:
o: the identity of the user who triggered it and their permissions
the name of the exception thrown, the origin of the exception, and the cause of the exception
the number of redundant components still available
the checksum of the affected memory region
questions.e: The mechanism employed depends largely on the programming environment, ranging from simple function return codes - error codes - to exception classes containing information helpful in fault correlation, such as the name of the exception thrown, the origin of the exception, and the cause of the exception thrown. Software can then use this information to mask the fault, usually by correcting the cause and retrying the operation.

questions.q: The rollback tactic permits the system to revert to a previous known good state, referred to as:
o: the recovery point
the checkpoint line
the shadow state
the rollback line
questions.e: Rollback permits the system to revert to a previous known good state, referred to as the rollback line, upon the detection of a failure; once the good state is reached, execution can continue.

questions.q: Rollback depends on the availability of what, and how may it be stored?
o: A full system image, stored only at system startup
A parameter fence, placed after each object
A heartbeat message, retained by the monitor
A checkpoint, a copy of a previous good state, stored in a fixed location and updated at regular intervals or at significant times in the processing
questions.e: Rollback depends on a copy of a previous good state - a checkpoint - being available to the components that are rolling back. Checkpoints can be stored in a fixed location and updated at regular intervals, or at convenient or significant times in the processing such as at the completion of a complex operation.

questions.q: Rollback is often combined with which other tactics?
o: Removal from service and transactions, so that failures are prevented
Active or passive redundancy, so that after a rollback a standby version of the failed component is promoted to active status
Sanity checking and parameter typing, so that the state is validated
Ping/echo and heartbeat, so that the failure is detected sooner
questions.e: Rollback is often combined with active or passive redundancy tactics so that after a rollback has occurred, a standby version of the failed component is promoted to active status.

questions.q: The goal of the software upgrade tactic is to:
o: detect faults introduced by a previous upgrade
achieve in-service upgrades to executable code images in a non-service-affecting manner
replace the entire system during a scheduled outage
roll back to a previous version of the software
questions.e: The goal of the software upgrade tactic is to achieve in-service upgrades to executable code images in a non-service-affecting manner; it may be realized as a function patch, a class patch, or a hitless in-service software upgrade.

questions.q: Which realizations of the software upgrade tactic are used to deliver bug fixes, and which delivers new features and capabilities?
o: The hitless in-service software upgrade delivers bug fixes, while function and class patches deliver new features
All three deliver only new features
Function patch and class patch deliver bug fixes, while the hitless in-service software upgrade delivers new features and capabilities
All three deliver only bug fixes
questions.e: In practice the function patch and class patch are used to deliver bug fixes, while the hitless in-service software upgrade is used to deliver new features and capabilities.

questions.q: The function patch tactic is used in procedural programming and employs:
o: an incremental linker/loader to store an updated software function into a pre-allocated segment of target memory
a redundant processor running the new version
a complete reload of the executable image
a class definition that includes a version identifier
questions.e: A function patch employs an incremental linker/loader to store an updated software function into a pre-allocated segment of target memory; the new version employs the entry and exit points of the deprecated function, and upon loading it the symbol table must be updated and the instruction cache invalidated.

questions.q: After loading a new software function via a function patch, which two housekeeping actions are required?
o: The checkpoint must be refreshed and the heartbeat restarted
The data cache must be flushed and the stack unwound
The symbol table must be updated and the instruction cache invalidated
The voter must be reset and the spare promoted
questions.e: Upon loading the new software function, the symbol table must be updated and the instruction cache invalidated.

questions.q: The shadow operation tactic involves:
o: upgrading a component's state before its return to service
running a previously failed component in shadow mode for a short time to make sure it mimics the behavior of the working components before restoring it to service
recording a consistent state periodically or in response to specific events
running a redundant component in parallel and discarding its output permanently
questions.e: Shadow operation is a reintroduction tactic: a previously failed component may be run in shadow mode for a short time to make sure it mimics the behavior of the working components before restoring it to service.

questions.q: The state resynchronization reintroduction tactic is required because:
o: the voter cannot compare states of differing ages
checkpoints cannot be stored for redundant components
the monitor cannot detect stale state
the passive and active redundancy tactics require the component being restored to have its state upgraded before its return to service
questions.e: State resynchronization is needed because the passive and active redundancy tactics require the component being restored to have its state upgraded before its return to service.

questions.q: A checkpoint, in the checkpoint/rollback reintroduction tactic, is:
o: a message emitted periodically by one component and heard by another
an asynchronous request/response pair between nodes
a recording of a consistent state created either periodically or in response to specific events
a data pattern placed after an object's variable-length parameters
questions.e: A checkpoint is a recording of a consistent state created either periodically or in response to specific events.

questions.q: The removal from service fault prevention tactic works by:
o: removing a component from operation to undergo activities that prevent anticipated failures, such as rebooting to prevent memory leaks from causing a failure
monitoring a component's conditions to detect faults
permanently deleting a faulty component from the system
promoting a standby component to active status
questions.e: Removal from service removes a component of the system from operation to undergo some activities to prevent anticipated failures; one example is rebooting a component to prevent memory leaks from causing a failure.

questions.q: The transactions fault prevention tactic defines a transaction as:
o: a checkpoint recorded at the completion of a complex operation
the bundling of several sequential steps such that the entire bundle can be undone at once
a message exchange between a client and a server
a single atomic read or write of shared data
questions.e: A transaction is the bundling of several sequential steps such that the entire bundle can be undone at once.

questions.q: The process monitor fault prevention tactic works by:
o: removing a component from service for preventive maintenance
monitoring the conditions of a device to detect faults early
deleting a faulty process and creating a new instance of it, initialized to some appropriate state
bundling steps so that they can be undone at once
questions.e: A monitoring process can delete the faulty process and create a new instance of it, initialized to some appropriate state.

questions.q: The main goal of modifiability tactics is controlling:
o: the probability of detecting an attack
the response time of the system under load
the time and cost to implement, test and deploy changes
the number of modules in the architecture
questions.e: Modifiability's main goal is controlling the time and cost to implement, test and deploy changes.

questions.q: Modifiability tactics are organised into which three groups?
o: Resist, detect and recover
Localize modifications, prevent the ripple effect and defer binding time
Detect, recover and prevent
Input/output and internal monitoring
questions.e: The modifiability tactics are organised into three groups: localize modifications, prevent the ripple effect, and defer binding time.

questions.q: Semantic coherence refers to:
o: the agreement between a module's documentation and its code
the consistency of naming conventions across modules
the degree to which a module's interface matches its implementation
the relationships among responsibilities in a module, with the goal that all responsibilities work together without excessive reliance on other modules
questions.e: Semantic coherence refers to the relationships among responsibilities in a module; the goal is to ensure that all of these responsibilities work together without excessive reliance on other modules. One way of achieving or measuring this is coupling and cohesion, but they lack the context of a change.

questions.q: Why are coupling and cohesion said to be insufficient for measuring semantic coherence?
o: They measure performance rather than modifiability
They lack the context of a change, so semantic coherence should be measured against a set of anticipated changes
They cannot be computed for object-oriented systems
They apply only at the architectural level
questions.e: One way of achieving or measuring semantic coherence is coupling and cohesion, but they lack the context of a change; semantic coherence should be measured against a set of anticipated changes.

questions.q: Within semantic coherence, abstracting common services means to:
o: provide them through specialised modules
remove them from the architecture
duplicate them in each module that needs them
move them into the client code
questions.e: Within maintaining semantic coherence, one abstracts common services and provides them through specialised modules; this also includes the use of application frameworks and other middleware software.

questions.q: The 'anticipate expected changes' tactic is concerned with:
o: measuring the cost of changes already made
minimizing the effects of the changes, and is normally used in conjunction with semantic coherence
eliminating the need for any future changes
predicting the exact date each change will be requested
questions.e: The tactic of anticipating expected changes is concerned with minimizing the effects of the changes; it is normally used in conjunction with semantic coherence.

questions.q: The 'limit possible options' tactic reduces the effect of modifications by, for example:
o: restricting modifications to a single developer
restricting the system to a single module
restricting the number of users who may request changes
restricting processor changes to members of the same family
questions.e: Restricting the possible options will reduce the effect of modifications; restricting processor changes to members of the same family limits the possible options.

questions.q: The 'generalise the module' tactic works because:
o: a general module has no dependencies on other modules
a general module contains fewer lines of code
a general module can compute a broader range of functions based on input, so the requested change can be made by adjusting the input language rather than the module
a general module can be replaced at runtime
questions.e: A general module can compute a broader range of functions based on input; the input can be treated as a processing language for the module, so the requested change can be made by adjusting the input language rather than the module.

questions.q: Why is deferring binding time needed in addition to localizing modifications and preventing the ripple effect?
o: Those two techniques cannot localize changes at all
Those two techniques increase coupling
Those two techniques apply only to hardware
Those two techniques cannot reduce the time to deploy, and support for changes by non-developers is also required
questions.e: With the previous two techniques one cannot reduce the time to deploy; support to make changes by non-developers is also required. Late binding can support both features, and two kinds of binding are important: deployment time bindings and run-time bindings.

questions.q: Which two kinds of binding are identified as important for deferring binding time?
o: Design time bindings and build time bindings
Static bindings and dynamic bindings
Deployment time bindings and run-time bindings
Compile time bindings and link time bindings
questions.e: Two kinds of binding are important: deployment time bindings and run-time bindings.

questions.q: What advantage does runtime binding give over the developer's normal modification process?
o: It guarantees that changes cannot introduce faults
It removes the need for testing the changes
It removes the time lag between making changes and their availability to the user, because the end user or administrator can make the changes and see them immediately
It allows changes to be made without any system preparation
questions.e: Developers' modifications follow a process of changes, testing and distribution, which incurs a time lag between making the changes and when they become available to the user. In runtime binding the system is prepared for that binding, so the end user or administrator can make the changes and the changes are visible.

questions.q: The runtime registration tactic supports plug-and-play operation at what cost?
o: Loss of polymorphic dispatch
Additional overhead to manage the registration
A requirement for a new compiler
Loss of the ability to change configuration files
questions.e: Runtime registration supports plug-and-play operation, with the additional overhead of managing the registration; publish/subscribe registration, for example, can be implemented at either runtime or load time.

questions.q: Publish/subscribe registration can be implemented at which times?
o: Only at compile time
Only at design time
Only at build time
Either runtime or load time
questions.e: Publish/subscribe registration can be implemented at either runtime or load time.

questions.q: The configuration files tactic works by:
o: recompiling the system with new switches
replacing components at load time
allowing late binding of method calls
setting parameters at startup, as in an Apache server configuration file
questions.e: Configuration files set parameters at startup, for example an Apache server configuration file.

questions.q: Which modifiability tactic allows late binding of method calls?
o: Configuration files
Component replacement
Polymorphism
Runtime registration
questions.e: Polymorphism allows late binding of method calls; component replacement is load time binding, and adherence to defined protocols gives runtime binding of independent processes.

questions.q: Component replacement, as a binding tactic, is categorised as:
o: compile time binding
design time binding
runtime registration
load time binding
questions.e: Component replacement is a form of load time binding.

questions.q: Adherence to defined protocols provides which kind of binding?
o: Load time binding of components
Design time binding of modules
Compile time binding of libraries
Runtime binding of independent processes
questions.e: Adherence to defined protocols gives runtime binding of independent processes.

questions.q: Security tactics are organised around which three aspects?
o: Prevention, detection and prosecution
Authentication, authorization and auditing
Confidentiality, integrity and availability
Resisting attacks, detecting attacks and recovering from attacks
questions.e: The three aspects of security are resisting attacks, detecting attacks and recovering from attacks.

questions.q: Which goals are identified in the security characterization?
o: Authentication, authorization, accounting and auditing
Nonrepudiation, confidentiality, integrity and assurance
Availability, reliability, safety and maintainability
Prevention, detection, response and recovery
questions.e: Nonrepudiation, confidentiality, integrity and assurance are the goals in the security characterization.

questions.q: Authentication is defined as:
o: ensuring that data is delivered as intended
ensuring that an authenticated user has the rights to access or modify data or services
ensuring that a user or remote computer is actually who it purports to be
ensuring that limited services are available on each host
questions.e: Authentication is ensuring that a user or remote computer is actually who it purports to be; passwords, one-time passwords, digital certificates and biometric identifications provide authentication.

questions.q: Which mechanisms provide authentication?
o: Virtual private networks and SSL
Checksums and hash results
Passwords, one-time passwords, digital certificates and biometric identifications
Firewalls and service allocation
questions.e: Passwords, one-time passwords, digital certificates and biometric identifications provide authentication. Checksums and hashes maintain integrity, while VPN, SSL and encryption keys maintain data confidentiality.

questions.q: Authorizing users means:
o: ensuring that an authenticated user has the rights to access and modify either data or services
encrypting data and communication links
ensuring that a user is who they claim to be
detecting intrusions by comparing traffic patterns
questions.e: Authorizing users means ensuring that an authenticated user has the rights to access and modify either data or services; access control patterns are mentioned in this connection.

questions.q: Maintaining data confidentiality is achieved through:
o: encryption of data and communication links, using mechanisms such as VPN, SSL and encryption keys
allocation of services to hosts and firewalls
maintaining an audit trail
checksums and hash results
questions.e: Maintaining data confidentiality is achieved by encryption of data and communication links, with VPN, SSL and encryption keys given as mechanisms.

questions.q: Maintaining integrity means that data should be delivered as intended, achieved using:
o: checksums or hash results
audit trails and redundant copies
encryption keys and SSL
firewalls and service allocation
questions.e: Maintaining integrity means data should be delivered as intended; checksums or hash results are the mechanisms given.

questions.q: The 'limit exposure and access' tactic responds to which observation about attacks?
o: Attacks always target the user interface first
Attacks always originate from external, unauthenticated sources
Attacks typically depend on exploiting a single weakness to attack all data and services on a host
Attacks are only possible when data is unencrypted
questions.e: Attacks typically depend on exploiting a single weakness to attack all data and services on a host, so the tactic is to allocate services to hosts such that limited services are available on each host, and to use firewalls to limit access.

questions.q: An intrusion detection system detects attacks by:
o: authenticating every remote computer
maintaining redundant copies of administrative data
comparing network traffic patterns to a database
encrypting all inbound traffic
questions.e: An intrusion detection system works by comparing network traffic patterns to a database.

questions.q: Which component should an intrusion detector have?
o: A control console so that the analyst can modify intrusion detection actions
A rollback line for reverting to a known good state
A voting component to resolve inconsistencies
An encryption key store for confidential data
questions.e: Intrusion detectors should have some sensor to detect attacks, managers to do sensor fusion, databases for storing events for later analysis, tools for offline reporting and analysis, and a control console so that the analyst can modify intrusion detection actions.

questions.q: In an intrusion detector, what is the role of the managers?
o: To generate offline reports
To do sensor fusion
To store events for later analysis
To modify detection actions
questions.e: Intrusion detectors should have sensors to detect attacks, managers to do sensor fusion, databases for storing events for later analysis, tools for offline reporting and analysis, and a control console.

questions.q: Tactics for recovering from attacks are related to which two concerns?
o: Monitoring conditions, and raising exceptions
Encrypting data, and authenticating users
Detecting intrusions, and limiting exposure
Restoring state, and attacker identification for either preventive or punitive purposes
questions.e: The tactics for recovering from attacks relate to restoring state and to attacker identification, for either preventive or punitive purposes.

questions.q: The security tactic for restoring state overlaps with which other quality attribute's tactics?
o: Testability
Performance
Availability
Modifiability
questions.e: Tactics for restoring state overlap with those of availability; they include maintaining redundant copies of system administrative data such as passwords, access control lists, domain name services and user profile data.

questions.q: Which data is kept in redundant copies as part of restoring state after an attack?
o: Performance metrics and latency measurements
System administrative data such as passwords, access control lists, domain name services and user profile data
Network traffic captures and intrusion signatures
Application source code and build artifacts
questions.e: Restoring state includes maintaining redundant copies of system administrative data such as passwords, access control lists, domain name services and user profile data.

questions.q: The tactic for identifying an attacker is to:
o: require biometric authentication for all users
maintain an audit trail, keeping a copy of each transaction applied to the data together with identifying information
encrypt all inbound and outbound traffic
allocate services across multiple hosts
questions.e: The tactic for identifying an attacker is to maintain an audit trail: maintain a copy of each transaction applied to the data in the system together with identifying information.

questions.q: Maintaining an audit trail helps with which three things?
o: Tracking the actions of an attacker, non-repudiation and system recovery
Fault detection, fault recovery and fault prevention
Encryption, authentication and authorization
Latency reduction, throughput improvement and load balancing
questions.e: An audit trail helps in tracking the actions of an attacker, non-repudiation and system recovery.

questions.q: Usability tactics fall into which two categories?
o: A detection category and a recovery category
A runtime category supporting the user during system execution, and a design category supporting the interface developer at design time
A localize category and a defer binding category
An input/output category and an internal monitoring category
questions.e: The two categories of usability tactics are the runtime category, which supports the user during system execution, and the design category, which is based on the iterative nature of user interface design and supports the interface developer at design time. The latter is strongly related to the modifiability tactics.

questions.q: The design category of usability tactics is strongly related to which other tactics?
o: The availability tactics
The security tactics
The performance tactics
The modifiability tactics
questions.e: The design category of usability tactics is based on the iterative nature of user interface design and supports the interface developer at design time; it is strongly related to the modifiability tactics.

questions.q: Cancelling a command is said to demonstrate 'mixed initiative' because:
o: the system cancels on the user's behalf without being asked
neither the user nor the system has control of the interaction
both the user and the system issue the cancel simultaneously
the user issues the cancel, which is user initiative, while the system may put up a progress indicator, which is system initiative
questions.e: The three aspects of human-computer interaction are user initiative - the user issues the cancel - and system initiative - during the cancel the system may put up a progress indicator. Thus cancel demonstrates mixed initiative.

questions.q: The runtime usability tactic 'maintain a model of the task' is used to:
o: determine context, for example knowing that sentences usually start with capital letters so a lower-case letter in that position can be corrected
separate the user interface from the rest of the application
determine the expected system behavior so appropriate feedback can be given
determine the user's knowledge of the system and expected response time
questions.e: The task model is used to determine context; for example, knowing that sentences usually start with capital letters would allow an application to correct a lower-case letter in that position.

questions.q: The runtime usability tactic 'maintain a model of the user' determines:
o: the expected system behavior for feedback purposes
the user's knowledge of the system, the user's behavior in terms of expected response time, and other aspects specific to a user or class of users
the division of the interface from the application
the context in which an input occurs
questions.e: Maintaining a model of the user determines the user's knowledge of the system, the user's behavior in terms of expected response time, and other aspects specific to a user or a class of users; for example, it allows the system to pace scrolling so that pages do not fly past faster than they can be read.

questions.q: Pacing scrolling so that pages do not fly past faster than they can be read is an example of which usability tactic?
o: Maintain a model of the task
Separate the user interface from the application
Maintain a model of the user
Maintain a model of the system
questions.e: Maintaining a user model allows the system to pace scrolling so that pages do not fly past faster than they can be read.

questions.q: The runtime usability tactic 'maintain a model of the system' determines:
o: the expected system behavior so that appropriate feedback can be given to the user, such as the time needed to complete the current activity
the context in which a keystroke occurs
the user's expected response time
which parts of the interface are likely to change
questions.e: Maintaining a model of the system determines the expected system behavior so that appropriate feedback can be given to the user; for example, the time needed to complete the current activity.

questions.q: The design-time usability tactics are to separate the user interface from the rest of the application and to localize expected changes, using which patterns?
o: Model-View-Controller and Presentation-Abstraction-Control
Observer and Strategy
Broker and Microkernel
Layers and Pipes and Filters
questions.e: The design-time tactics are to separate the user interface from the rest of the application and to localize expected changes, using Model-View-Controller and Presentation-Abstraction-Control.

questions.q: The goal of performance tactics is to:
o: eliminate all blocking in the system
maximise the number of components that can run concurrently
minimise the total resources the system consumes
generate a response to an event arriving at the system within some time constraint
questions.e: The goal of performance tactics is to generate a response to an event arriving at the system within some time constraint; the event can be single or a stream and is the trigger for a request to perform computation.

questions.q: Which of the following can be the triggering event for a performance request?
o: The completion of a development phase
A developer's wish to modify functionality
An attempt to access protected data
The arrival of a message, the expiration of a time interval, or the detection of a significant change of state in the system's environment
questions.e: The event triggering a request to perform computation can be the arrival of a message, the expiration of a time interval, or the detection of a significant change of state in the system's environment.

questions.q: Each phase of processing an event contributes to:
o: the overall latency of the processing of that event
the jitter in the response
the throughput of the whole system
the blocked time of the computation
questions.e: An event goes through various steps of processing, each consuming some sort of resource such as CPU, bandwidth or an entity; each phase contributes to the overall latency of the processing of that event.

questions.q: In the described processing path, what is the term the Object Management Group uses for the transformation of a message after it is placed in a buffer?
o: Marshalling
Packing
Encoding
Serialization
questions.e: A message is generated by one component, placed on the network, arrives at another component, is placed in a buffer, and is transformed in some fashion - marshalling is the term the Object Management Group uses for this transformation - processed according to some algorithm, transformed for output, placed in an output buffer, and sent onward.

questions.q: A computation can be blocked from using a resource for which reasons?
o: Only the expiration of a time interval
Contention for the resource, the resource being unavailable, or dependence on the result of another computation not yet available
Only contention for the resource
Only unavailability of the resource
questions.e: A computation can be blocked from using a resource because of contention for it, because the resource is unavailable, or because the computation depends on the result of other computation which is not yet available.

questions.q: Event streams are the source of demand. Which two characteristics of that demand matter?
o: The number of components and the number of threads
How often a request is made in a stream, and how much of a resource is consumed by each request
The latency and the jitter
The queue size and the execution time bound
questions.e: Event streams are the source of demand: how often a request is made in a stream, and how much of a resource is consumed by each request.

questions.q: Under 'control resource demand', which two approaches reduce the resource required?
o: Managing the sampling rate and limiting the event response
Bounding execution times and bounding queue sizes
Increasing computational efficiency and reducing computational overhead
Introducing concurrency and maintaining multiple copies
questions.e: To reduce the resource required one increases computational efficiency, improving algorithms to decrease latency, and reduces computational overhead - no request for a resource means less processing needed, for example using Java classes instead of RMI, or removing an intermediary to reduce the processing of an event.

questions.q: Using Java classes instead of remote method invocation is an example of:
o: reducing computational overhead
introducing concurrency
increasing computational efficiency
managing the sampling rate
questions.e: Reducing computational overhead is illustrated by using Java classes instead of RMI and by removing an intermediary to reduce the processing of an event.

questions.q: Under 'control resource demand', which two approaches reduce the number of events processed?
o: Introducing concurrency and increasing available resources
Scheduling resources and assigning priorities
Managing the sampling rate and limiting the event response
Increasing computational efficiency and reducing overhead
questions.e: To reduce the number of events processed one manages the sampling rate, reducing the sampling frequency at which certain variables are monitored with some loss of detail, and limits the event response, so that queued requests can be sampled at a predefined rate. Other ways are to bound execution times and bound queue sizes.

questions.q: Managing the sampling rate reduces the number of events processed at what cost?
o: Increased blocked time
Greater contention for resources
Some loss of detail
Loss of concurrency
questions.e: Managing the sampling rate reduces the sampling frequency at which certain variables are being monitored, with some loss of details.

questions.q: Besides managing the sampling rate and limiting the event response, which other ways of controlling resource demand are given?
o: Separating interface from implementation
Bounding execution times and bounding queue sizes
Introducing concurrency and caching
Scheduling resources and assigning priorities
questions.e: The other ways given are to bound execution times and bound queue sizes.

questions.q: Under resource management, introducing concurrency achieves what?
o: Replicating data in different repositories
Processing requests in parallel to reduce blocked time, by processing streams of events on different threads
Reducing the number of events that must be processed
Avoiding contention by scheduling resources
questions.e: Introducing concurrency means processing requests in parallel to reduce blocked time, processing streams of events on different threads.

questions.q: Caching is described as a tactic in which:
o: requests are processed in parallel on different threads
data is replicated in different repositories, which reduces contention
resources are scheduled to avoid contention
the sampling rate of monitored variables is reduced
questions.e: Maintaining multiple copies of data and computation covers maintaining multiple copies of either data or computations; caching is a tactic in which data is replicated in different repositories, which reduces contention. Consistency and synchronisation of data is an issue, besides the requirement for load balancing.

questions.q: What issues accompany maintaining multiple copies of data?
o: Loss of concurrency and increased blocked time
Increased jitter and miss rate
Consistency and synchronisation of data, besides the requirement for load balancing
Reduced computational efficiency
questions.e: Consistency and synchronisation of data is an issue when maintaining multiple copies, besides the requirement for load balancing.

questions.q: The purpose of resource arbitration is to:
o: reduce the number of events the system must process
schedule resources to avoid contention for a resource
replicate data across repositories
increase the resources available to the system
questions.e: Resource arbitration schedules resources to avoid contention for a resource.

questions.q: A scheduling policy has which two parts?
o: A latency target and a throughput target
A sampling rate and a response limit
A queue size and an execution time bound
A priority assignment and dispatching
questions.e: A scheduling policy has two parts: a priority assignment and dispatching.

questions.q: Which of the following is a scheduling policy named among the resource arbitration tactics?
o: Dynamic priority scheduling
Least-recently-used replacement
Round-robin load balancing
Shortest-path routing
questions.e: The scheduling policies named are first-in/first-out, fixed-priority scheduling, dynamic priority scheduling and static scheduling.

questions.q: The goal of testability tactics is to:
o: reduce the number of test cases required
guarantee that the software contains no faults
automate the generation of test data
allow for easier testing when an increment of software development is completed
questions.e: The goal of tactics for testability is to allow for easier testing when an increment of software development is completed.

questions.q: Why is architectural attention to testability worthwhile despite receiving less attention than other fields?
o: Because testing consumes such a high percentage of system development cost that anything the architect can do to reduce it yields significant benefit
Because testability is the only quality attribute that can be measured
Because testability determines the system's performance
Because testability is required by all standards
questions.e: Architectural techniques for enhancing software testability have not received as much attention as more mature fields such as modifiability, performance and availability, but since testing consumes such a high percentage of system development cost, anything the architect can do to reduce this cost will yield a significant benefit.

questions.q: Testability tactics fall into which two major categories?
o: Unit testing and integration testing
Detection and recovery
Static analysis and dynamic analysis
Input/output, that is providing input and capturing output, and internal monitoring
questions.e: The two major categories of tactics for testing are input/output - providing input and capturing output - and internal monitoring.

questions.q: How many tactics are there for managing input and output for testing?
o: Two
Four
Three
Five
questions.e: There are three tactics for managing input and output for testing: record/playback, separate interface from implementation, and specialize access routes or interfaces.

questions.q: The record/playback tactic refers to:
o: replaying a recorded session to demonstrate a defect to a user
recording the state of a component for later rollback
capturing performance metrics for later analysis
capturing information crossing an interface and using it as input into the test harness
questions.e: Record/playback refers to both capturing information crossing an interface and using it as input into the test harness; information crossing an interface during normal operation is saved in some repository and represents output from one component and input to another. Recording it allows test input for one component to be generated and test output to be saved for later comparison.

questions.q: Separating the interface from the implementation, as a testability tactic, allows:
o: the capture of information crossing an interface for replay
the component to maintain state accessible through an interface
the scheduling of resources to avoid contention
substitution of implementations for various testing purposes, including stubbing and substituting a specialized component as a test harness
questions.e: Separating the interface from the implementation allows substitution of implementations for various testing purposes: stubbing implementations allows the remainder of the system to be tested in the absence of the component being stubbed, and substituting a specialized component allows the replaced component to act as a test harness for the remainder of the system.

questions.q: Stubbing an implementation allows:
o: the system's performance to be measured under load
the remainder of the system to be tested in the absence of the component being stubbed
the stubbed component to be tested in isolation
the capture of information crossing the stubbed interface
questions.e: Stubbing implementations allows the remainder of the system to be tested in the absence of the component being stubbed.

questions.q: The specialize access routes or interfaces tactic allows:
o: the substitution of alternative implementations at runtime
the component to record events when monitoring states are activated
the recording of information crossing an interface for later replay
the capturing or specification of variable values for a component through a test harness, independently of its normal execution
questions.e: Having specialized testing interfaces allows the capturing or specification of variable values for a component through a test harness as well as independently from its normal execution; for example, metadata might be made available through a specialized interface that a test harness would use to drive its activities.

questions.q: What rule applies to specialized access routes and interfaces?
o: They should be removed before the system is deployed
They should be kept separate from the access routes and interfaces for required functionality
They should be identical to the production interfaces
They should replace the access routes used for required functionality
questions.e: Specialized access routes and interfaces should be kept separate from the access routes and interfaces for required functionality.

questions.q: What is the benefit of having a hierarchy of test interfaces in the architecture?
o: The system's performance improves under test
The number of test cases is reduced
Test cases can be applied at any level in the architecture, and the testing functionality is in place to observe the response
Test interfaces can be removed before deployment without effort
questions.e: Having a hierarchy of test interfaces in the architecture means that test cases can be applied at any level in the architecture and that the testing functionality is in place to observe the response.

questions.q: The built-in monitors tactic allows a component to maintain which information, accessible through an interface?
o: Only performance metrics
Only security audit records
Only its current state
State, performance load, capacity, security or other information
questions.e: With built-in monitors the component can maintain state, performance load, capacity, security or other information accessible through an interface; a common technique is to record events when monitoring states have been activated.

questions.q: What drawback accompanies the built-in monitors tactic, and how is it judged?
o: Monitoring states cannot be switched off at all
Monitoring states can increase the testing effort since tests may have to be repeated with monitoring off, but the increased visibility usually more than outweighs the cost
Monitoring states prevent the use of a test harness
Monitoring states slow the system permanently, which outweighs any benefit
questions.e: Monitoring states can actually increase the testing effort since tests may have to be repeated with the monitoring turned off; however, the increased visibility into the activities of the component usually more than outweighs the cost of the additional testing.

questions.q: What is the relationship between tactics and patterns?
o: Tactics and patterns are interchangeable terms
Tactics replace patterns in modern architecture practice
A pattern acts as a building block from which tactics are created
A tactic acts as a foundational building block of design, from which architectural patterns and strategies are created
questions.e: A tactic acts as a foundational building block of design, from which architectural patterns and strategies are created. An architect usually chooses a pattern or collection of patterns designed to realize one or more tactics.

questions.q: When an architect chooses a pattern to realize particular tactics, what follows?
o: The pattern implements exactly the tactics chosen and no others
The pattern implements no tactics until configured
The pattern must be modified to implement any tactic
Each pattern implements multiple tactics, whether desired or not, often concerned with different quality attributes
questions.e: An architect usually chooses a pattern or a collection of patterns designed to realize one or more tactics; however, each pattern implements multiple tactics, whether desired or not. Any pattern implements several tactics, often concerned with different quality attributes, and any implementation of the pattern also makes choices about tactics.

questions.q: Maintaining a log of requests to an active object could serve which purposes simultaneously?
o: Authenticating, authorizing and encrypting
Reducing latency, increasing throughput and lowering jitter
Localizing modifications, preventing ripple effects and deferring binding
Supporting recovery, maintaining an audit trail, and supporting testability
questions.e: This is the example given of a pattern implementing several tactics concerned with different quality attributes: an implementation could maintain a log of requests to the active object for supporting recovery, maintaining an audit trail, or supporting testability.

questions.q: Refactoring is defined as a disciplined technique for restructuring an existing body of code:
o: altering its external behavior without changing its internal structure
adding new functionality while preserving performance
altering its internal structure without changing its external behavior
converting it to a different programming language
questions.e: Refactoring is a disciplined technique for restructuring an existing body of code, altering its internal structure without changing its external behavior.

questions.q: What is refactoring's relationship to bugs?
o: It introduces bugs that must then be fixed by testing
It has no relationship to bugs whatsoever
It fixes bugs as a direct consequence of restructuring
It does not fix bugs, but it may help find bugs by scrutinizing code and may reduce the further introduction of bugs by cleaning up code
questions.e: Refactoring does not fix bugs, but it may help find bugs by scrutinizing code; it may also reduce the further introduction of bugs by cleaning up code.

questions.q: What is refactoring's relationship to new functionality?
o: It prevents new functionality from being added
It replaces the need to add new functionality
It adds new functionality as a side effect of restructuring
It does not add new functionality, but it will ease the further adding of new functionality
questions.e: Refactoring does not add new functionality to the system, but it will ease the further adding of new functionality.

questions.q: Refactoring is described as an essential part of which development approaches?
o: Agile software development such as Extreme Programming, and incremental development
Waterfall and V-model development
Formal methods and model checking
Big-bang integration and acceptance testing
questions.e: Refactoring is an essential part of agile software development such as Extreme Programming or incremental development, and ought to be done continuously as bad smells are encountered during programming.

questions.q: When should refactoring be done?
o: Only when a defect report requires it
Continuously, as bad smells are encountered during programming
Only during a dedicated maintenance phase
Only at the end of a project, before release
questions.e: Refactoring ought to be done continuously as bad smells are encountered during programming.

questions.q: Bad smells, also called anti-patterns, are defined as portions of design or code that are:
o: proven to contain defects
characterized as potentially confusing and identified as refactoring targets
written in an obsolete programming language
untested and undocumented
questions.e: Bad smells, or anti-patterns, are portions of design or code that are characterized as potentially confusing and identified as refactoring targets.

questions.q: Who first coined the term 'bad smells', and where?
o: Larry Constantine, in a paper on structured programming
Martin Fowler, in Kent Beck's Extreme Programming book
Joey Paquet, in a set of refactoring lecture notes
Kent Beck, in Martin Fowler's Refactoring book
questions.e: The term was first coined by Kent Beck in Martin Fowler's Refactoring book.

questions.q: A smell is said to be, by definition, something that is:
o: hidden deep in the code and found only by careful analysis
detectable only by automated tools
always an actual defect in the code
quick to spot, or sniffable, such as a method of more than a dozen lines
questions.e: A smell is by definition something that's quick to spot, or sniffable: a long method is a good example, since one need only look at the code of a method with more than a dozen lines.

questions.q: Which statement about smells and problems is correct?
o: Smells aren't inherently bad on their own; they are often an indicator of a problem rather than the problem itself
Smells are unrelated to problems in the code
Every smell indicates a definite problem that must be fixed
A smell is always the problem itself rather than an indicator
questions.e: Smells don't always indicate a problem - some long methods are just fine, and one has to look deeper to see whether there is an underlying problem. Smells aren't inherently bad on their own; they are often an indicator of a problem rather than the problem themselves.

questions.q: What makes a smell one of 'the best'?
o: It can be removed automatically by a tool
It is easy to spot and leads you to really interesting problems
It always corresponds to a serious defect
It appears in every class of the system
questions.e: The best smells are something that's easy to spot and leading you to really interesting problems; data classes - classes with all data and no behavior - illustrate this.

questions.q: A class with all data and no behavior is an example of:
o: a parallel inheritance hierarchy
a middleman passing calls to other classes
a lazy class with too little functionality
a data class, a good smell to look for
questions.e: Data classes - classes with all data and no behavior - are the kind of easily spotted smell that leads to interesting problems.

questions.q: Which of these is a reason to refactor, under the heading of improving quality?
o: Improving maintainability and extensibility, and improving sustainability of development
Eliminating the need for version control
Reducing the number of classes in the system
Improving the system's response time under load
questions.e: Refactoring is done to improve quality - improving design quality, maintainability and extensibility; to improve sustainability of development, since it requires proper testing and so improves testability and helps find bugs; and to improve productivity, by improving code readability and comprehensibility and simplifying code structure.

questions.q: Which reasons to refactor fall under improving productivity?
o: Improving design quality and maintainability
Improving extensibility and sustainability
Improving testability and helping to find bugs
Improving code readability and comprehensibility, and simplifying code structure
questions.e: Under improving productivity, refactoring improves code readability and comprehensibility and simplifies code structure.

questions.q: Each refactoring is implemented as a small behavior-preserving transformation. How is behavior preservation achieved?
o: Through pre- and post-transformation testing, in a test-refactor-test process
Through automatic verification by the compiler
Through formal proof of equivalence
Through code review by a second developer
questions.e: Each refactoring is implemented as a small behavior-preserving transformation; behavior preservation is achieved through pre- and post-transformation testing. The refactoring process is test-refactor-test.

questions.q: What is the cost overhead drawback of refactoring, and what mitigates it?
o: It requires a larger team, mitigated by outsourcing
It requires rewriting all documentation, mitigated by omitting documentation
It permanently slows the software, mitigated by later optimisation
It incurs extra cost in time, effort and resource allocation, mitigated by doing it sparingly on key issues and by using automated documentation, code browsing, refactoring and testing tools
questions.e: Refactoring is an add-on activity and will incur extra cost in the form of time, effort and resource allocation, especially if elaborate design and code documentation is maintained. However, when done sparingly and only on key issues its benefits are greater than its overhead, and automated documentation tools, code browsing tools, refactoring tools and testing tools diminish the overhead.

questions.q: What is the expertise drawback of refactoring, and what mitigates it?
o: It requires expertise, experience and considerable effort, especially if proper testing is involved, minimized by using refactoring tools and automated testing such as a unit testing framework
It requires formal training in mathematics, minimized by hiring consultants
It requires knowledge of multiple languages, minimized by standardising on one
It requires architectural authority, minimized by delegation
questions.e: Refactoring requires some expertise and experience and considerable effort in going through the process, especially if proper testing is involved; however, this overhead can be minimized by using refactoring tools and automated testing such as with a unit testing framework.

questions.q: Which statement about refactoring in practice is correct?
o: Refactorings are only valid in waterfall development
All published refactorings improve code quality unconditionally
Some refactorings are controversial and some can be counter-productive when applied blindly, especially in iterative development where design is evolving
Refactorings should always be applied blindly for consistency
questions.e: Some refactorings are controversial; some are arguably not improving code quality; and some can be counter-productive when applied blindly, especially in iterative development where design is evolving. A team should adopt a set of refactorings to be applied and ensure they are applied in a productive manner.

questions.q: What is recommended regarding a team's use of refactorings?
o: Forbid refactoring except during a maintenance phase
Apply every published refactoring at least once
Let each developer choose their own refactorings freely
Have the team adopt a set of refactorings to be applied, applied in a productive manner and in combination with design patterns
questions.e: The guidance is to have your team adopt a set of refactorings to be applied and make sure they are applied in a productive manner, to apply them in combination with the application of design patterns, and to use refactoring tools to automate changes, for example Eclipse refactoring and the JUnit testing framework.

questions.q: In iterative development, when should a major refactoring stage take place?
o: After the new build has been released
In parallel with the addition of new functionality
Preceding the beginning of the development of a new build, to remove slight design problems and ease the addition of further functionality
Only at the very end of the project
questions.e: When using iterative development a major refactoring stage should precede the beginning of the development of a new build; this removes slight design problems and eases the addition of further functionality. Refactoring counterbalances the productivity-driven software development practices implied by agile incremental development.

questions.q: Refactoring is said to counterbalance which pressure?
o: The quality-driven practices implied by formal methods
The cost pressure implied by fixed-price contracts
The productivity-driven software development practices implied by agile incremental development
The documentation burden implied by regulated industries
questions.e: Refactoring counterbalances the productivity-driven software development practices implied by agile incremental software development.

questions.q: The Mysterious Name smell concerns the fact that:
o: names should be as short as possible to reduce typing
one of the most important parts of clear code is good names, and a good name can save hours of puzzled incomprehension in the future
names should be chosen by a naming committee
names should encode the type of the variable
questions.e: One of the most important parts of clear code is good names, so a lot of thought goes into naming functions, modules, variables and classes so they clearly communicate what they do and how to use them; a good name can save hours of puzzled incomprehension in the future.

questions.q: Which refactoring methods address the Mysterious Name smell?
o: Extract Function, Slide Statements and Pull Up Method
Encapsulate Variable and Combine Functions into Class
Change Function Declaration, Rename Variable and Rename Field
Replace Temp with Query and Introduce Parameter Object
questions.e: The refactoring methods for Mysterious Name are Change Function Declaration, used to rename a function, Rename Variable, and Rename Field.

questions.q: Why is duplicated code a problem for reading as well as for changing?
o: Duplicated code cannot be placed under version control
Every time you read the same code you must read it carefully to see whether there is any difference
Duplicated code prevents the use of inheritance
Duplicated code always compiles more slowly
questions.e: If you see the same code structure in more than one place, the program will be better if you find a way to unify them. Duplication means that every time you read the same code, you need to read it carefully to see if there's any difference; and if you need to change the duplicated code, you have to find and catch each duplication.

questions.q: The simplest duplicated code problem is when:
o: the same expression appears in two different programs
duplicate fragments appear in subclasses of a common base class
you have similar but not identical code in unrelated classes
you have the same expression in two methods of the same class
questions.e: The simplest duplicated code problem is when you have the same expression in two methods of the same class; the remedy is Extract Function.

questions.q: Which refactoring addresses the same expression appearing in two methods of the same class?
o: Extract Function
Pull Up Method
Slide Statements
Replace Temp with Query
questions.e: Same expression in two methods of the same class is addressed by Extract Function. Code that is similar but not quite identical is first arranged with Slide Statements so the similar items are together for easy extraction, and duplicate fragments in subclasses of a common base class are addressed by Pull Up Method.

questions.q: Which refactoring is used to arrange code so that similar items are all together for easy extraction?
o: Split Loop
Extract Function
Pull Up Method
Slide Statements
questions.e: If you have code that's similar but not quite identical, Slide Statements arranges the code so the similar items are all together for easy extraction.

questions.q: Which refactoring addresses duplicate fragments found in subclasses of a common base class?
o: Pull Up Method
Slide Statements
Extract Function
Decompose Conditional
questions.e: If the duplicate fragments are in subclasses of a common base class, Pull Up Method is used.

questions.q: Why did older languages discourage the use of small functions, and what has changed?
o: Older languages carried an overhead in subroutine calls, which modern languages have pretty much eliminated for in-process calls
Older languages required functions to be declared before use
Older compilers could not inline functions, and modern ones can inline everything
Older languages had no support for functions at all
questions.e: Older languages carried an overhead in subroutine calls, which deterred people from using small functions; modern languages have pretty much eliminated that overhead for in-process calls. The programs that live best and longest are those with short functions, which are easy to explain, share and choose.

questions.q: Programs that live best and longest are said to be those with:
o: short functions
the most comments
the deepest inheritance hierarchies
the fewest classes
questions.e: The programs that live best and longest are those with short functions; the advantage is that they are easy to explain, share and choose.

questions.q: For a long function with lots of parameters and temporary variables, which refactoring eliminates the temps?
o: Replace Temp with Query
Introduce Parameter Object
Preserve Whole Object
Replace Function with Command
questions.e: If you have a function with lots of parameters and temporary variables, Replace Temp with Query eliminates the temps; long lists of parameters can be slimmed down with Introduce Parameter Object and Preserve Whole Object.

questions.q: For a long function, which refactoring is described as the worst case scenario remedy?
o: Decompose Conditional
Replace Function with Command
Split Loop
Extract Function
questions.e: For a long function, the worst case scenario remedy is Replace Function with Command.

questions.q: Which refactoring deals with conditional expressions inside a long function?
o: Replace Conditional with Polymorphism
Decompose Conditional
Extract Variable
Split Loop
questions.e: Conditionals and loops also give signs for extractions; Decompose Conditional deals with conditional expressions. A big switch statement can be converted to a single function call with Extract Function, and if there is more than one switch statement switching on the same condition, Replace Conditional with Polymorphism applies.

questions.q: If there is more than one switch statement switching on the same condition, which refactoring applies?
o: Replace Conditional with Polymorphism
Consolidate Conditional Expression
Extract Function
Decompose Conditional
questions.e: If there's more than one switch statement switching on the same condition, Replace Conditional with Polymorphism applies; a single big switch statement can be converted to a single function call with Extract Function.

questions.q: If an extracted loop is hard to give a name to, what does that suggest and which refactoring follows?
o: It is too short, so it should be inlined again
It should be replaced with recursion
It may be doing two different things, so Split Loop breaks out the separate tasks
It needs more parameters, so Introduce Parameter Object applies
questions.e: With loops one extracts the loop and the code within it into its own method using Extract Function; if you find it hard to give an extracted loop a name, that may be because it's doing two different things, so Split Loop breaks out the separate tasks.

questions.q: For a long parameter list, if one parameter can be obtained by asking another parameter for it, which refactoring applies?
o: Remove Flag Argument
Replace Parameter with Query
Preserve Whole Object
Introduce Parameter Object
questions.e: If you can obtain one parameter by asking another parameter for it, Replace Parameter with Query removes the second parameter.

questions.q: Rather than pulling lots of data out of an existing data structure to pass as parameters, which refactoring applies?
o: Combine Functions into Class
Preserve Whole Object
Replace Parameter with Query
Remove Flag Argument
questions.e: Rather than pulling lots of data out of an existing data structure, Preserve Whole Object passes the original data structure instead.

questions.q: If several parameters always fit together, which refactoring applies?
o: Introduce Parameter Object
Remove Flag Argument
Replace Parameter with Query
Preserve Whole Object
questions.e: If several parameters always fit together, Introduce Parameter Object combines them.

questions.q: If a parameter is used as a flag to dispatch different behavior, which refactoring applies?
o: Introduce Parameter Object
Remove Flag Argument
Replace Parameter with Query
Preserve Whole Object
questions.e: If a parameter is used as a flag to dispatch different behavior, Remove Flag Argument is used.

questions.q: When multiple functions share several parameter values, which refactoring captures those common values as fields?
o: Encapsulate Variable
Introduce Parameter Object
Extract Function
Combine Functions into Class
questions.e: Classes are a great way to reduce parameter list sizes, particularly when multiple functions share several parameter values; Combine Functions into Class captures those common values as fields.

questions.q: Why is global data described as one of the most pungent odors likely to be encountered?
o: It cannot be placed under version control
It prevents the use of inheritance
It occupies the largest amount of memory
It can be modified from anywhere in the code base, leading to bugs, and tracing the source of a change is difficult and time consuming
questions.e: Global data can be modified from anywhere in the code base leading to bugs, and tracing the source of a change is difficult and time consuming. The issue is not restricted to global variables: class variables and singletons are also included.

questions.q: Besides global variables, which constructs are included in the global data smell?
o: Constants and enumerations
Class variables and singletons
Interfaces and abstract classes
Local variables and parameters
questions.e: The issue is not restricted to global variables; class variables and singletons are also included.

questions.q: What is the key defence against global data, and what follows it?
o: Extract Function, after which the data should be duplicated locally
Split Loop, after which the data should be made read-only
Rename Variable, after which the data should be documented
Encapsulate Variable, after which the scope should be limited as much as possible by moving the data within a class or module
questions.e: The key defence is Encapsulate Variable, always the first move when confronted with data open to contamination by any part of a program: wrapped by a function, you can start seeing where it is modified and control its access. Then it is good to limit its scope as much as possible by moving it within a class or module where only that module's code can see it.

questions.q: The Encapsulate Downcast refactoring applies when:
o: a method returns a value that is never used
a method returns an object that needs to be downcast by its callers, and the downcast is moved to within the method
a method takes a parameter that must be upcast by its callers
two subclasses have the same field
questions.e: Encapsulate Downcast applies when a method returns an object that needs to be downcasted by its callers; refactor by moving the downcast to within the method, so that for example 'Object lastReading() { return readings.lastElement(); }' becomes 'Reading lastReading() { return (Reading) readings.lastElement(); }'.

questions.q: The Consolidate Conditional Expression refactoring applies when:
o: the same fragment of code appears in all branches of a conditional
a conditional expression is hard to understand
you have a sequence of conditional tests with the same result, which are combined into a single conditional expression and extracted
there are several switch statements on the same condition
questions.e: Consolidate Conditional Expression applies when you have a sequence of conditional tests with the same result; refactor by combining them into a single conditional expression and extracting it, so three separate early returns of 0 become 'if (isNotEligibleForDisability()) return 0;'.

questions.q: The Consolidate Duplicate Conditional Fragments refactoring applies when:
o: two subclasses have the same field
a method's name does not reveal its purpose
a sequence of conditional tests all have the same result
the same fragment of code is in all branches of a conditional expression, and it is moved outside the expression
questions.e: Consolidate Duplicate Conditional Fragments applies when the same fragment of code is in all branches of a conditional expression; refactor by moving it outside the expression, so that a send() call appearing in both branches is moved after the if-else.

questions.q: Given 'if (isSpecialDeal()) { total = price * 0.95; send(); } else { total = price * 0.98; send(); }', what is the refactored form?
o: if (isSpecialDeal()) total = price * 0.95; else total = price * 0.98; send();
send(); if (isSpecialDeal()) total = price * 0.95; else total = price * 0.98;
if (isSpecialDeal()) { total = price * 0.95; } else { total = price * 0.98; send(); }
if (isSpecialDeal()) { send(); total = price * 0.95; } else total = price * 0.98;
questions.e: Because send() appears in both branches, it is moved outside the conditional expression and placed after the if-else; the assignments, which differ, remain in their branches.

questions.q: The Rename Method refactoring applies when:
o: two methods in different classes do the same thing
the name of a method does not reveal its purpose, so the name is changed
a method is too long to understand
a method has too many parameters
questions.e: Rename Method applies when the name of a method does not reveal its purpose; refactor by changing the name, so that 'int getInvCdtLmt()' becomes 'int getInvoiceableCreditLimit()'.

questions.q: The Pull Up Field refactoring applies when:
o: behavior on a superclass is relevant only for some of its subclasses
a class has too many fields of primitive type
two subclasses have the same field, which is moved to the superclass
two classes have fields with the same name but different types
questions.e: Pull Up Field applies when two subclasses have the same field; refactor by moving the field to the superclass.

questions.q: Which refactoring applies when behavior on a superclass is relevant only for some of its subclasses?
o: Pulling the behavior up to a higher superclass
Extracting the behavior into a new class
Moving that behavior down to those subclasses
Renaming the behavior to reflect its narrow use
questions.e: When behavior on a superclass is relevant only for some of its subclasses, it is refactored by moving it to those subclasses. This is the Push Down Method refactoring, the counterpart of Pull Up Method; note that it is sometimes mistakenly written 'Pull Down Method'.

questions.q: The Extract Method refactoring addresses which problem?
o: You place the result of an expression in a local variable for later use
Your methods contain a repeating group of parameters
You have a code fragment that can be grouped together, which is moved to a separate new method with a call left in its place
You have an expression that is hard to understand
questions.e: Extract Method addresses a code fragment that can be grouped together; the solution is to move this code to a separate new method or function and replace the old code with a call to the method.

questions.q: Which smells does Extract Method eliminate?
o: Comments only
Long Parameter List, Data Clumps and Primitive Obsession only
Long Method and Duplicate Code only
Duplicate Code, Long Method, Feature Envy, Switch Statements, Message Chains, Comments and Data Class
questions.e: Extract Method eliminates Duplicate Code, Long Method, Feature Envy, Switch Statements, Message Chains, Comments and Data Class.

questions.q: Refactoring 'void printOwing(){ printBanner(); // Print details. System.out.println("name: " + name); System.out.println("amount: " + getOutstanding()); }' by Extract Method produces:
o: printOwing with the two println calls replaced by a single combined println
printOwing unchanged, with a new method added that is never called
printOwing with printBanner inlined into it
printOwing calling printBanner() and printDetails(getOutstanding()), with printDetails taking the outstanding amount as a parameter
questions.e: The detail-printing fragment is moved into a new method printDetails(double outstanding), and printOwing then calls printBanner() followed by printDetails(getOutstanding()). The explanatory comment is replaced by the method's name.

questions.q: The Extract Variable refactoring addresses which problem, and which smell does it eliminate?
o: A long method with intertwined local variables; it eliminates Long Method
A repeating group of parameters; it eliminates Data Clumps
A code fragment that can be grouped together; it eliminates Duplicate Code
An expression that's hard to understand; it eliminates Comments
questions.e: Extract Variable addresses an expression that's hard to understand; the solution is to place the result of the expression, or its parts, in separate variables that are self-explanatory. It eliminates the Comments smell.

questions.q: A banner-rendering method tests 'platform.toUpperCase().indexOf("MAC") > -1 && browser.toUpperCase().indexOf("IE") > -1 && wasInitialized() && resize > 0'. How does Extract Variable improve it?
o: The condition is split into nested if statements
The condition is replaced by a lookup table
The whole condition is moved into a separate method with no variables
Each part is assigned to a self-explanatory variable such as isMacOS, isIE and wasResized, which are then used in the condition
questions.e: Extract Variable places the result of the expression or its parts in separate self-explanatory variables: final boolean isMacOS, final boolean isIE and final boolean wasResized, which are then combined in the if condition along with wasInitialized().

questions.q: The Replace Temp with Query refactoring addresses which problem?
o: Your methods contain a repeating group of parameters
You place the result of an expression in a local variable for later use in your code
You have an expression that's hard to understand
You get several values from an object and pass them as parameters
questions.e: Replace Temp with Query addresses placing the result of an expression in a local variable for later use; the solution is to move the entire expression to a separate method and return the result from it, then query the method instead of using a variable, incorporating the new method in other methods if necessary.

questions.q: Which smells does Replace Temp with Query eliminate?
o: Comments only
Long Parameter List and Data Clumps
Long Function or Method, and Duplicate Code
Primitive Obsession and Data Class
questions.e: Replace Temp with Query eliminates the Long Function or Method smell and Duplicate Code.

questions.q: Applying Replace Temp with Query to 'double calculateTotal() { double basePrice = quantity * itemPrice; if (basePrice > 1000) return basePrice * 0.95; else return basePrice * 0.98; }' gives:
o: calculateTotal taking basePrice as a parameter
a basePrice() method returning quantity * itemPrice, with calculateTotal calling basePrice() in place of the temporary variable
basePrice promoted to a field of the class
a single return statement using a ternary operator on the temporary variable
questions.e: The expression is moved into a separate method, 'double basePrice() { return quantity * itemPrice; }', and calculateTotal queries basePrice() instead of using the local variable.

questions.q: The Introduce Parameter Object refactoring addresses which problem?
o: An expression is hard to understand
Your methods contain a repeating group of parameters, which are replaced with an object
A long method has intertwined local variables
You get several values from an object and pass them as parameters to a method
questions.e: Introduce Parameter Object addresses methods containing a repeating group of parameters; the solution is to replace these parameters with an object. It eliminates Long Parameter List, Data Clumps, Primitive Obsession and Long Method.

questions.q: Which smells does Introduce Parameter Object eliminate?
o: Duplicate Code, Feature Envy and Switch Statements
Long Parameter List, Data Clumps, Primitive Obsession and Long Method
Long Method and Message Chains only
Comments and Data Class only
questions.e: Introduce Parameter Object eliminates Long Parameter List, Data Clumps, Primitive Obsession and Long Method.

questions.q: The Preserve Whole Object refactoring addresses which problem?
o: Your methods contain a repeating group of parameters that should become an object
A method returns an object that callers must downcast
A local variable holds the result of an expression for later use
You get several values from an object and then pass them as parameters to a method, so instead you pass the whole object
questions.e: Preserve Whole Object addresses getting several values from an object and then passing them as parameters to a method; instead, try passing the whole object. It eliminates Primitive Obsession, Long Parameter List, Long Method and Data Clumps.

questions.q: Refactoring 'int low = daysTempRange.getLow(); int high = daysTempRange.getHigh(); boolean withinPlan = plan.withinRange(low, high);' by Preserve Whole Object gives:
o: boolean withinPlan = plan.withinRange(new Range(low, high));
boolean withinPlan = plan.withinRange(daysTempRange);
boolean withinPlan = plan.withinRange(daysTempRange.getLow());
boolean withinPlan = daysTempRange.withinRange(plan);
