questions.e: Instead of extracting the low and high values and passing them separately, the whole object is passed: 'boolean withinPlan = plan.withinRange(daysTempRange);'.

questions.q: The Replace Method with Method Object refactoring addresses which problem?
o: A method whose name does not reveal its purpose
A repeating group of parameters across several methods
An object that must be downcast by its callers
A long method in which the local variables are so intertwined that Extract Method cannot be applied
questions.e: Replace Method with Method Object addresses a long method in which the local variables are so intertwined that you can't apply Extract Method; it eliminates the Long Method smell.

questions.q: How does Replace Method with Method Object work?
o: The method's local variables are promoted to parameters
The method is moved into the class whose data it uses most
The method is replaced by a sequence of smaller methods in the original class
The method is transformed into a separate class so that the local variables become fields of that class, after which the method can be split into several methods within the same class
questions.e: The solution is to transform the method into a separate class so that the local variables become fields of the class; then you can split the method into several methods within the same class.

questions.q: Applying Replace Method with Method Object to an Order class whose price() method declares primaryBasePrice, secondaryBasePrice and tertiaryBasePrice and performs a long computation gives:
o: a static utility method taking the three prices as parameters
an Order class with the three values promoted to fields and price() unchanged
three separate methods on Order, one per base price
a PriceCalculator class holding those three values as private fields, constructed from the Order and exposing a compute() method
questions.e: The method becomes a class: PriceCalculator holds primaryBasePrice, secondaryBasePrice and tertiaryBasePrice as private fields, takes an Order in its constructor to copy the relevant information, and performs the long computation in a compute() method.

questions.q: A Range class whose includes method reads 'return arg >= low && arg <= high;' is refactored to 'return arg >= getLow() && arg <= getHigh();' with accessors added. This illustrates:
o: replacing a temporary variable with a query
consolidating a conditional expression
self-encapsulating the fields so that access goes through accessor methods
extracting a new class for the range bounds
questions.e: The refactoring introduces getLow() and getHigh() accessors and has the class's own method use them in place of direct field access, so that access to the fields is routed through accessor methods.

questions.q: A Person class with a private name field plus getName and setName methods is contrasted with a Person class whose name field is simply public. Which smell does the second version exhibit?
o: A data class with public data members, which blurs the interface and violates encapsulation
A parallel inheritance hierarchy
A middleman that merely passes calls through
A long parameter list
questions.e: A class with all data and no behavior is the data class smell, and making the field public rather than hiding it behind accessors removes the encapsulation that the getter and setter version provides.

questions.q: Which tools are named for automating refactoring changes and testing them?
o: NetBeans refactoring and the CppUnit framework
Eclipse refactoring and the JUnit testing framework
IntelliJ refactoring and the NUnit testing framework
Visual Studio refactoring and the TestNG framework
questions.e: The guidance is to use refactoring tools to automate changes, naming Eclipse refactoring and the JUnit testing framework.

questions.q: Which reference work on refactoring is attributed to Fowler, Beck, Brant, Opdyke and Roberts?
o: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture
Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code
Software Architecture in Practice
Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software
questions.e: Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code, by Martin Fowler, Kent Beck, John Brant, William Opdyke and Don Roberts, Addison-Wesley Professional, 1999.
